#6599. Schmaltzy Chicken and Stuffing Skillet

While you might think of instant stuffing as a once-a-year darling that makes an annual appearance like Punxsutawney Phil, this recipe is a case study of why this product should be put to use throughout the year. (Boxes of the dried mix can be found near the breadcrumbs any month.) Here, it’s called into action to prop up skin-on, bone-in chicken thighs in a bed of savory stuffing that’s bolstered by aromatics and sweet-tart dried cranberries. Starting with a cold pan ensures even rendering of the chicken fat and crispy skin. The lot gets baked together, allowing the savory drippings from the chicken to soak into the stuffing. Serve with a side of cranberry sauce, a fresh salad, or all by itself for a one-pan dinner that recalls Thanksgiving any night of the week.

More delicious skillet dinners this way: Chicken Thighs With Spiced Couscous and Carrots; Ruffled Mushroom Pot Pie; and One-Skillet Chicken Pot Pie.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Season 2 lb. skin-on, bone-in chicken thighs (about 4 medium) on both sides with kosher salt and freshly ground pepper. Pour 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil into a cold large stainless-steel skillet and swirl to coat bottom of pan. Arrange chicken, skin side down, in pan and place over medium-high heat. Cook undisturbed, rotating pan around on burner often to promote even browning, until skin is browned and chicken releases easily from pan, 7–10 minutes. Transfer to a rimmed baking sheet or large plate and arrange skin side up.

Combine 1 large onion, finely chopped, 2 celery stalks, finely chopped, and 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter in same pan and cook over medium-high heat, stirring often, until onion is softened and just starting to turn golden, 8–12 minutes. Add one 6-oz. box instant stuffing mix, ½ cup unsweetened dried cranberries, and 1¼ cups water, then finely grate in zest from 1 lemon and set lemon aside. Mix until stuffing is hydrated. Remove pan from heat and push stuffing to sides to create wells for chicken to rest in. Nestle thighs, skin side up, into stuffing. Transfer pan to oven and bake until chicken is cooked through and top of stuffing is golden brown and crisp, 45–55 minutes.

Top chicken and stuffing with more dried cranberries and reserved celery leaves. Cut reserved lemon into wedges and serve alongside for squeezing over.

#6598. Japanese Sweet Potato Chaat

Every cuisine has a sauce that’s an absolute essential—a ride or die, if you will. For South Asian food, this is a cilantro mint green chutney. It brings a punchy, herb-packed burst of flavor that goes with pretty much everything. This recipe combines cilantro, mint, and just the right amount of heat from green chiles, creating a balance of spice and freshness. Lime juice adds brightness, while cumin, sugar, and chaat masala add complexity. Use this as a zesty topping for your favorite dish or as a base for pani puri water (just add 1½ cups [360 ml] of water and strain), or make it creamy with yogurt or sour cream to use for spreading and dipping.

Slow-roasting Japanese sweet potatoes flesh-side down releases their natural sugars, caramelizing and deepening their sweetness. The flesh becomes incredibly tender, almost custard-like in texture, while the skin turns a rich golden brown and becomes slightly crispy. So don’t bother peeling them! Top them with tamarind concentrate (I like Tamicon, Cock Brand, Pure Indian Foods, or Dragonfly—anything without citric acid), green chutney, fresh onions, tomatoes, and cilantro for a chaat-inspired appetizer.

To a blender or food processor, add 2 bunches cilantro (about 6 oz. [170 g]), leaves and stems, 1 bunch mint (about 2 oz. [55 g]), leaves and tender stems, 6 green Thai chiles or 2 serranos, stemmed (more if you want it spicier), ½ cup (120 ml) lime juice (from about 5 limes), 2 tsp. cumin seeds, 1½ tsp. fine sea salt, 1 tsp. sugar, and 1 tsp. chaat masala. Pulse for a few seconds in intervals until the ingredients are pulverized into a smooth paste. Transfer to an airtight container and store until ready to use, up to 1 week in the refrigerator or 1 month in the freezer.

Preheat the oven to 375°F (190°C) and line a baking sheet with parchment paper.

Drizzle the sheet with extra-virgin olive oil and place 1½ lb. (680 g) Japanese or Korean sweet potatoes, ends trimmed, halved lengthwise, cut-side down. Bake for 60 to 70 minutes, until golden and caramelized on the cut side and cooked through and tender; a knife inserted into the center of the potato should slide through easily. Let rest for 5 to 8 minutes. Once cool enough to handle, cut the sweet potatoes into 1" to 2" [2.5 to 5 cm] pieces.

To a small bowl, add ½ cup (120 g) plain whole-milk yogurt or sour cream and ½ tsp. fine sea salt and whisk to combine. If you’re using sour cream, thin it out with a little water.

Place the sweet potatoes on a serving platter and drizzle the yogurt, ½ cup Evergreen Chutney, 3 Tbsp. tamarind concentrate or paste, and 2 Tbsp. lime juice evenly all over. Sprinkle with 1 medium red tomato (5 oz. [140 g]), finely chopped, 1 small red onion (7 oz. [200 g]), finely chopped, 2 Tbsp. chopped cilantro leaves and tender stems, 1 tsp. chaat masala, 3 green Thai chiles or 1 serrano, stemmed, thinly sliced, and crispy sev and serve immediately.

Do Ahead: You can make the individual components a day ahead of time and store them in airtight containers in the refrigerator, then assemble to serve.

#6593. Failproof Homestyle Chicken Kari

This recipe is inspired by the garam masala my mother used to make back in India. Just a pinch adds incredible depth and flavor to both meat and vegetable dishes—it’s the secret ingredient that often leaves my guests wondering why my Indian food tastes so exceptional. And now you can use it too! This version perfectly balances the warming notes of cloves and nutmeg, and it’s the one I return to time and time again. If you prefer a sweeter blend, add more cinnamon and fennel seeds; if you want a spicier kick, increase the black pepper and cloves.

In a small bowl, toss 12 dried bay leaves, 12 whole cloves, 5 black cardamom pods, 4 whole star anise pods, three 3" (7.5-cm) cinnamon sticks, 1 whole nutmeg, 3 Tbsp. coriander seeds, 3 Tbsp. whole mace fronds, 2 Tbsp. cumin seeds, 1 Tbsp. black peppercorns, and 2 tsp. white poppy seeds to combine.

Heat a medium dry skillet over low heat until hot. Add the spice mixture and toast until slightly fragrant, about 45 seconds. Transfer back to the bowl and let cool.

Transfer the whole nutmeg to a mortar and break into smaller pieces with a pestle (this is just to make it easier to grind, so don’t worry about being too precise!). Repeat with the cinnamon. Tear the bay leaves into smaller pieces. Transfer all of the spices to a spice grinder and grind into a fine powder (it will be slightly warm when you remove the lid). Transfer to an airtight container (do not cover yet) and let cool completely. Then close the lid.

Do Ahead: Garam masala can be made 1 month ahead. Cover and store in a cool, dark place.

To a small heatproof bowl, add 1 medium yellow onion (9 oz. [255 g]), halved, thinly sliced into half-moons, 2 Tbsp. lime juice, 2 Tbsp. Kashmiri red chili powder, 2 tsp. chaat masala, ½ tsp. cayenne powder, and ½ tsp. fine sea salt.

In a small pan over medium-high heat, warm 2 Tbsp. peanut oil or any vegetable oil or avocado oil until it shimmers. Add 1 tsp. cumin seeds and cook until fragrant and they start to turn brown, about 1 minute. Be careful not to let the seeds burn or they will taste bitter. Remove from the heat and pour the hot oil over the onions. Toss to coat the onions in the spice mixture.

Serve immediately or let cool and store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 1 week.

To a mortar and pestle or food processor, add one 2" (5-cm) piece fresh ginger, chopped, 4 garlic cloves, peeled, and 3 green Thai chiles or 1 serrano, stemmed, chopped, and pound or pulse into a chunky paste. To a medium bowl, add 2 lb. (910 g) boneless, skinless chicken thighs, excess fat trimmed, cut into 2" [5-cm] pieces, along with the ginger-garlic paste and 1 tsp. fine sea salt and toss to combine. Cover and place in the refrigerator to marinate for a minimum of 1 hour or overnight.

In a medium heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven over medium-low heat, warm ⅓ cup (80 ml) vegetable oil or avocado oil, then add 1 tsp. cumin seeds, ½ tsp. black mustard seeds, ½ tsp. black peppercorns, 5 whole cloves, 1 fresh or dried bay leaf, 1 star anise, and one 3" [7.5-cm] cinnamon stick, broken into small pieces, and lightly toast and until fragrant, about 1 minute. Increase the heat to medium, add 1 medium red or yellow onion (9 oz. [255 g]), finely chopped, cover, and cook until the onion is translucent and beginning to turn brown around the edges, stirring halfway through, about 10 minutes.

Add 1 Tbsp. ground coriander, 1 Tbsp. Kashmiri red chili powder, 1 Tbsp. Garam Masala, 2 tsp. cayenne powder, and 1 tsp. powdered turmeric. Stir to combine and cook until fragrant, about 1 minute. Drain off the excess marinade from the chicken, then add it to the pot along with 3 Tbsp. tomato paste, 1 Tbsp. packed fresh fenugreek leaves, and remaining 1½ tsp. fine sea salt and stir until everything is mixed thoroughly and the chicken is covered with the spices and tomato paste. Add ½ cup (120 ml) water and mix again. Cover and cook until the chicken is cooked through and tender, 30 minutes, stirring halfway through.

Remove from the heat and sprinkle with the remaining 1 tsp. Garam Masala, remaining 1 tsp. fresh fenugreek leaves, and cilantro leaves. Serve immediately with lime wedges, Insanely Addictive Pickled Onions, and steamed rice or Indian flatbread.

Do Ahead: Store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days or in the freezer for up to 1 month.

#6592. One More Bite

Here at Taste of Home, there's nothing we love more than trying a new recipe. But sometimes that means buying an ingredient or two that isn't part of our regular dinner rotation—which can mean leftover condiments, sauces or spices we don't know what to do with. The question is: What's the next bite?

That's where One More Bite comes in. We're exploring how to use one ingredient in multiple ways, so nothing goes to waste. A single new ingredient can transform weeknight meals, weekend favorites and simple snacks, and might just find a permanent spot on our grocery list.

We often see chili crisp spooned over dumplings, soups and rice bowls, but there are so many uses for this crunchy, fiery oil-based sauce. We love mixing chili crisp into biscuit batter, layering it on grilled cheese sandwiches and cooking it with eggs.

Many people buy tahini for dips like hummus or baba ghanoush, then wonder what to do with the rest of the jar. Not us. The creamy sesame paste never lasts long in our kitchen—it blends beautifully into sweet and savory recipes.

Hot honey didn't exactly invent sweet heat—but it sure did make it easy to drizzle on everything. This swicy condiment is sweet enough to hook you and spicy enough to keep you coming back.

Pistachio cream is like a green version of Nutella, but sweeter, more spreadable and decidedly more decadent. When pistachio cream went viral alongside Dubai chocolate, it sparked a wave of creative recipes that lean into its rich, nutty flavor.

Served raw, the punchy flavor of kimchi cuts through rich foods, lightening up dishes like mac and cheese or burgers. Cooked, its acidity mellows and the umami notes deepen, turning a last-minute stir-fry or grain bowl into a dish that tastes layered and intentional.

When we think of pesto as a garlicky herb sauce, the ways to use it become endless. We've spooned it over garlic bread, tucked it into a stuffed chicken breast and whisked it into mayo for a quick sandwich spread.

Brittle sheets of rice paper become bendable and stretchy when dipped in water, allowing them to be wrapped around all kinds of fillings. They have a chewy finish when served fresh, a crunchy texture when fried, and a wafer-like bite when dipped in egg and stacked.

Nothing swirls, spreads or steals the spotlight quite like our favorite retro ingredient: marshmallow creme. No matter the recipe, marshmallow creme brings its signature lightness and gooey pull, adding a soft finish that never goes out of style.

Za'atar, a Middle Eastern spice blend, tastes woodsy, tart, bright and crunchy all at once. There are plenty of traditional recipes that call for za'atar, some as simple as mixing it with oil to make a dip. But it can also be used more broadly, in place of a single dried herb.

When a stew we had been simmering for hours tasted flat, we added a spoonful of miso and the broth took on a richness it had previously lacked. Once we started using it more, we realized that it belongs in sweet and salty desserts, easy sides and main dishes that need a little oomph.

Because it needs to be harvested by hand and yields only a tiny amount, saffron is one of the most expensive ingredients you can buy—so the last thing you want to do is let it sit in your pantry and collect dust.

You don't need to save fish sauce for your favorite Thai recipes or other Southeast Asian dishes. We sprinkle it into marinara sauce and Caesar dressing, when more salt would just make it salty instead of adding depth.

Reducing balsamic vinegar concentrates the sugars, creating a sweet, tangy reduction. Balsamic glaze brightens up watermelon salads, adds nuance to grilled cheese and creates a dazzling finish for baked chicken.

#6588. Maple Bourbon Chicken With Brussels Sprouts

If you, like most people, hear the term “bourbon chicken” and have no idea what it is, let me call it by its more common name: toothpick chicken. Yes, the suspiciously delicious chicken shelled out at mall food courts on toothpicks is most likely bourbon chicken. Popular at American Chinese or Cajun-style Chinese restaurants, the sticky-sweet chicken is the utter definition of delicious, luring weary shoppers into food courts to find refuge from the bubblegum pink sweatpants and ripped denim. This version takes cues from the classic but swaps in some autumnal ingredients to make it fit for the season. Charred brussels sprouts leaves and pecans add bulk, while maple syrup and apple cider vinegar give it that delightful tart-sweet flavor we know and love. Serve it over rice or noodles or all by its lonesome for a hearty dinner that will take you back to the '90s.

More chicken dinner winners here: Sheet-Pan Hot Honey Chicken and Peaches; Basil Chicken Stir-Fry; and Ginger-Garlic Chicken and Vegetable Stir-Fry.

Whisk one 1½" piece ginger, peeled, finely grated, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, ⅓ cup bourbon, ⅓ cup pure maple syrup, ¼ cup apple cider vinegar, ¼ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes, 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, ¼ cup low-sodium soy sauce, and ½ cup water in a small bowl to combine. Set sauce aside.

Toss 1½ lb. skinless, boneless chicken breasts, halved crosswise, thinly sliced against the grain, remaining 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, and remaining 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce in a medium bowl until chicken is coated; set aside.

Heat 2 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large skillet over medium-high. Add 1 lb. brussels sprouts, halved through stems, leaves separated, and cook, stirring very occasionally, until just tender and blackened in spots, about 5 minutes. Transfer to another medium bowl.

Add more oil if pan looks dry and, working in batches if needed, arrange reserved chicken in a single layer and cook, turning occasionally, until golden brown and cooked through, about 5 minutes. Transfer to bowl with brussels sprouts.

Add reserved sauce to same pan and bring to a simmer. Cook, stirring constantly, until thickened, about 1 minute. Remove pan from heat and return brussels sprouts and chicken to pan; top with 1 cup salted roasted pecans, coarsely chopped. Toss to coat in sauce. Serve chicken and brussels sprouts with steamed white rice if desired.

#6586. Chicken Pozole Verde

This chicken pozole verde recipe puts a whole bird to work, making a fragrant broth and plenty of tender shredded meat in one go. Roasted tomatillos and a mix of green chiles give the Mexican stew its tang and heat; a final swirl of cilantro purée adds fresh flavor and turns the whole pot brilliantly green.

The tomatillos and peppers roast while the chicken simmers. Toasting the canned hominy—a tip from Test Kitchen alum Rick Martinez—gives it a flavor “almost like a corn nut.” But if that’s one step too many, skip it—the stew will still be awesome.

Set out red onion, cilantro, dried oregano, and lime wedges, and let everyone load up their own bowl. Add avocado for creaminess, or shredded cabbage, sliced radishes, and crushed tortilla chips for crunch.

Canned white or golden hominy works here. These plump, chewy corn kernels give the stew its hearty texture. Dried hominy needs to be cooked separately before adding it to the pot.

Mexican oregano is a different herb from Mediterranean oregano, with floral, citrusy notes and a hint of anise. We prefer it in this pozole, but regular dried oregano works too.

No. The whole chicken simmers in water with onion, garlic, and spices to make the broth. Before adding the shredded chicken and cilantro purée, taste the broth and season with salt and pepper.

Can I make pozole verde ahead or freeze it?

Yes. Cook the chicken up to 3 days ahead and refrigerate it in its broth, then finish the recipe when you’re ready to serve. You can also freeze the finished pozole. Take Rick’s advice and stash a quart for your next weeknight dinner emergency.

Heat ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil in a large Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium. Cook 1 large yellow onion, finely chopped, and 6 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, seasoning with kosher salt and stirring occasionally, until very tender, 12–15 minutes. Add 2 tsp. ground coriander, 1 tsp. ground cumin, and ½ tsp. dried oregano, preferably Mexican, and cook, stirring constantly, until very fragrant, about 1 minute.

Place one 3½–4-lb. whole chicken in pot and pour in 12 cups water. Bring to a simmer and cook chicken, uncovered and reducing heat as needed to maintain a very gentle simmer (and turning once or twice if it isn’t completely submerged), until cooked through and legs wiggle easily in their joints, 40–50 minutes.

Meanwhile, preheat oven to 425°. Spread out 4 poblano chiles, 2 Cubanelle peppers or 2 more poblano chiles, 3 serrano chiles, and 1½ lb. tomatillos, husks removed, rinsed, on a large rimmed baking sheet. Roast, tossing once or twice, until chiles and peppers are browned and collapsing and tomatillos are tender, 30–40 minutes. Let cool.

Transfer chicken to a cutting board; set broth in pot aside. Let chicken sit until cool enough to handle. Pull meat from bones and shred into bite-size pieces; discard chicken skin and bones.

Split open chiles and peppers; remove stems and seeds and discard. Remove any skin that can be easily peeled off and discard. Transfer chiles and peppers to a blender and add tomatillos; reserve baking sheet. Blend until smooth. Stir chile purée into reserved broth and bring to a simmer. Reserve blender.

Spread out two 15-oz. cans golden or white hominy, rinsed, in an even layer on reserved baking sheet and roast, tossing halfway through, until very fragrant and hominy around edges of baking sheet are just beginning to brown, 12–18 minutes. Scrape into pot with broth.

Season broth with salt and freshly ground black pepper and simmer, uncovered, until flavors come together and broth is rich tasting, about 20 minutes. Ladle ½ cup broth into reserved blender. Add 2 cups cilantro leaves with tender stems and purée until smooth and very bright green, at least 1 minute. Add chicken to broth and cook until heated through, then stir in cilantro purée. Taste posole and season with more salt if needed.

Divide posole among bowls. Top with ½ small red onion, thinly sliced, and more cilantro leaves and dried oregano. Serve with lime wedges for squeezing over.

Do Ahead: Chicken can be cooked 3 days ahead. Let cool in broth; cover and chill.

#6585. Roxie Nafousi’s 5 Biggest Business Lessons From Closing Her Fragrance Brand

Roxie Nafousi knows a thing or two about turning an audience into a business. The self-development coach and manifestation author has sold two million books since 2022, all the while building a lucrative ecosystem spanning an app, workshops and other products like journals and affirmation cards all centered on personal development. Translating that community into a successful consumer brand, however, proved a different challenge.

With Alia, her fragrance line, Nafousi set out to create something that could extend beyond her own personal brand. “I genuinely believed that we could create a major international fragrance brand,” she says over Zoom. “I hoped it would expand beyond fragrance into candles and incense. I thought the sky was the limit, and I felt so full of hope and excitement.”

The reality was a little more complicated: production delays, disagreements with a business partner and a resulting larger-than-expected financial commitment (£300,000 in total, against an originally expected £50,000 investment) all put pressure on the business. And while a high-profile launch that included celebrity events and retail placements seemed promising, delayed inventory and lackluster sales compounded the challenges. A cease-and-desist letter from a global brand ultimately brought the venture to a close, which Nafousi announced earlier this week on her personal Instagram.

Speaking to Vogue Business exclusively in the days after, Nafousi says a big part of the struggle was comparing online narratives of success with her own journey. “Social media is full of stories about people who create a brand and sell out overnight. There’s so much of that, and not nearly enough of the reality that it’s really hard and sometimes things don’t work out,” she says. “I really want people to make sure they understand what they’re getting into.”

“During the first few months [of launching Alia], when sales were trickling in and things weren’t really happening, I felt ashamed,” Nafousi adds. “I thought, ‘Oh my God, I’m irrelevant. I was so stupid to think I could make this work.’ I was comparing myself with these amazing brands, so it took me time to realize that not succeeding in my fragrance business wasn’t a failure. It was an amazing lesson.”

Here, Nafousi reveals her five biggest business lessons off the back of the brand.

The rise of the creator-founder has fueled a popular narrative whereby building a social media following is a natural precursor to building a consumer business. Big online followings can theoretically bypass some of the traditional barriers to launching a brand, from customer acquisition to building trust, but appetite for someone’s content or recommendations does not necessarily translate into demand for an entirely different category.

“It’s absolutely not a given that you can have an audience for one thing and expect them to transfer easily over to another,” Nafousi says. “Attention is not the same as demand. So many people confuse the number of followers they have with the number of people who actually want to spend their own money on something they create.”

In Alia’s case, Nafousi believed there was a natural connection between the fragrance brand and the world she built around self-development and empowerment, with scent offering another way for women to embody different parts of themselves. Its debut Alter Ego collection featured fragrances named Main Character, Power House and Scene Stealer, reflecting the themes that had become central to Nafousi’s personal brand across her Manifest and Confidence books.

“I did think that, because the messages were aligned, it would make sense,” she says. “I talk about empowerment and becoming the best version of yourself, and to me, Alia was just an extension of that. I definitely thought my audience would understand it.”

In hindsight, Nafousi believes more market and consumer research could have established whether fragrance was the right category in the first place. “People’s money is precious, and the way they spend it is changing. You need to do the research into what they actually want from you. What’s missing from their lives? What do they need? And just because you love something doesn’t mean someone else will,” she says. “I’d probably challenge myself more.”

Initially expected to invest £50,000 in Alia through a 50-50 partnership, Nafousi unfortunately found herself having to buy out her business partner when the relationship became strained. Her initial investment effectively doubled, while costs continued to mount as she took on additional responsibilities within the business. Nafousi found herself having to recruit additional support, bringing unexpected recruitment fees and a new salary into the equation alongside lawyers and accountants.

“The money and investment required were far greater than I’d imagined. There just seemed to be bills coming out of nowhere. I remember getting a bill for £70,000 in January this year, and I couldn’t understand where it had come from. It was production costs,” she says. The financial pressure then extended to decisions around how much inventory to commit to. For Nafousi, having sold two million copies of her book, 12,000 starting units felt relatively modest by comparison, but surplus stock and resulting production delays quickly became an issue.

“That was a big mistake, ordering far too much stock at the beginning,” she says. There were also problems with the timing of production: the perfumes arrived late, missing the initial momentum. “I really wouldn’t do it alone. I’d find the right partner, someone I’d gone through some shit with first. I’d really ask them how they deal with conflict and get to know their communication style, to make sure we could handle things together as a team.”

“For me, the most interesting thing was that we had all the ingredients you’d expect to work,” Nafousi says. “We had incredible press and huge events attended by so many wonderful celebrities, influencers and other people. All the ingredients were there for a great launch that should have translated into sales.”

Yet generating attention is only part of the challenge. With consumers becoming more selective about their spending and competition for visibility intensifying, brands face growing costs to acquire customers. “In general, we’re seeing that consumers are much more mindful of their spending,” Nafousi says. “It takes a lot more to acquire a customer than it used to. There’s so much competition, and consumers are bombarded with things. You can’t simply post something on your Stories or your feed and say, ‘Guys, I’ve got this thing,’ and expect that to be enough anymore.”

The unpredictability of organic reach can also lead to brands spending heavily on content and imagery without necessarily engaging a meaningful audience. For founders, this makes it important to diversify their marketing efforts rather than relying on social media alone, testing different ways to reach and engage potential customers. “The algorithm fucks us all, really. I might have spent so much money on social media and having someone create beautiful imagery for Alia, but nobody’s seeing it. Maybe 100 people are seeing it.”

Nafousi also found that some of the launch strategies commonly used by similar brands — such as gifting products to influencers — generated visibility without necessarily prompting purchases. What proved more effective was a direct appeal to her own community. Nafousi invited followers who genuinely wanted to try Alia to receive the product in exchange for sharing their thoughts. The resulting user-generated content, often from those with relatively small audiences, performed better than traditional gifting.

In-person activations also helped bridge the gap between awareness and purchase. At her Manifest Live show, a pop-up store allowed attendees to smell the fragrance and interact with the product, an experience she says performed particularly well.

For many emerging brands, securing a retail partnership can feel like a major milestone. “Having spoken to a lot of other founders, I’ve heard the same thing repeatedly. They get so excited about getting into retail that they don’t realize how much money they then have to spend to maintain their position and earn their place on the shelves,” she says. Retailers want to see that brands are generating sales, Nafousi explains, yet driving those conversions can require more spending on marketing and in-store visibility.

Early on, Alia supplied Lookfantastic with around 3,000 specially made 10ml fragrances for its advent calendar — assuming it would influence the decisions of further retailers and consumers to buy into the brand. While the initiative put the product into thousands of consumers’ hands, it didn’t directly drive sales. “I was so excited, because it was right at the beginning of the journey. We were getting the product into the hands of around 3,000 people, which was really fun,” Nafousi says. “But it was also quite a big expense.”

There were exceptions. Violet Grey, the US beauty retailer known for its tightly curated selection, performed particularly well for Alia. Nafousi believes the retailer’s niche positioning and trusted relationship with its customers helped the brand connect with the right audience. The value of a retail partnership, therefore, depends not simply on the number of doors a brand enters, but on whether the retailer’s customer base and positioning align with the product.

For founders, persistence is often celebrated, but knowing when to stop investing in a business can be just as important as having the conviction to start one.

Although production delays and packaging issues created friction in the early stages, Nafousi saw them as common setbacks. “At that point, I thought, ‘You know what? Every founder has these issues,’ so I wasn’t particularly worried about it,” she says. The bigger concern came when sales failed to gain traction. “I wanted to close it down when we launched. I think we made about two sales in the first week. The following week, there were no sales. Then, there was one sale. It was so deflating.”

Still, discovery sets were yet to launch and a forthcoming Space NK listing offered another opportunity to build momentum. Nafousi continued experimenting with sampling and brand activations, but soon realized that greater investment in advertising and awareness was needed. “I just thought, ‘God, I don’t know if I’m ready to invest even more money when I don’t know whether it’s going to work,’” she explains.

Nafousi was also approached by potential investors midway through the journey, but turned them down to keep her autonomy. “If I wanted to say, ‘You know what? I’m going to close this down,’ I didn’t want to lose that freedom,” she says. Ultimately, the decision to close Alia was made for her when she received a cease-and-desist letter from another brand operating under a similar name, giving her until December 31 to sell all remaining stock. Although she could have rebranded to continue trading, Nafousi saw it as a sign that it was time to move on. “I genuinely believe I manifested it in some way. I think it was a gift from the universe.”

Now, she is viewing the experience as one of growth. “The way I see it is that every entrepreneur will have something along their journey that doesn’t work out the way they hoped,” she says.

In her confidence book, one of the central tenets is learning to do hard things. “It’s not about feeling like you’re able to do everything or that you’re amazing at everything. A big part of confidence is knowing that even when things go wrong, you can handle it. That’s the resilience part. It’s knowing that I’m going to be able to cope with whatever comes my way, and I feel that now more than ever.”

#6583. Vietnamese Coffee Martini

You get dessert and a cocktail all in one with this Vietnamese coffee martini, which adds sweetened condensed milk to the classic espresso martini for a rich, frothy sip.

Whipping up a Vietnamese coffee martini after dinner means two things: You don’t have to make dessert, and you aren’t going to sleep anytime soon. This cocktail is next-level sweet and caffeinated, and it makes your regular espresso martini look like child’s play. Sure, this cocktail shares some of the same elements (vodka, coffee liqueur and espresso), but it includes sweetened condensed milk for a rich, luxurious texture, signature caramel sweetness and super-frothy finish.

Vietnamese coffee is typically made with dark-roasted robusta beans, which taste bolder and more chocolatey than the arabica beans in most coffee blends. In traditional preparations, the grounds drip slowly through a small metal filter called a phin, straight into a glass with a layer of sweetened condensed milk waiting at the bottom. Fresh milk was hard to come by and didn’t keep well in Vietnam’s heat, so canned milk became the go-to. It’s almost as thick as syrup and tastes a little like melted caramel. Shaken into a cocktail, it lands somewhere closer to a creamy Baileys espresso martini than a classic one, only richer.

Fill a cocktail shaker three-fourths full with ice. Add the vodka, espresso, sweetened condensed milk and Kahlua. Cover the shaker and shake hard until condensation forms on the outside, 10 to 15 seconds.

Strain the cocktail into a glass and top with the coffee beans. Serve immediately, while the foam is at its fluffiest.

Editor’s Tip: Chill your martini glass or coupe for 10 to 15 minutes before you start mixing. A frosty glass keeps the cocktail colder longer and helps the foam hold its shape.

Enjoy a Vietnamese coffee espresso martini right after you shake it, since the foam starts to deflate as it sits. If you’ve mixed up a little extra, store the unshaken mixture of vodka, coffee, condensed milk and Kahlua in a sealed jar in the refrigerator for up to two days. Give it a good stir, then shake it over fresh ice right before serving to revive the froth.

Making Vietnamese coffee martinis ahead of time is a smart move for hosting. Brew and chill the espresso or cold brew up to a day ahead, then mix the cocktail without ice. Refrigerate the batched cocktail until guests arrive. When it’s go time, shake each drink to order with fresh ice so every glass gets that signature foamy top.

For a dairy-free Vietnamese coffee martini, swap the regular sweetened condensed milk for sweetened condensed coconut milk. You should be able to find it in most grocery stores near the baking aisle. It shakes up just as creamy and sweet, with a subtle toasted coconut flavor that plays beautifully with the coffee. Kahlua is dairy-free, so the rest of the recipe stays the same.

Vietnamese coffee is usually made with robusta beans, which have nearly twice the caffeine of the arabica beans used in most espresso blends. Ounce for ounce, phin-brewed Vietnamese coffee can rival a shot of espresso, which is why it stands up so well to sweet condensed milk.

The foam comes from the oils in freshly brewed coffee, so espresso gives you the most dramatic froth, while cold brew and instant coffee create a slightly thinner layer. The condensed milk helps, too, adding body that traps air bubbles as you shake. Use plenty of ice, shake like you mean it and strain right away into a chilled glass so the foam settles on top in a smooth, creamy cap.

#6582. Hugo Boss Sales Drop 5% Amid Frasers Takeover

Hugo Boss attributed the 5% sales decline to its ongoing Claim 5 Touchdown turnaround plan. The strategy was implemented in December 2025 by group CEO Daniel Grieder, focusing on brand positioning, targeted distribution and enhanced operations, but is proving a drag on current growth.

The results follow Frasers Group’s takeover of Hugo Boss and its two sub-brands — Boss, which is marketed at millennials, and Gen Z-focused Hugo — on October 23. The acquisition followed a rejected takeover bid in the summer, though the British retail conglomerate continued its efforts, gradually raising its holding and eventually securing majority ownership of the German company.

During Tuesday’s earnings call, Grieder addressed the working relationship with Frasers. “We have regular and constructive dialog with Frasers Group, and we really value them as a significant long-term shareholder,” he told analysts and investors. “As with all shareholders, our engagement is guided by the objective of supporting the long-term success of Hugo Boss, and that is their intention also. So it’s not a short-term investment for them.” Frasers Group CEO Michael Murray assumed the Hugo Boss chair position in September, after Stephan Sturm stepped down.

On the struggles to reach long-term success, Grieder acknowledged a difficult macroeconomic and geopolitical environment, as well as weak consumer demand. While he remained positive about the future of Hugo Boss in its “new constellation” — it will become a subsidiary of Frasers Group — he emphasized the importance of honed distribution, profitability, and cost discipline.

“Our strategic direction on the Claim 5 touchdown [strategy] remains unchanged, and I firmly believe that we are doing the right things. Nevertheless, there is still work ahead of us, and benefits of the related initiatives will take time to materialize,” said Grieder. “But let me stress that we are convinced they will strengthen our business in the long term.”

Hugo Boss’s division into its two sub-labels was formally introduced in early 2022 as part of a seismic rebrand and marketing overhaul. For this quarter, Boss sales fell 3% to €813 million, while Hugo sales fell 17% to €133 million. The company continues to invest in marketing to build brand equity across both businesses, noting the new Boss by Beckham capsule, which provided an uptick in consumer engagement.

Sales across the company’s retail segments — comprising bricks-and-mortar, the brand website, and online concessions — were down 8% to €516 million, while wholesale and licenses both fell 2% to €406 million and €24 million, respectively.

Across regions, numbers were down. Europe, Middle East, and Africa (EMEA) declined the most, down 7%, a tumble symptomatic of soft demand in the UK and France, despite some resilience in Germany. The conflict in the Middle East also dragged on store traffic, eating into sales performance. The Americas fell 3%, with strongest performance in the US, offset by light decline in Latin America. Grieder explained that the US, nonetheless, had “very good results” for both brands, especially in department stores. The Asia-Pacific region was down 2%, impacted by sales slowdown in China, Southeast Asia and the Pacific cluster.

The new guidance for 2026 forecasted a high-single-digit decline, attributed to weakened demand and ongoing uncertainty. As such, Hugo Boss’s predicted EBIT now sits between €250-300 million for the full year, down from the initial estimate of €300-350 million.

“My focus is on the long term rather than the next quarter, and I see my role as setting the right financial and operational course for Hugo Boss,” said CFO and COO Ivica Maric, who is newly appointed but has been with the company since 2005. “I will use the coming period to review our strategic KPIs as well as the way we manage our balance sheet and cash flows. This is a continuous process aimed at keeping our financial framework aligned with the current market environment and our strategic priorities under Claim 5 Touchdown.”

#6579. 23 Thanksgiving Bread Recipes: Rolls, Biscuits, and More

Pies get most of the Thanksgiving baking glory. But these Thanksgiving bread recipes make a strong case for saving some oven space for buttery dinner rolls, flaky biscuits, and midnight-sandwich-ready loaves. Think golden sweet potato buns soft enough to nap on, buttermilk cornbread to eat with butter or bake into dressing, and tender sweet loaves to nibble on Thanksgiving morning. Several recipes have make-ahead options too.

There’s no need to overhaul a classic. Adapted from The Fannie Farmer Baking Book, these Parker House rolls have buttery folds, golden tops, and a finish of flaky salt. Bake enough for seconds.

These pillowy rolls get their warm color and gentle sweetness from mashed sweet potato. Bake and freeze them up to a month ahead, then reheat and brush with melted butter before serving.

Butter tucked inside each roll melts as it bakes, crisping the bottom. “If you can imagine a warm dinner roll meeting a flaky croissant, you’re getting closer,” says Hana Asbrink.

Pillowy rolls swirled with sweet-salty pork floss, mayo, scallions, and furikake. Bake and freeze them up to three months ahead, then warm them through while everyone finds a seat.

A tangzhong—a cooked flour-and-milk paste—helps these sour cream and chive rolls stay exceptionally soft. Tear one off to mop up gravy, then save a few for tomorrow’s turkey sandwiches.

Garlic bread, meet buttery dinner roll. Fresh and dried dill work their way into these pillowy buns, which get a generous brushing of garlic butter after baking. Save one for a gravy swipe.

So many layers, you’ll feel like a geologist unearthing them. Claire Saffitz’s biscuits get their height from a cut-and-stack technique. Another reason to love them: You can freeze the unbaked biscuits up to a month ahead.

All the herby goodness of Thanksgiving stuffing, packed into a biscuit: sage, rosemary, fennel seed, and scallions. Save a few for breakfast the next morning, preferably under a generous ladle of leftover gravy.

No rolling pin, no biscuit cutter, no problem. Canned creamed corn keeps these drop biscuits tender, while Calabrian chile honey butter brings a little heat.

For the guest who always takes the biggest piece of garlic bread: flaky buttermilk biscuits loaded with Parmesan and parsley. Freeze them unbaked, then bake straight from frozen when the oven frees up.

Biscuits or cornbread? This cheesy mash-up means you don’t have to choose. Sharp cheddar and fresh sage work their way into flaky, buttery layers that feel right at home on the Thanksgiving table.

Looking to start a fight? Declare a cornbread recipe “best.” This version strikes a balance: a tender crumb, buttermilk tang, and a touch of sweetness. Eat it with butter—or turn it into cornbread dressing.

Cheddar, caramelized corn, and hot honey butter take this cornbread well beyond the usual. Nervous about the flip? “Don’t be afraid of flipping the bread—I promise you can do it,” says former BA food editor Rachel Gurjar.

Pumpkin purée gives this fall-ish rendition of our no-knead focaccia recipe its golden color and gentle sweetness. Finish with rosemary and flaky salt, then tear off a piece for dipping in olive oil. You can bake it a day ahead.

Leave the oven to the turkey. These flaky, skillet-cooked parathas have brown butter and sage tucked between their layers. Parcook them a day ahead, then fry until golden just before dinner.

A garlic knot with centerpiece ambitions. This braided loaf wraps buttery dough around garlic, Parmesan, and parsley, then gets another garlicky brush after baking. Start the dough a day ahead.

Leave the stand mixer where it is. This focaccia asks for a little patience, not much elbow grease, to produce its airy crumb and golden crust. An overnight rise gets you started; garlic butter finishes the job.

Focaccia’s leaf-shaped French cousin deserves a turn in the Thanksgiving bread basket. Green olives, rosemary, and lemon zest bring plenty of flavor. And yes, the dough comes together in one bowl.

In this crusty yeast bread recipe, apple juice replaces water. The apple flavor is subtle, but the appeal of a warm slice with butter is not.

Oats and chia seeds give this gluten-free loaf a dense, chewy crumb. No kneading, shaping, or scoring; just be sure to use the gluten-free oats and oat flour specified in the recipe.

Give Thanksgiving morning the sticky-bun treatment. This pull-apart bread packs tender apples between cinnamon-sugar-coated bites, with tangy cider caramel coating the whole thing. Put on a pot of coffee and let everyone help themselves.

Chocolate or vanilla? Rick Martinez’s conchas give you both, with a two-tone sugar topping over buttery Mexican sweet buns. Another reason to love them: You can bake them up to three days ahead.

Start the holiday with a thick slice of ginger-spiked pumpkin bread and a generous schmear of salted maple butter. You can bake the loaf up to four days ahead, leaving Thanksgiving morning for coffee and slicing—and, uh, all that other prep.

Maple-glazed turkey, garlicky mashed potatoes, pumpkin chiffon pie, and more recipes worthy of your Thanksgiving table.

Like brown-butter brussels sprouts with gochujang, green bean salad with Parmesan dressing, our best-ever mashed potatoes, and more reasons to rebrand the holiday “Sidesgiving.”

From hot toddies to big-batch punch, these festive drinks will get you in the holiday spirit.

Like pumpkin flan de queso, rosemary-pear snacking cake, Amish pecan cream pie, and more.

#6578. Can Money Buy You A Better Brain?

We’ve spent years optimizing everything from our glucose levels and gut microbiomes to our sleep scores and biological ages. Full-body MRIs, smart rings and an arsenal of light therapies have turned our bodies into wired-up machines for monitoring, measuring and fine-tuning. But what about the organ responsible for making sense of it all? As anxieties mount over how a life spent online — and increasingly outsourced to AI — is eroding our ability to think, wellness has a new obsession: the brain.

As with so many wellness tech trends, the Kardashians were ahead of the curve. In a 2022 episode of The Kardashians, Kendall Jenner took Khloé to Amen Clinics for a SPECT scan, a type of imaging that measures blood flow in the brain. Her results were interpreted as revealing anxiety and the effects of past emotional trauma. At the time, it seemed over the top, a scientifically contentious form of indulgent self-examination, most fitting for people with money to burn.

Now, brain health is moving beyond celebrity curiosity and into luxury wellness, from neurofeedback sessions at Mandarin Oriental Mayfair to Clinique La Prairie’s seven-day cognitive longevity program in Switzerland, costing just under CHF 30,000 ($36,000). Meanwhile, neurotechnology companies are bringing brain monitoring and stimulation into specialist clinics and at-home devices, hoping to make cognitive fitness as routine as going to the gym.

Consumers appear hungry to know more. According to McKinsey’s 2025 Future of Wellness report, 61% of respondents consider cognitive function very important, yet brain health remains one of the areas where consumer demand is going unmet. Younger consumers, especially Gen Z, reportedly feel that gap the most.

“For a long time, it was all about physical performance, having beautiful top-performing bodies as late as possible in life,” says Olga Donica, longevity innovation director at luxury longevity clinic Clinique La Prairie. “Now, we are switching to something much more advanced, complex and sophisticated, and this for sure is the brain.”

Part of the appeal lies in growing research into neuroplasticity, which has overturned the idea that the brain becomes fixed in adulthood, revealing its capacity to rewire itself and adapt throughout life. For wellness brands, it’s an enticing proposition: if they’ve built lucrative businesses helping us optimize our bodies to perform better for longer, why not our brains?

In June, Mandarin Oriental Mayfair added a Brain Gym residency to its wellness offering, led by Natalia Ramsden, performance psychologist and founder of Sofos Associates, a cognitive performance consultancy. The experience begins with a 75 to 90-minute brain-mapping assessment, during which clients wear a cap fitted with 24 sensors that record electrical activity as they rest and complete short cognitive tasks. The results inform personalized recommendations and, for those who want to continue, a course of 10 to 20 neurofeedback sessions, where an on-screen game responds to their brain activity in real time. Some clients return for maintenance sessions and repeat assessments. “You don’t get fit in one session at the gym, and the brain is no different,” Ramsden says.

It’s a far cry from a doctor’s office. Sessions take place in the hotel’s private residences and suites, though most bookings come from external clients rather than hotel guests — largely business leaders, founders, and entrepreneurs based around Mayfair.

“My work is with leaders, founders, and investors who are already performing well and want to keep doing so under sustained pressure,” she says. “Many come to us running on high alert. They can’t switch off, their sleep suffers, and under pressure their attention narrows when they most need to see the bigger picture.”

Ramsden calls this investment in mental performance “cognitive capital”. With longer working lives and growing dependence on technology fueling anxieties about mental sharpness, Ramsden says, her clients are getting younger, too. “We’ve spent years talking about lifespan and healthspan. Now, people are starting to talk about brainspan,” she adds. For luxury hotels, this could mean a new frontier in wellness, offering a way to build lasting relationships with affluent clients beyond the occasional stay.

Where Sofos caters to professionals hoping to maintain their mental edge, Clinique La Prairie addresses a related anxiety: what happens when that edge begins to dull with age?

Clinique La Prairie in Switzerland, where clients can undergo a seven-day ‘Brain Potential’ program focused on cognitive longevity. Photos: Courtesy of Clinique La Prairie

Donica says the retreat’s Brain Potential program attracts predominantly affluent professionals in their late 40s to early 60s, often at the height of their careers but beginning to notice changes in their cognitive performance. They report problems with memory, stress, recovery and decision-making. “They run big companies, they own big things. So they need to be cognitively sharp,” Donica says.

Developed over two years, in collaboration with Lausanne University Hospital, the seven-day program at the clinic’s Montreux property combines brain MRI and volumetric analysis with cognitive testing, genetic screening, inflammation markers, gut microbiome analysis, and cardiovascular examinations. Guests receive a calculated “cognitive age”, with the results used to devise personalized nutrition, exercise and cognitive training plans. Each has a dedicated team of five: a doctor, nutritionist, therapist, movement expert, and guest-relations specialist. Guests leave with a personalized, three-month cognitive training plan, while follow-up assessments allow the clinic to adjust its recommendations over time.

But the ability to measure more aspects of brain health does not necessarily mean the ability to improve them. Donica says the clinic is gathering observations from guests, while acknowledging that these are not sufficient to make scientific claims about the program’s effectiveness. It’s a revealing tension: the higher the price and the more sophisticated the diagnostics, the more compelling the promise of personalization — even as evidence of lasting cognitive benefits remains limited.

At the more accessible end of the market, businesses are looking to turn brain health from an occasional luxury splurge into a regular part of consumers’ wellness routines.

London-based Naya Health, founded in 2025 by Daniel and Emily Honeywell, is among a new wave of clinics bringing brain stimulation into the wellness market. It offers repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS), a non-invasive treatment that uses magnetic pulses to stimulate targeted brain regions, for clinical conditions and now also marketed toward cognitive optimization. The co-founders are bullish on the technology’s potential, touting benefits from alleviating depression, anxiety and chronic fatigue to sharpening focus, improving decision-making and boosting athletic performance.

Honeywell likens brain stimulation to physiotherapy — “a workout for the brain” — that needs to be tailored to a person’s condition, rather than administered at a fixed intensity. Rather than treating stimulation as a one-off intervention, the clinic encourages clients to return for maintenance sessions, with some executives and athletes also booking “top-up” appointments ahead of important meetings or competitions.

Currently, around 80% of Naya’s clients are seeking treatment for chronic conditions, while 20% come for optimization. Optimization sessions cost around $300, while sessions for chronic conditions cost approximately $470. Some longer treatment courses can amount to around $10,700.

A patient receives an rTMS treatment at Naya Health’s London clinic. Photo: Courtesy of Naya Health

“The traditional model is transactional: people feel sick, then they receive treatment,” Daniel says. “People increasingly want long-term prevention and proactive care that keeps them well, in the same way they go to the gym to maintain their physical health. In five years, asking someone about their brain health routine will be as normal as asking about their skincare.”

And it’s not just brain stimulation attracting investment. Neurotechnology company Myndspan is building a business around measuring the brain rather than treating it, offering £600 assessments using magnetoencephalography (MEG), a technology traditionally confined to hospitals and research laboratories. The scans record magnetic signals generated by neural activity, giving customers a snapshot of their brain function and an estimated cognitive age.

Co-founder and CEO Caitlin Baltzer says her longer-term ambition is to make brain scans a recurring health check rather than a specialist medical procedure. “The value today is the information it provides and the ability to build a personal history,” Baltzer says. “Demonstrating the longer-term benefit is the work ahead for us.”

Beyond luxury hospitality and specialist clinics, dozens of neurotechnology companies are bringing brain monitoring and stimulation into everyday wearables.

Muse, the EEG (electroencephalogram, a technology that measures the brain’s electrical activity) headband maker, launched Brain Age earlier this month — a feature reminiscent of Whoop’s most popular feature, the Whoop Age — that estimates whether Muse’s 500,000 users’ brain activity appears younger or older than their biological age. Ongoing weekly assessments require a premium subscription, creating another potential revenue stream. While consumer EEG sacrifices some signal strength compared with laboratory equipment, CMO Nadia Kumentas argues that repeated measurements offer a different advantage. “In return, you get data from real life, night after night,” she says.

Muse is a consumer-grade EEG headband that claims to help users improve focus, relaxation, and meditation through neurofeedback that monitors brainwave activity in real time. Photo: Courtesy of Muse

Neurotechnology company Neurable has embedded EEG sensors into $499 noise-canceling headphones to monitor focus and cognitive fatigue, but founder and CEO Ramses Alcaide sees greater potential in licensing the technology to other manufacturers — including mainstream wearables brands. “We believe brain sensing will eventually become a standard feature in wearables, much like heart rate and sleep tracking today,” he says.

Others are moving beyond measurement to intervention. Pulsetto, which produces neck-worn vagus nerve stimulation devices, saw revenue rise from approximately $9 million in 2024 to more than $40 million in 2025, according to co-founder and CEO Povilas Sabaliauskas. “Data on its own doesn’t change how you feel, and now, consumers need a practical way to act on all their health information,” Sabaliauskas says.

It mirrors the broader trend in the longevity tech and wellness market — after years of selling consumers information about their bodies, they’re increasingly selling interventions to change how they function. As the technology becomes more portable, and the price barrier is lowered, there are more opportunities for consumer wellness brands, as well as luxury hospitality and spas, to sell the promise of a sharper brain.

But experts warn that identifying a market is one thing; proving these products actually work is another, particularly when sophisticated neuroscience-adjacent therapeutic applications are supposedly re-packaged in consumer-grade devices for at-home use.

Isaac Treves, a postdoctoral research fellow at Columbia University who studies neuroimaging, mindfulness and resilience, is particularly skeptical of consumer neurofeedback devices such as Muse. Beyond the challenges of capturing reliable EEG signals outside a laboratory, he questions whether those signals can tell us much about more subjective, complex mental states. “We don’t actually know how to predict whether you are paying attention or meditating peacefully with brain signals,” he says, arguing that “the Muse algorithm is mostly guesswork”.

“Unfortunately, the evidence base for neurofeedback devices like Muse is extremely limited, and most likely contaminated by placebo effects,” he adds.

None of this means brain health is destined to become another discarded wellness fad. Concerns about cognitive aging are real, and Treves remains optimistic about the potential of technologies that measure and influence brain activity.

But the industry’s commercial momentum is running ahead of the evidence for some of its most ambitious claims. Treves believes increasingly personalized neuroscience, supported by larger datasets and AI, could eventually produce meaningful advances. For now, though, his advice for improving cognitive wellbeing involves no re-wiring of the brain. “Good sleep and exercise habits, good social connection, seeking out meaning in your life, and all those obvious points that our parents tell us,” he advises.

Pulsetto’s vagus nerve stimulator is one of an emerging category of at-home consumer devices promising to regulate the nervous system and brain. Photo: Courtesy of Pulsetto

For luxury wellness and hospitality brands, the stakes are reputational: when selling a better brain, scientific credibility matters more than hyperpersonalization or luxurious surroundings.

There’s also a more uncomfortable question: whether the pursuit of brain ‘optimization’ risks becoming another demand on our already overstretched minds. “There’s a general anxiety about doing the latest thing, being the best, and capturing and quantifying everything,” says Sofos founder Ramsden. “Tracking can be very useful, but it can also backfire.”

#6576. Wildly Delicious Weeknight Dinners To Keep You Cozy All November Long

There’s more than just Thanksgiving to plan for.

November is the month when comfort food season really kicks into full gear. It’s the last month that really feels like fall before those pleasantly chilly evenings turn teeth-chattering, the leaves are still colorful and on the trees, and, of course, we can’t forget about Thanksgiving, so we’re not letting it get away without celebrating all it has to offer. Join us this November as we cook up cozy, comforting meals for both weeknights and special occasions. We’ve got 40 recipes to help inspire you to make dinner this November—one for every day of the month, and then some.

We’ve included a good mix of entirely new recipes, like our lasagna alla vodka skillet and our sheet-pan chicken tagine, as well as some old cold-weather classics like our chicken & dumplings, our broccoli cheddar gnocchi soup, and our chili mac.

Looking for cozy recipes for November? Check out our favorite one-pan fall dinners, under-an-hour comfort foods, and easy comfort food recipes.

Lasagna and penne alla vodka are two Italian-American staples that go hand in hand. Because our one-pot lazy lasagna skillet is a weeknight favorite, it only felt right to consolidate these two classics in one pan.

This version of chicken biryani is inspired by Hyderabadi biryani, which is one of the most popular and iconic dishes in South Asia. This streamlined version stays as true as possible to the authentic flavors, using readily available grocery store ingredients, but cuts down on the time by finishing things in the oven.

We can never get enough of beef and broccoli. In this easy, hands-off version, we’re cooking thinly-sliced steak low and slow in a rich broth until it’s fall-apart delicious, and then throwing in the broccoli near the end so it cooks just long enough to become tender.

This sheet-pan chicken tagine is the ultimate glow-up, transforming the complex, slow-simmered flavors of the classic North African dish into a streamlined meal perfect for busy evenings or an effortless dinner party.

This pumpkin pot pie is basically a pumpkin coconut curry baked beneath a flaky, golden crust that turns out equal parts comforting and festive. The carved Jack-o'-lantern top transforms a simple pot pie into a showstopping centerpiece that's almost too cute to cut into.

Carbonara always feels like a luxurious dish, but it's made with the simplest ingredients: eggs, spaghetti, Pecorino Romano, and pork. Add a bottles of Shaoxing and soy sauce, and you've got yourself an unforgettable meal.

In the world of all of our Marry Me Chicken variations, this just may be our new favorite version. We have a soft spot for risotto because it feels elevated, but it’s also soothing to stand there and stir until the rice hits the right tenderness. This version is extra luxurious with sun-dried tomatoes and a touch of cream.

Pizza is our guilty pleasure, but sometimes we want the flavors of the classic dish with a little more protein, without ordering a meat lovers. This vegetarian dinner has everything you love about pizza—slightly sweet tomato sauce, Italian herbs, and plenty of cheese—but makes a protein-packed swap by substituting the crust for cannellini beans.

One spoonful instantly made me think of my childhood. This easy comfort food recipe is perfect on a cold night, and simple enough to whip up when you don't feel like making anything (like on a weeknight after a weekend full of potlucks and Friendsgivings).

Slow-cooked turkey legs are this year’s ultimate Thanksgiving hack (we're not stopping you the rest of the month either!). No basting, no inevitable dry meat—no fuss at all. All you have to do is make an easy festive herb butter, wrap everything in foil, and let it roast unsupervised.

When you combine chili and mac and cheese, incredible things happen. We started with our preferred chili variation—white chicken chili, of course—and added in all the creamy, cheesy goodness of mac and cheese for the perfect weeknight dinner for indecisive families.

This recipe combines the rich, smoky flavors of traditional barbacoa with a cheesy topping and buttery biscuits for an irresistible meal. At the heart of this dish is succulent beef chuck roast, slow-cooked in a blend of fire-roasted tomatoes, chipotle chiles, and a medley of spices.

If you love stovetop mac 'n' cheese, you’ve got to try this creamy butternut squash orzo. Butternut squash and Parmesan join forces with orzo to create a cheesy pasta skillet that hits every nostalgic note.

The real magic in this sheet-pan dinner is in the savory-sweet, spoonable sauce that the onions transform into. Blending the chicken fat-roasted, charred onions with butter, sweet white vinegar, and crushed red pepper yields a creamy, umami-rich sauce that makes the chicken even more succulent.

If you’re looking for a vegetarian dinner centerpiece, then you can’t beat a whole roasted cauliflower. Gorgeously browned outside and meltingly tender in the middle, its stunningly simple goodness can’t be topped at any vegetarian Thanksgiving dinner.

Nothing satisfies a meat-and-potatoes craving quite like a classic, hearty shepherd’s pie. In this comfort food staple, ground beef is cooked with aromatics and red wine before being combined with corn and peas, all covered with velvety, rich mashed potatoes and topped with Parmesan before being broiled until golden brown.

Want taco night without the multiple pans and (semi-?) controlled chaos of a build-your-own dinner? Make this taco skillet. Saucy, spiced sweet potatoes and black beans are tossed with crushed potato chips and topped with melty cheese for a simple one-pan meal that will be your new weeknight go-to this November.

The heavy cream cuts the robust, earthy pumpkin in this soup, making it one of the most comforting soups for a chilly fall day. Load up on the garlic, cook the tomato paste to eliminate any rawness and release its sweet side, and get ready to thoroughly enjoy this pumpkin tortellini soup (in under 30 minutes!).

Broccoli cheddar soup is the ultimate comfort food—it’s rich, creamy, and packed with cheesy goodness—and we're taking it to the next level with pillowy gnocchi, making it heartier and more satisfying without any extra hassle. The gnocchi cooks right in the same pot, so you’re not stuck washing another dish.

This one-pot meal is a perfect way to warm up during the colder months, so go ahead and make it in the dead of winter to awaken your soul and grab a spoon to dig in! The best part? This hearty favorite is ready to enjoy in just 30 minutes, making it the perfect go-to weeknight dinner.

#6575. The Vogue Business AI Tracker

The Vogue Business AI Tracker keeps a record of the most important AI developments that will influence our industry and our world, each week. From venture capital investments and startup launches to product drops and regulatory updates, we’ll make sure you never miss a beat when it comes to the AI news that matters.

Why it matters: Prada has launched a ChatGPT plugin allowing users in the US, the UK and Italy to discover products, explore collections and find stores using information sourced directly from the brand. As AI assistants become a gateway to product discovery, the move gives Prada a more authoritative presence in conversations it might otherwise struggle to influence. “Conversational experiences represent a natural evolution of traditional e-commerce,” said Prada Group digital director Laura Campanella. “Through this pilot initiative, we are exploring a new territory for customer engagement.”

The news coincides with the launch of Prada’s Christmas campaign this week, featuring hand-drawn animation by Disney veteran John Pomeroy. These two contrasting moves reflect a broader distinction emerging in luxury: AI for product discovery, and human craftsmanship for consumer-facing brand storytelling.

The news: Anthropic’s IPO filing reveals the huge costs and risks of the AI boom.

Why it matters: Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO filing offers a rare look inside the economics — and extraordinary risks — of the AI industry. As the Claude AI maker prepares for a potential $2 trillion valuation, the Financial Times reports that its revenues exceeded $33 billion in the first nine months of 2026, while its computing costs have fallen dramatically relative to sales, all suggesting a path to profitability. Yet Anthropic has also committed more than $800 billion to computing infrastructure through 2045, much of it supplied by technology giants including Amazon and Google, who are also major investors.

Crucially, the prospectus devotes 92 pages to risks, warning that future AI models could resist shutdown, manipulate information or cause harm too large for insurers to cover. For businesses embedding AI into everything from creative production to customer service, the filing exposes a central contradiction: the technology is becoming commercially indispensable even as its developers acknowledge profound uncertainty over its long-term risks.

The news: Anthropic plans European AI consultancy.

Why it matters: Anthropic is reportedly partnering with private equity firm Hg to launch a European consultancy that’ll place AI engineers and advisers in external businesses to help them integrate Anthropic’s technology, according to the Financial Times. Expected to launch by the end of 2026, hubs are currently planned in London and Berlin, with the Claude developer likely using the venture to accelerate corporate AI adoption — and even capture some of the work traditionally handled by consultancies such as Accenture and the Big Four.

Fashion and luxury businesses, many of which are still grappling with how to deploy AI, could be fertile ground for these services. But the model raises an obvious tension: while companies may welcome direct access to AI expertise, how independent can the advice be when the consultancy is backed by a company with a commercial interest in driving adoption of its own technology?

The news: Anthropic launches Claude Duet AI agent to rival OpenAI and Meta.

Why it matters: Anthropic has released Claude Duet, an AI agent rivaling Meta’s consumer-focused Muse and OpenAI’s more enterprise-oriented Dots; the Duet has both brand and consumer use cases for fashion. It can purchase products on consumers’ behalf using Shopify’s Shop Pay and Stripe Link, while merchants can instruct the agent to set up, design and manage their Shopify stores, including inventory and orders, Anthropic announced in a blog post. Meanwhile, a “richer visual editor” — which allows brands to design and preview their storefronts within the agent’s interface before anything goes live — is “coming soon”.

It was only a matter of time until Anthropic followed Meta and OpenAI in launching a personal AI assistant. Now, the battle is on between these tech companies to capture both consumer and brands’ trust, so that the integration these agents depend on across stores and payment providers is realized. The growing competition here signals a shift towards AI-mediated purchases, potentially reducing direct customer interactions for brands and making product visibility and seamless checkout across AI platforms increasingly important.

The news: Major banks and retailers block AI shopping agents like Meta Muse.

Why it matters: A growing list of US banks and retailers are blocking AI agents like Meta Muse and Instinct from acting on their websites. Amazon and Ebay have both prohibited these models from browsing or purchasing items on their respective marketplaces, while Citigroup, Bank of America, JPMorgan and Charles Schwab have each moved to prevent outside agents from logging into customer accounts and transacting on their behalf.

“We have to make sure we protect our customers in the right way [and] we’re building tools to do that,” JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon said on the company’s third-quarter earnings call last week. “In the meantime, we’re not going to allow just any outside agent to come inside the company, because that’s too risky for clients and for JPMorgan.”

While much of the fashion industry runs its direct-to-consumer sites via platform providers like Shopify — which has opened its network to AI agents unless a brand explicitly opts out — the growing calls from prominent banking officials to introduce legislation point to a bigger unresolved question: when an AI agent makes a purchase that a consumer later disputes, who is responsible for putting it right? For now, experts say much of that burden may still land with the retailer.

The news: OpenAI UK employees received £2.3 million on average in pay and shares in 2025.

Why it matters: OpenAI employees in the UK received an average of £2.3 million in pay and shares last year, according to newly filed UK accounts. The ChatGPT developer distributed £255 million in salary and equity compensation among 110 staff — more than double the previous year’s average package. The figures reflect fierce competition for specialist AI talent, although remuneration varies significantly between employees, with leading researchers commanding the largest pay.

It’s another sign that the AI bubble is far from bursting, with these salaries incentivizing employees for longer and reflecting the budgets of the venture capitalists funding the company. (OpenAI’s most recent funding round reached $122 billion in March 2026, at an $852 billion post-money valuation.)

OpenAI’s UK revenue more than tripled to £293 million in 2025, as London becomes an increasingly key international AI research and commercial hub.

The news: Pinterest launches AI-powered beauty guides.

Why it matters: Pinterest has launched Beauty Guides, an AI-powered feature that analyzes hair and nail Pins to generate personalized salon instructions, at-home tutorials and product recommendations. Available first to US iOS users, Pinterest says the tool aims to close the gap between discovering a beauty look and recreating it.

While competitors like Google Lens already use AI-powered visual search to identify and shop products, Pinterest is extending the concept to practical beauty advice. The move reflects a broader shift from AI-powered discovery to AI-assisted decision-making, while helping Pinterest turn its vast repository of visual inspiration into greater shopping intent and potential commercial opportunities for beauty brands. It also builds on the platform’s recent push into visual search advertising, giving it more ways to connect inspiration with purchases.

The news: OpenAI releases virtual try-on in ChatGPT.

Why it matters: OpenAI is introducing AI-powered virtual try-on and product-saving features to ChatGPT, deepening its push into fashion e-commerce. Users can upload photos of themselves to visualize how clothing and accessories might look on, while a new Favorites feature lets them save products and try-on images for later.

Powered by ChatGPT Images 2.5 (OpenAI’s latest image generator, released in September) the tools will roll out globally across consumer plans, with purchases still completed on merchants’ websites. The launch puts ChatGPT in more direct competition with visual shopping platforms such as Google and Pinterest, as AI assistants evolve from product discovery tools into personalized shopping destinations.

For fashion brands, it raises the prospect of ChatGPT becoming an increasingly influential touchpoint in the customer journey. Luxury brands have been hesitant to adopt virtual try-on on their own channels, largely because the tech hasn’t met their visual standards — but the latest advances in AI are rapidly improving the realism of these digital models.

The news: TikTok launches AI shopping assistant and one-click checkout.

Why it matters: TikTok has launched an AI-powered shopping assistant that provides personalized product guidance, answering questions about sizing, availability and delivery directly within the app. Alongside this, a new one-click checkout feature allows users to purchase directly from brands on their FYP, without leaving TikTok.

Developed in partnership with commerce and payment providers including Shopify, Salesforce and Stripe, the features mark an expansion beyond TikTok Shop’s existing marketplace model, more deeply embedding AI-assisted shopping and direct brand purchases into the social platform. Its aim is to create a more seamless journey from inspiration through discovery, to purchase.

The launch comes against a wider shift towards AI-powered, end-to-end shopping experiences, alongside Meta’s Muse AI agent, Pinterest’s growing shopping investment, and ChatGPT’s new virtual try-on capabilities. For brands, the challenge becomes how to surface in these AI products, where checkout is handled outside their own channels.

The news: Trump orders the US government to stop calling AI “AI”.

Why it matters: President Donald Trump has signed an executive order instructing the US government to replace “artificial intelligence” and “AI” with “super intelligence” and “SI” across all official communications and policy documents, arguing that the new terminology better reflects the tech’s rapidly advancing capabilities and economic potential. The language notably echoes Mark Zuckerberg’s vision of “personal super intelligence”, which he made central to Meta’s AI strategy last year.

The rebrand comes amid a much bigger debate over who should be responsible for keeping increasingly powerful AI systems in check. Ahead of signing the executive order, Trump convened some of the industry’s most powerful figures — including Meta’s Zuckerberg, xAI’s Elon Musk, Google’s Sundar Pichai, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, OpenAI’s Greg Brockman, and Anthropic’s Dario Amodei — to sign a voluntary AI safety accord.

The accord puts the onus on companies to develop internal safeguards, subject their systems to independent audits and provide board-level oversight, in line with the Trump administration’s preferred “self-policing” versus a coordinated slowdown. Amodei has been among the most vocal advocates for slowing down, while OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Microsoft and xAI have backed calls for greater restraint.

The bosses at Anthropic, Google, xAI, Meta, OpenAI, and Nvidia all signed Trump’s voluntary accord.

The news: Oura delays IPO, citing market uncertainty.

Why it matters: Smart ring maker Oura has postponed its hotly anticipated IPO, citing “uncertainty in the IPO market” despite strong demand for its wearables offering. The company had been targeting a valuation of as much as $14 billion, and expected to raise as much as $2.2 billion in the public listing.

The timing points to a broader AI-driven shake-up in public markets. Investors are increasingly scrutinizing the vast cash being poured into AI infrastructure and lofty tech valuations, even as prospective mega-listings from AI companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI threaten to command an outsized share of investor attention and capital. Oura’s delay offers an early glimpse of the potential divide between the tech companies attracting extraordinary sums and those competing for what’s left.

Plus, as of last week, OpenAI announced that it won’t be joining the IPO rush this year. CEO Sam Altman has said going public now would be ill-advised given the safety work still ahead.

The news: Meta unveils kawaii-coded wearable pendant to house its Muse AI assistant.

Why it matters: Just when we thought Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg had finished announcing his slew of smart glasses and AI updates during the annual connect conference, there was “just one more thing”: another wearable device designed to house its new Muse AI agent, the Muse Charm. It’s a tamagotchi-esque, palm-sized totem on a looped cord designed to attach to keychains or fit into the wearer’s pocket.

The Muse Charm has a small screen to display the user’s selected Muse AI avatar. It’s unlocked via fingerprint and can be spoken into for instructing their agent to carry out tasks. Zuckerberg is still “finalizing” the components, but promised that the device will be ready to ship before the holidays.

The Muse Charm is Meta’s latest attempt at a new form factor designed to get its AI agent into the hands of as many consumers as possible. “We packed the whole muse experience, including the real-time voice and avatar stack into something that fits on a key chain and is always available to talk to,” Zuckerberg said. “So if you’re not wearing glasses, this is going to be by far the fastest way to talk to your Muse and show [it] what’s going on around you.”

It feeds into Zuckerberg’s promise of “personal superintelligence”, and may offer itself as a successor to the smartphone.
