Why it matters: After launching ChatGPT-5 in August this year, OpenAI has quickly followed with a significant update: Chat GPT-5.2, pitched as its smartest LLM model yet, across its writing, coding and reasoning capabilities.

OpenAI dropped the model just a few days after CEO Sam Altman announced an internal “code red” announcement, which the company’s head of applications, Fidji Simo, told journalists on Thursday was to signal that OpenAI wanted to “marshal resources” into ChatGPT. All of this comes as the company faces rapidly increasing competition from rival LLM makers, including Perplexity, Anthropic and Google, who are fast refining their own models. Google, which has received positive reviews for Gemini 3, released last month, is intensifying its shopping-focused efforts. Just last week, it released an update to its virtual try-on tool, so that US consumers needn’t take a full-body shot to try any item they find in Google’s AI Mode on, in the run up to the holidays.

The news: Trump signs executive order blocking states from enforcing their own AI rules.

Why it matters: President Donald Trump has ramped up his push for America to become the global AI market dominator, this time by signing an executive order to prevent federal governments passing their own statewide AI regulations. It’s a move that will be welcomed by US tech giants like OpenAI and Meta, who have pushed for nationwide rather than statewide rules, which they fear could slow their pace of AI innovation. Trump’s nationwide approach to AI regulation is characterized by a hands-off approach, all but deregulating the industry. It’s yet another stark reminder for fashion companies operating globally to establish their own AI guardrails that align with their brand values: legal experts suggest brands use the more intensive European approach to AI regulation as a blueprint instead.

The news: McDonald’s pulls AI Christmas ad after audience backlash.

Why it matters: A 45-second holiday ad released by McDonald’s on the company’s Netherlands YouTube channel on December 6 promptly sparked online social media backlash. Consumers labeled it “AI slop”, and creatives criticized the ad as threatening job displacement in the industry, where real actors and filmmakers were absent from its production. The ad has since been removed.

Melanie Bridge, CEO of The Sweetshop Films, the company that made the AI-generated ads, took to LinkedIn to defend the video’s production. In a post that has also since been deleted, she wrote: “It’s never about replacing craft, it’s about expanding the toolbox. The vision, the taste, the leadership… that will always be human,” adding that the film took her 10-person team five weeks of full-time work to make.

So far, brands’ creative experiments with AI have drawn more critique when the output is something that consumers believe could have been made just as well without the tech. More surreal adverts leaning into AI models’ entropic tendencies, like Valentino’s recent DeVain bag campaign, have proven slightly less divisive. “This moment serves as an important learning as we explore the effective use of AI,” McDonald’s told the BBC in a statement confirming it had removed the ad.

The news: Meta acquires AI pendant maker Limitless in further wearables push.

Why it matters: It’s been a huge week for Meta when it comes to the company’s AI wearables ambitions. A day after CEO Mark Zuckerberg announced a new creative studio within its Reality Labs division, the group confirmed it’s shifting some resources from its metaverse team into AI glasses and wearables. Then, on Friday, it announced its acquisition of Limitless, a startup that makes AI-powered “all listening” pendants, for an undisclosed amount.

So far, Zuckerberg has been bullish on smart glasses as the ultimate form factor for AI-powered wearables, but the Limitless acquisition suggests the company is exploring other form factors that take in more context (like audio as well as visual information) from the wearer’s environment, as part of its push into its “superintelligence” vision. It comes after Amazon bought a similar startup, Bee, in July, acquiring its wristworn “all listening” device technology, too. In a statement accompanying the news, Limitless said: “Meta recently announced a new vision to bring personal superintelligence to everyone and a key part of that vision is building incredible AI-enabled wearables. We share this vision and we’ll be joining Meta to help bring our shared vision to life.”

The news: ELC and Jo Malone London launch AI-powered scent advisor.

Why it matters: They say that shopping for fragrance is one of the most personal tasks, so it makes sense that this would be an area of focus for AI innovation within beauty groups. Jo Malone’s new AI-powered scent advisor is designed to “digitally recreate the Jo Malone London’s signature in-store consultation experience”, the companies said, by inviting customers to describe the kind of scent they’re searching for, and whether it’s for themselves or a gift. The beauty company has partnered with Google to use the tech group’s Gemini and Google Cloud Vertex AI platform, which interprets customers’ natural language prompts and generates bespoke fragrance recommendations after analyzing the beauty brand’s olfactory data combined with that of customers.

It’s touted as particularly useful for first-time buyers of the brand, who may want more information about a scent before purchasing, and represents the next step in olfactory-focused AI applications. Expect other fragrance brands to follow suit.

The news: Meta poaches senior designer from Apple to build out its new creative studio.

Why it matters: Alan Dye, who has spent the last 19 years at Apple and the last 10 as its VP of user interface design, is leaving the company to become Meta’s chief design officer. Alongside this hire, Meta also announced it is establishing a creative studio within Reality Labs — the division that houses its wearables and metaverse businesses — which Dye will lead. The hire was announced on Threads by Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, who wrote: “The new studio will bring together design, fashion and technology to define the next generation of our products and experiences. We plan to elevate design within Meta, and pull together a talented group with a combination of craft, creative vision, systems thinking, and deep experience building iconic products.” Meanwhile, on X, Meta CTO Andrew Bosworth revealed the company is poaching another of Apple’s senior design leads, Billy Sorrentino, to join the new creative studio.

Zuckerberg has been recruiting several senior hires from its biggest competitors in the AI race, including OpenAI, as it doubles down on its goals to create the first truly mass-adopted AI wearable. By poaching senior designers from Apple and launching a creative studio at the same time, Meta is sending a strong signal that it’s prioritizing the design and feel of its devices in-house. So far, Meta has relied on its partnership with eyewear group EssilorLuxottica to provide the design stripes necessary for AI smart glasses that people actually want to wear. All fashion eyes will be on what kind of wearable the new creative studio designs in-house.

The news: Topshop plots “AI-driven” fashion show in February 2026.

Why it matters: Topshop has teamed up with creative agency THG Studios, Paypal and Google to launch what it’s pitching as the “world’s first AI-driven fashion show” in February next year. The high street brand, which made its return to the runway after seven years this August, will host the show, involving real-life models, in Manchester at THG’s studios. Topshop says that the fashion show will be shoppable, and that the audience will be able to “co-create” the show by interacting with a dedicated app, which generates a “digital wardrobe” for each guest and guides them through the event space, alerting them to certain items or moments that are most relevant to their tastes. Each look will appear on the app the moment it appears on the runway, allowing guests to click and buy it through the app. Guests will also be able to “like” looks as they see them, which will feed into trending items across apps users.

It’s the latest sign that brands are exploring how AI can personalize the shopping experience for customers, this time blending the in-person and online experiences together, as a way to increase engagement with a collection.

The news: OpenAI responds to lawsuit over teenager’s suicide saying it was down to “misuse” of ChatGPT.

Why it matters: The family of a 16-year-old boy, Adam Raine, who committed suicide in April have filed a lawsuit against ChatGPT maker OpenAI, alleging that the chatbot had functioned as a “suicide coach” that told him how to take his own life and even wrote a suicide note. OpenAI this week responded to the lawsuit for the first time, denying the allegations and saying the teenager had engaged in “misuse, unauthorized use, unintended use, unforeseeable use, and/or improper use of ChatGPT”, in a filing to the California Superior Court of San Francisco. Filings from Raine’s family show that the chatbot discouraged Raine from seeking mental health advice, but did offer up a suicide hotline number in some conversations.

OpenAI said the teenager had bypassed its rules requiring parental consent for under-18s. This signals that the tech company places the onus on users’ interactions with its chatbots, rather than the availability of potentially harmful information on its platform, and serves as an important reminder for brands working with OpenAI to have their own AI guardrails in place, where no regulation currently exists.

The news: OpenAI launches new shopping research feature within ChatGPT.

Why it matters: The biggest players in AI search have been announcing new shopping-focused features in quick succession ahead of the Black Friday shopping weekend. OpenAI’s latest shopping update gives users a step-by-step product discovery journey, designed like a conversation, so that users can have a back-and-forth with the chatbot to refine the “personalised buying guide” it eventually delivers. The tool gives users options for budget range, finds the best deals on products, and lets them respond “not interested” or “more like this” to product images it suggests. All of this was possible on ChatGPT previously through users’ conversations with the chatbot, but with the new feature, OpenAI is giving users a dedicated space within the app that’s wholly focused on shopping.

It comes as the company is gradually rolling out an integrated checkout within its app for US users, so consumers can discover products and complete purchases without ever leaving the app. By signposting consumers to a dedicated shopping research tool, OpenAI is doubling down on its positioning as an AI-powered personal shopper, a move that primes ChatGPT for future in-app advertising opportunities.

The news: Perplexity launches free “agentic” integrated checkout product ahead of holiday sales.

Why it matters: Following in the footsteps of OpenAI’s ChatGPT, AI platform Perplexity has partnered with PayPal so that all its US users can now make direct purchases without having to click through to retailers’ sites. It’s a move that removes friction for shoppers, so they can research a product and make a purchase in fewer steps. Perplexity’s chief business officer, Dmitry Shevelenko, told CNBC in an interview that “most people still want to do their own research,” so the platform has kept that step within consumers’ hands, and made the payments process “agentic” to simplify the buying journey.

The platform says it’s also refined its AI model to better understand purchase intent and deliver more personalised recommendations based on users’ search history. Perplexity has not disclosed whether it will earn revenue from sales completed on its platform, according to ChatGPT. It’s the latest sign that AI platforms are doubling down on shopping as a key driver for growth — and aiming to keep consumers on their platforms for longer and longer.

The news: Google CEO warns “no company is immune” if the AI bubble bursts.

Why it matters: As more and more billions of investment are poured into AI platforms and the companies that power their infrastructure, investors have been growing increasingly wary in recent weeks that we’re in an “AI bubble” that could echo the 2000 dot-com crash. Google is one of the biggest players in AI, so CEO Sundar Pichai’s warning that “no company is going to be immune, including us”, if the bubble bursts, shows that even the leaders at the forefront of the AI race are conscious that valuations are inflated and investment is extremely concentrated in AI.

Pichai did, however, draw comparisons with the dawn of the internet to show that even if AI companies are overvalued, and we’re heading for a crash, the technology itself is so fundamental that it will change the way we interact digitally forever. This view is shared by most proponents of the technology, who promise that it has the potential to reach humanlike intelligence and improve society. When AI chipmaker Nvidia beat expectations by $1.8 billion when it posted $57 billion in revenues for the third quarter last week, AI and tech stocks rallied, suggesting investors aren’t totally spooked by the idea of an AI bubble. Experts advise fashion companies to tread cautiously and continue investing in AI tools that demonstrate a clear use case for their business in the meantime.

The news: Daydream launches AI agent shopping app for iPhone.

Why it matters: Julie Bornstein’s startup Daydream, which describes itself as the “first chat-based AI shopping agent built exclusively for fashion”, is designed to make shopping easier for consumers. Previously only available in beta as a desktop website, Daydream is now launching an iPhone shopping app. It’s chosen to go deep on iOS integration by incorporating Apple’s visual intelligence — the AI-powered feature that allows users to point their cameras at objects and texts to identify them — so that Daydream users can search and shop directly from any screenshot on their phone. In practice, Daydream says this means consumers can screenshot an Instagram post and insert the image into the app to identify and shop featured products, closing the loop between visual inspiration and purchase.

The news: Snapchat owner inks deal with Perplexity to introduce AI search.

Why it matters: Snap Inc, the parent company of Snapchat, saw its shares surge up to 16% this week, after announcing a $400 million partnership with Open AI rival Perplexity AI, to integrate its AI search engine within the Snapchat app. From early 2026, Perplexity will appear in the Snapchat Chat interface, so that its nearly one billion monthly active users can ask questions on any topic and yield real-time conversational answers, powered by Perplexity’s generative AI.

The deal opens up a big new revenue stream for Snap, which will charge Perplexity $400 million over the course of a year to access its user base. Perplexity has recently been embroiled in a number of copyright infringement cases, including from News Corp, as well as a recent lawsuit from Amazon over the use of its AI agent to shop on customers’ behalves without their consent. The deal with Snap gives the platform some timely validation. In a statement announcing the news, Snap made clear its AI ambitions, saying: “The partnership underscores Snap’s growing role as a trusted platform for AI partners to reach a large, engaged, mobile-native audience.” Meanwhile, Snapchat will also use the conversations users have with Perplexity to “help enhance personalization on Snapchat”, doubling as a clear in-app ad revenue driver.

The news: Pinterest CEO says platform is exploring the potential for agentic shopping.

Why it matters: On Pinterest’s Q3 earnings call, investors wanted to know what the social platform is planning for the future of agentic commerce. CEO Bill Ready told investors that Pinterest already offers “push button-type shopping” through its partnership with Amazon, and it is gathering data to see if users actually want its AI model to “push the button for them”. The questions come a couple of weeks after Pinterest announced it will soon launch a voice-enabled AI shopping assistant, which allows Pinterest users to talk to the platform about what they’re searching and shopping for. This will yield personalized recommendations drawing from users’ saved pins and collections.

The news: Nvidia becomes the world’s first $5 trillion company

Why it matters: Three years ago, before the arrival of generative AI chatbots like ChatGPT, Nvidia’s valuation was $400 billion. Last week, it became the first $5 trillion company in the world. Nvidia makes software and hardware like graphics processing units (GPUs) and chips that power AI models. CEO Jensen Huang said the company had already secured $500 billion in orders of its AI chips for the next five quarters, which sent its stock rallying. Nvidia’s record-breaking valuation signals just how much promise investors believe AI technology has — but it also comes at a time when there is limited data showing how AI has improved efficiencies. Talks of an AI bubble are rife, and every bubble has to burst. Fashion companies using AI tools may not be affected by an investor bubble bursting, but it would send shockwaves through markets if the tech doesn’t live up to its promise.

The news: Amazon cuts 14,000 jobs amid AI push

Why it matters: Last week, Amazon joined the growing cohort of blue-chip companies across the world announcing sweeping workforce cuts. The Big Tech company said it would cut up to 14,000 jobs from its corporate workforce. It comes a week after Target announced it was cutting 8% of its corporate staff (around 1,800 jobs) in its first major round of layoffs in 10 years. Although neither company directly attributed the cuts to AI, analysts have pointed to what they both have in common: the cuts are being made to white-collar roles within corporate teams, which are viewed as particularly ripe for AI automation, rather than jobs within their factories. It’ll be interesting to see if more retailers follow suit — and if this corporate focus becomes a trend.

The news: Aerie releases “real people” anti-AI campaign.

Why it matters: Aerie, American Eagle Outfitters’s lounge and lingerie brand, last week released an Instagram campaign with a strong anti-AI message. “Real creativity at its best. Here’s our team, behind the scenes of our holiday shoot. No retouching. No AI. 100 per cent Aerie Real,” read the caption accompanying the campaign launch post, which features BTS shots of Aerie’s festive campaign shoot cast and crew. The brand, which previously swore off Photoshop in its campaigns, has been known to centre its messaging around human “realness”; this latest effort underscores how divisive AI-made campaigns have become.

While some advocates for AI images argue they get rid of creative constraints, the biggest backlash against brand experiments with AI-generated images so far has surrounded campaigns that seem like they could have been made without AI. Some analysts say that human-made content will soon become the ultimate marker of luxury. Will more brands follow Aerie’s lead this festive season?

The news: Meta is reportedly laying off 600 employees from its AI division.

Why it matters: Facebook and Instagram owner Meta is cutting some 600 staff from its so-called Superintelligence unit, the company’s AI division, according to multiple reports. The news was first reported by Axios, who cited an internal employee memo. “By reducing the size of our team, fewer conversations will be required to make a decision, and each person will be more load-bearing and have more scope and impact,” Meta’s chief AI officer Alexandr Wang wrote in the memo to employees, according to Axios’s report. It’s a turnaround after the company went on an AI hiring spree earlier this year, that included the hiring of Wang himself, and comes amid broader speculation that the tech industry is heading for an “AI bubble” that has seen AI companies receive mega investment before delivering on business fundamentals. Investors’ eyes will be closely watching Meta’s competitors to see if they soon follow suit.

The news: Frasers Group partners with Commercetools to build out agentic AI capabilities.

Why it matters: In September, ChatGPT launched its “agentic commerce protocol” (ACP), an open-source tech standard that allows various AI agents from companies like Perplexity, Google and Microsoft to interact with each other, connect to different commerce systems and complete purchases, in partnership with Shopify and Commercetools. Now, Frasers Group is working with Commercetools to become one of the first European retailers to roll out two agentic commerce products, AI Hub and Agent Gateway.

The company said this partnership will allow shoppers to discover and purchase products from Frasers Group’s retailers like Sports Direct and Flannels directly within AI shopping channels such as ChatGPT and Google AI when their integrated checkout features land in Europe. It’s the first major announcement from a European retailer indicating an intention to launch AI shopping agents — which would search, select and purchase products on behalf of the customer — when the tech is ready.

The news: Pinterest introduces the option for users to remove AI-generated content from their feeds.

Why it matters: Pinterest’s new controls allow users to personalise their feeds and opt out of seeing AI-generated imagery across specific categories, including home decor and beauty, as well as men’s, women’s and children’s fashion. The tech company said it will also make its existing AI-generated labels more noticeable in the coming days. For Pinterest, it’s a move that indicates just how business-critical transparency is around AI, and gives us an idea of the intensity of the backlash the platform has received against such content — a highly controversial subject when it comes to creative forms like image and video.

The news: Revolve launches AI-powered personal styling tool.

Why it matters: The US multi-brand retailer tapped fashion entrepreneur Sandy Sholl’s AI startup Zelig to power its new ‘Build a Look’ onsite feature. Revolve customers can now mix and match items from the site and style them on digital avatar models — all enabled by Zelig’s combination of generative AI and computer vision, as well as input from IRL stylists, the brands claim. Revolve has also launched a “digital closet” feature for shoppers to save desired items as well as those purchased. It’s the latest personalisation play from an online retailer, as they race to enhance their websites with the latest AI capabilities, to retain engagement as more shoppers adopt AI search. While individual brands like Ralph Lauren and Moncler are investing in bespoke features that replicate their in-store experiences online, for multi-brand players, retaining a USP in the age of AI is an even tougher challenge.

The news: OpenAI’s Sora app hits one million downloads, faster than ChatGPT.

Why it matters: OpenAI exec Bill Peebles, who is in charge of the tech firm’s new Sora video-generation app, announced that Sora reached one million app downloads in under five days — a faster take-up than when the company released ChatGPT in November 2022. It gives us an idea of just how high consumer demand is for visual experiments through AI — the app is currently invite-only and available exclusively to users in North America. It also comes amid creator copyright concerns over the AI’s use of their work. If the app grows rapidly before the company has proper controls and protections in place, there could soon be a vast amount of AI-generated content published with likenesses to original works.

The news: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman promises creators more “granular” controls over Sora 2’s content usage.

Why it matters: Just four days after OpenAI launched Sora 2, its new invite-only video generation app, CEO Sam Altman took to his online blog to promise creators of copyrighted characters more “granular” controls, “similar to the opt-in model for likeness but with additional controls”, over the use of their creations by the app. He said the company had been “taking feedback” from rightsholders and app users and would work to “fix the missteps very quickly” as it develops OpenAI’s video generation tools. This prompt response from Altman reflects just how contentious image use for AI tools is right now, while wider regulation to protect creatives’ IP is yet to be seen. For now, legal experts say for brands wanting to experiment with AI images and video, the onus is on them to establish permissions from creators and properly attribute their use, to avoid individual copyright cases.

The news: California Governor Gavin Newsom signs AI safety law.

Why it matters: It’s the first in-nation law that forces developers at major US-based AI companies to publicly disclose their AI safety and security protocols, and includes whistleblower protections for AI workers, in what analysts are saying could set a benchmark for other states to follow. But it also moves in direct opposition to Trump’s recent AI action plan, which all but deregulates the development of AI at these companies on a national level. As the state that houses much of the Silicon Valley tech companies at the forefront of AI development, California is the closest to their inner workings, but brands operating at a national level will need to watch how other regional governments react, and if this policy influences the ongoing regulation battle at a federal level.

The news: OpenAI launches ChatGPT Checkout.

Why it matters: Instant Checkout removes the friction for ChatGPT users — where they previously searched and discovered products on ChatGPT, before clicking through to make the purchase on a brand’s own site, this new feature omits that final step, shortening the purchase journey. It has big implications for brands’ partnership decisions, advertising strategies, and how they design their websites to appeal to both human customers and LLM “crawlers”. Find out more about what it means for fashion here.

The news: Meta debuts three new AI smart glasses models, but demos fail.

Why it matters: At Meta’s annual Meta Connect conference on 17 September in California, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg unveiled the first AI smart glasses with an in-lens display, the Meta Display glasses, designed to replace the wearer’s need to get out their phone. But the live tech demos featured a couple of glitches. A demo of the AI glasses’ ability to interpret cooking ingredients in front of the lenses and give the wearer recipe instructions misinterpreted the selection of raw ingredients as a half-cooked dish, and the glasses failed to pick up a live Whatsapp video call demo between Zuckerberg and Meta CTO Andrew Bosworth.

Bosworth later took to Instagram to explain why the demos went wrong. It wasn’t down to the Wi-Fi, as Zuckerberg suggested onstage, but down to the amount of Meta AI glasses in close proximity during the demo, which caused a flood of traffic to Meta’s live AI server, according to Bosworth. It’s a reminder of just how many pieces of the puzzle are required for this nascent tech to function. At $799 a pop, consumers will expect their buzzy AI glasses to work, so Meta has its work cut out to fix any bugs before they become available for US consumers at the end of the month.

The news: US Federal Trade Commission launches inquiry into AI ‘companions’ used by teens.

Why it matters: Tech companies including OpenAI, Meta and Google are being probed by the US regulator over AI chatbots that provide “companionship”, after a series of high-profile suicides and harm among young people linked to their interactions with the tech. The US Federal Trade Commission (FTC) has ordered the companies to share information about how their AI chatbots develop characters and personas, and how they monetise this kind of engagement. It’s also asking tech firms to disclose what measures they have in place to avoid harm, especially among young people, and how they handle personal data from the conversations.

Given that a primary hesitation among luxury brands in their adoption of AI is the risk of losing consumer trust, the industry should watch the case closely. As user trust in conversations with generative AI grows, analysts say this trust will extend to other online activities like shopping. But as AI regulation becomes increasingly fragmented, more of the onus is on brands to develop their own guardrails. The results of the inquiry should provide key insights for brands that are grappling with developing their own AI ethics, and could inform industry standards in future.

The news: Fraudsters use AI to fake defects on resale platforms.

Why it matters: A disturbing trend has been called out on fashion social media this week — some buyers on resale platforms are using AI image generators to fake defects on received items to get refunds. On resale platforms, trust hangs in the balance between a seller’s description of their garment condition and what the item actually looks like. Although a number of the fake defect attempts called out on social media are amusingly bad, some are more realistic, thanks to recent improvements in AI image generators and their usage becoming more commonplace. When Vogue Business reached out to the main resale platforms, they said this was not yet a business concern — suggesting that this type of fraud is still in its infancy. But in order to retain trust, resale platforms will have to stay on the front foot of this new risk, which could mean investing in an enhanced verification process like videos for buyers making defect claims, which is an added cost for the platforms that could be passed onto users. Vinted told Vogue Business it is “closely monitoring the evolving use of AI among our members to ensure it remains consistent with the platform’s usage guidelines”.

The news: Shein appears to use an AI Luigi Mangione as a T-shirt model.

Why it matters: Shein has opened an internal investigation after the product image for a men’s shirt listing on its website featured a model that resembled Luigi Mangione, the person accused of killing UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson last year. The online retailer has now taken down the image, and told press in a statement: “The image in question was provided by a third-party vendor and was removed immediately upon discovery.” But the image was online long enough to be shared widely on social media, with speculation surrounding whether it was generated using AI. Mangione has amassed a cult following among some in the US who frame him as a folk hero, in opposition to the US healthcare system. This fuelled a surge of clothing emblazoned with Mangione’s face and name being sold online on retailers like Etsy and Ebay. Connecting the dots, this incident is a stark reminder of the importance of human oversight at brands experimenting with AI for more routine image needs like product listings. And it’s a very stark reminder of how undiscerning the AI image generators themselves are at this point — they crawl the good, the bad and the ugly of the internet to produce their images.

The news: Amazon launches Lens Live instant AI image scanning tool.

Why it matters: Amazon already had a visual search tool, Amazon Lens, which allowed customers to upload images or scan barcodes to discover products. But this new live component brings the retailer more in line with Google Lens and Pinterest Lens — shoppers can now point their phones at things they see before them in the real world, and Amazon’s app will suggest similar or matching products on its platform. The new feature will initially be rolled out to “tens of millions” shoppers in the US, and the company has not said when it will be rolled out to further US customers or into other markets. The live lens feature will also integrate with Amazon’s AI shopping assistant Rufus for more product information. It’s clear that Amazon is investing big in its AI-powered shopping features, and this represents the biggest multimodal search development on a retailer’s own platform thus far. How long until competitors follow suit?

Why it matters: The initial buzz around the launch of ChatGPT-5 and its “PhD-level” knowledge this month has wound down, amid criticisms of the update as somewhat underwhelming. Social media users, tech influencers and journalists abound have commented on the tool’s tendency to “hallucinate” as well as only marginal improvements in its natural language style. One thing that could benefit fashion, however, is OpenAI’s big new emphasis on health — the company wants users to consult ChatGPT like their doctor. But why does this affect fashion brands? Experts tell me that when users are confiding in the tool about their health, and it’s giving them useful recommendations, their trust in the tool will increase exponentially. Trust will likely then extend to other avenues, such as shopping queries and style advice. Let’s see how this plays out in the coming months.

The news: J Crew sparks backlash for unlabelled AI campaign imagery.

Why it matters: This week, newsletter Blackbird Spyplane published a visual investigation of J Crew’s latest campaign — the launch of a collab with Vans — in which the images gave a strong indication they’d been generated by AI. Spyplane managed to uncover the creator of the images — AI photographer Sam Finn. This sparked widespread backlash on social media and within fashion communities, partly because the brand hadn’t credited the use of AI for its images, and partly because, as Spyplane put it, J Crew had “used AI to counterfeit their own vibes”. The images in question resemble J Crew’s catalogue imagery from its late ’80s to early ’90s heyday, which made the use of AI for such an authentic vintage aesthetic even more puzzling to internet critics. The brand has yet to confirm its use of AI, but it did update the campaign instagram post to credit Finn for the “digital art”. (J Crew has not responded to Vogue Business’s request for comment on the campaign.) It’s the latest in a string of AI image controversies across fashion that shows just how thorny the issue is within creative communities. Is there a way that fashion brands can get AI images right?

The news: Meta partners with Midjourney on AI images and video.

Why it matters: Meta made its first move into AI image generation last year, when it launched image generation tool Imagine on its Facebook, Instagram and Messenger platforms. Now, it’s partnering with Midjourney — which is widely viewed as one of the best AI image generation tools on the market — to “bring beauty to billions”, according to chief AI officer Alexandr Wang. It’s the latest move from Meta in its huge AI investment push, and could now enable it to develop image and video products that compete with Google’s Veo and OpenAI’s Sora — and could impact the visual content consumers grow more accustomed to seeing on its social platforms.

The news: Meta is implementing an AI hiring freeze, according to a report from The Wall Street Journal.

Why it matters: After spending the past few months hiring over 50 AI researchers, Meta has hit pause, the tech giant confirmed to The Wall Street Journal. The hiring freeze coincides with a wider restructuring of Meta’s AI teams, which involves splitting them into four divisions. As AI becomes an increasing priority, businesses are not only competing in an AI talent war, but they are having to figure out the internal infrastructures, too. Already, investors are concerned about the stock-based compensation tech giants are offering AI talent, which could dilute shareholder value.

The news: Google adds agentic capabilities to AI Mode search function.

Why it matters: The agentic update allows AI Mode to make restaurant reservations with multiple constraints and preferences (“I only have an hour and need a quick lunch spot, any suggestions?”). The feature will soon expand to local service appointments and event tickets. The update signals a major step towards AI assistants functioning as agents and navigating real-world systems, rather than just a smart search engine. AI Mode has previously only been available in the US, the UK and India, but now Google has rolled it out to over 180 additional countries.

The news: Meta is offering AI translations for creators to expand their global reach.

Why it matters: Meta AI translations — a tool that dubs and lip-syncs reels on Facebook and Instagram into another language — will now be available for English to Spanish and Spanish to English translations, with further languages in the pipeline. The move has the potential to help creators grow audiences in new markets, boosting the creator economy even further.

The news: ChatGPT-5 launches for businesses.

Why it matters: Hot on the heels of OpenAI’s rollout of ChatGPT-5 to consumers and developers last week, the company has extended the model to its enterprise customers. Spanish bank BBVA and Zara owner Inditex have already adopted the updated tool — Inditex data and AI lead Oscar Mateos took to LinkedIn to say, “GPT-5 feels less like a tool and more like an expert collaborator who’s always one step ahead.” Who will be the first luxury conglomerate to adopt the upgraded tech?

The news: Stitch Fix announces AI shopping updates in personalisation push.

Why it matters: Stitch Fix is seeking a competitive edge as several dedicated, AI-powered personal styling startups burst onto the scene — including Daydream, which was founded by former Stitch Fix COO Julie Bornstein, and has so far raised $50 million in funding to support its development. Stitch Fix has previously deployed AI to understand personal style and predict trends, but claims that a new suite of AI-powered personal styling features will “increase personalisation, convenience and inspiration” for its users. The updated features include: an AI style assistant for customers, which uses generative AI to suggest outfit inspiration based on the taste profile it builds from their data over time; a “Stylist Connect” platform for customers to chat to human stylists; virtual try-on “personalised AI style visualisation”; and AI design integration for its private brands.

The news: OpenAI launches ChatGPT-5, touting its knowledge as a “major upgrade” from ChatGPT-4.

Why it matters: We’ve been waiting for this update for a while (the last GPT-4 update was in March 2023), and the developments within OpenAI’s technology are a key indicator of how far AI has come, and what brands should know it can do. In OpenAI CEO Sam Altman’s words, “GPT-3 sort of felt like talking to a high school student, GPT-4, maybe it was like talking to a college student. But with GPT-5, now it’s like talking to an expert, a PhD-level expert in anything, any area you need, on demand.” OpenAI also says its new model beats the LLMs from competitors Google, X and Anthropic. Perhaps most interestingly for brands, Open AI says the new model is more conversational than ever, which could have implications for customer interactions with their brands both in ChatGPT search for shopping, and their chatbot interactions.

The news: Pinterest CEO pitches the platform as an “AI-enabled shopping assistant”.

Why it matters: In the company’s second-quarter earnings call, Pinterest CEO Bill Ready said the app’s users don’t necessarily think of it as a shopping platform, but that its experiments with AI mean they’re actually getting proactive recommendations for products that “align with their taste and their style, the way a really great personal shopping assistant would”. Ready said the platform is also using multimodal AI (combining text and images), AI for visual search, and AI for conversational search. It’s one to watch for brands, as consumers move to more niche social platforms for product discovery.

The news: Google says AI search is increasing, not decreasing, traffic to websites — but doesn’t share data to back up its claims.

Why it matters: Some industry analysts suggest that the rise in AI-powered conversational search is decreasing organic traffic to websites. This week, Google rebuffed these claims as “inaccurate”. “Average click quality has increased and we’re actually sending slightly more quality clicks to websites than a year ago (by quality clicks, we mean those where users don’t quickly click back — typically a signal that a user is interested in the website),” Google’s head of search Liz Reid wrote in a blog post. Yet the blog cited no data — and the reports it was challenging do. Google isn’t the only AI-powered search engine, either. ChatGPT is increasingly being used for consumers’ shopping searches. AI optimisation is emerging among marketers to try to increase their sites’ chances of appearing in search — here’s what brands need to know about the nascent practice.

The news: Mark Zuckerberg says those without AI smart glasses will be at a “significant cognitive disadvantage” in future.

Why it matters: Meta had a big week last week, beating revenue and profit expectations in its second-quarter earnings. It’s good news for CEO Mark Zuckerberg, who has been investing heavily in AI, and will be wanting to reassure investors that the company is in a position to do so. Zuckerberg seized the good news opportunity to go in even harder on the company’s AI ambitions. Not only did he announce that the company’s AI models will soon reach human-like “superintelligence”, but he reinforced his belief that AI-powered glasses will be the primary way humans interact with AI in coming years.

“I continue to think that glasses are basically going to be the ideal form factor for AI," Zuckerberg told investors on the earnings call. “I think in the future, if you don’t have glasses that have AI — or some way to interact with AI — you’re probably going to be at a pretty significant cognitive disadvantage.” Meta has something of a first-mover advantage in the world of smart glasses, but Google, OpenAI and Apple are among the other Big Tech players investing in wearables’ AI promise. Read more about Meta’s smart glasses moves here.

The news: Experts say AI is developing much faster than expected.

Why it matters: We’re used to tech CEOs shouting about the potential of AI. But when experts including Nobel Prize winner Geoffrey Hinton say the technology is developing much faster than they ever anticipated, it adds even more fuel to the fire. Examples of AI models’ accelerating developments are everywhere: this week, Meta’s model began correcting itself.

Since Trump more or less deregulated the sector in the US, there’s barely anything standing in these companies’ way. This means global brands need to get to work on developing internal AI guardrails, especially if they’re handling lots of consumer data across jurisdictions (like the EU) that are stricter on AI.

The news: Apple says it is “very open” to acquisitions this year to catch up to competitors on AI.

The news: Google launches AI shopping mode in the UK.

Why it matters: Google launched its AI Mode search feature for shopping in the US in May, and the UK rollout this week indicates its plans to expand the number of consumers who shop using the feature — and fast. AI Mode uses Google’s generative AI tool to produce a chat-style interface for users, giving them a conversational search experience in which they can converse back and forth, and ask more specific questions. Three other AI shopping features rolled out on Google in the US — virtual try-on, Gemini-powered personalised shopping recommendations, and agentic price-match comparisons — are yet to be announced in the UK.

It’s particularly relevant for shopping. Some 80 per cent of consumers now rely on AI-written results for at least 40 per cent of their searches, according to Bain & Co. All this means ad agencies and marketing teams have shifted their focuses from SEO (search engine optimisation) to what’s been coined “AIO” (AI optimisation). Learn more about emerging AIO practices in fashion here.

The news: UK government signs “strategic partnership” with OpenAI in AI investment push.

Why it matters: The UK is eager not to get left behind in the so-called ‘AI race’ between the US, Europe and China, and this is the latest sign it’s keen to attract more investment to Britain’s AI sector. The government’s plans to use more of OpenAI’s technology to deliver public services will likely mean that the technology is trained on citizen data. In turn, OpenAI is planning on hiring more UK staff for its research and engineering teams, and increasing the size of its London office, as per the plan. ChatGPT maker OpenAI is currently one of the most powerful companies in the world, and President Trump’s new AI Action Plan shows how eager each government is to persuade the tech company — and its competitors — to develop their tech on their soil.

The news: Trump unveils US AI Action Plan and signs three AI executive orders.

Why it matters: The 28-page ‘AI Action Plan’ aims to build out the country’s AI infrastructure, cement America’s dominance in the industry and prohibit all federal agencies from using AI contractors that don’t comply with the White House’s definition of “ideological neutrality”. The new policies reverse several Biden-era federal AI safeguards related to DEI (diversity, equity and inclusion) and climate change, block state-level regulations on AI and further relax export rules so that global companies rely deeper on US-built AI. The move to get rid of existing AI regulations places further onus on individual companies to establish their own AI guardrails, especially if they operate across countries and jurisdictions. The US-centric policy also presents key challenges for fashion’s global supply chain and consumer base, which you can read more about here.

The news: OpenAI has shown some brands a pilot of a checkout feature that would enable users to complete purchases within its ChatGPT platform, according to a report by the Financial Times. It would charge brands commission for sales made this way.

Why it matters: When users search for products, ChatGPT currently shows recommendations with links to click through to brands’ own e-commerce sites. Bypassing this step opens up a clear revenue stream for OpenAI, but could significantly impact brands’ online sales. Those whose websites are picked up easier by ChatGPT would hold a significant advantage over those whose aren’t. No one’s quite sure what makes large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT tick yet, but there are some key practices emerging that could help brands optimise for AI search.

The news: WeTransfer has U-turned on plans to use UGC to train AI, after a revision in its terms of service caused widespread backlash.

Why it matters: Copyright protection has long been in place to safeguard creatives like photographers against their work being used without permission. Tech companies’ training of AI models on their work is proving a thorny issue within the fashion and creative industries, as it poses a risk of copies, duplication and direct competition — ultimately threatening their source of income. Given that WeTransfer is widely used within the creative industries, the company’s U-turn represents the perceived reputational risk that openly training AI models on creative work can cause.

The news: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has said the company will build a data centre “the size of Manhattan” to fuel its planned development of AI products.

Why it matters: It’s the latest in a string of moves from Meta — which owns Instagram, Whatsapp and Facebook — that demonstrate the scale of the investment it’s making in developing AI products. Data centres are hugely expensive to build and maintain, and the size of what Zuckerberg is suggesting would cost billions of dollars. Zuckerberg has been very bullish on the potential for the company’s AI smart glasses in particular, and talk of Meta buying a stake in its Ray-Ban Meta AI glasses co-creator EssilorLuxottica has intensified in the last month.

#6574. The Cheesecake Factory Drama, Explained

Welcome to Open Tab, a weekly column covering the news, gossip, and stories that have stayed open in my tabs all week. Last time we covered Italy’s looming food shortage.

Well, it’s over. Last Ditch, the bar in Greenfield, Massachusetts, that became the center of a tornado of scrutiny, ridicule, discourse, and, er, media coverage a few weeks ago is now closed as it searches for new co-owners, or to sell the bar to new owners. If your memory needs a refresh, the TL;DR is that the bar relaxed its COVID-conscious mask restrictions, and it tore the local community apart.

The Boston Globe covered the drama, and the story quickly went viral. But despite—or perhaps because of—its newfound infamy, the bar couldn’t attract enough clientele to stay open. Could new owners resurrect the beleaguered business?

Also in the discourse this week: Washington, DC residents will be voting on a foie gras ban which has prominent chefs coming out as firmly pro-foie, despite public backlash. José Andrés argues that the American food system also mistreats many other animals—and that we have bigger issues, like child hunger, to address.

Also in today’s Open Tab: why The Cheesecake Factory has made headlines this week, how salmon could decide Alaska’s midterm elections, a delivery platform acquisition for the ages, and a look inside LA’s buzzy Skywalker Grill.

This week the Cheesecake Factory’s name was splashed across headlines in a handful of national magazines and newspapers—a feat that hasn’t happened since…ever? It’s hard to say.

This story starts last weekend, when former president Barack Obama made a joke at a campaign rally in Ohio. “[President Trump’s] got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory. Just gold everywhere,” he said.

Trump himself responded on Monday. “For you to say it’s a Cheesecake Factory, that just shows why you were a lousy president,” he told reporters. The White House X account followed up with some AI-generated trolling.

Rick McCormack, the chain’s former vice president of design, also weighed in. “I think it’s a little bit sad that the pettiness of politics would create that sound bite, knowing all our challenges going on in the country today,” he said.

Is the Cheesecake Factory designed to look like it was done by an Egypt-obsessed kid with an unrestricted budget and a lot of ambition? Yes. But that’s part of its charm. You need a maximalist setting to match a maximalist menu, a maximalist experience. As I see it, The Cheesecake Factory is designed as it is so that ordering an “all day morning cocktail” (?), or a slice of “Brownie Crunch Choc-o-Lot Cheesecake” suddenly doesn’t seem so crazy. The Cheesecake Factory, as we were reminded again and again this week, is an American institution. So, unfortunately, is a quips-based, sound-byte-heavy political system.

And don’t feel too bad about the beleaguered corporate chain, which operates 200-plus locations. The C-suite is laughing their way to the bank: Stock analysts were quick to point out it is among the highest performing stocks on the market.

A few weeks ago a friend who grew up in Alaska told me nonchalantly that the state’s upcoming primary would be decided by salmon. “It’s the only thing that matters,” he said.. According to a recent feature in the New Yorker, it looks like he was right.

For many Alaskans fishing is both a job and a way to nourish their family. The democratic candidate, Mary Peltola, even settled on the slogan ““Fish, Family, Freedom.” But in recent years, runs of king salmon and chum salmon have collapsed, and don’t seem to be recovering. Experts point to climate change, but activists point to the practice of trawling—a method of fishing that includes pulling an enormous net behind the boat— for pollack which also catches millions of salmon which get killed and discarded by fishermen.

“This is an ecological crisis, a cultural trauma, an economic emergency and a public-health disaster,” reads one op-ed in an Alaskan paper.

Today in sentences that a Victorian tween wouldn’t understand a single word of: Delivery platform DoorDash, most recently in the news for its new fleet of drones, will buy Instacart for $17 billion.

It’s hard to overstate just how enormous this deal will be. Instacart is among America’s dominant platforms for grocery delivery, and DoorDash corners the market on the country's restaurant delivery apparatus.

The size of the acquisition would, under most administrations, attract FTC scrutiny. This is a pretty big consolidation in the field, after all. But the Trump administration has been particularly permissive of giant companies coming together to maximize their joint slay. In this case “joint slay” means market share and monopoly.

Museums must have a buzzy restaurant attached these days, and Los Angeles’s Lucas Museum of Narrative Art is no different. That’s where you’ll find Skywalker Grill, which, despite its monied environs, features a menu that’s surprisingly approachable. As Bon Appétit contributor Khushbu Shah tells us, it’s quickly become one of the city’s hottest tables. She takes us inside the restaurant to break down its surprisingly accessible menu.

#6572. The Truth About ‘Natural Flavors’ On Food Labels Might Surprise You

The word “natural” comes with a few caveats.

I consider myself a pretty diligent ingredient-label reader. But there’s one phrase I see constantly that, until recently, I hadn’t given much thought to: “natural flavors.”

It’s printed on everything from flavored drinks to packaged snacks, and it sounds pretty straightforward. You’d probably assume that if something contains natural flavors, those flavors come directly from the foods they’re supposed to taste like. After all, that’s what natural suggests—except the actual definition is much broader than you might expect.

According to the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), natural flavors can come from a surprisingly long list of sources, including fruits, vegetables, spices, herbs, dairy products, meat, seafood, and even certain fermentation products. And while those ingredients must come from qualifying sources, turning them into flavorings can be far more involved than simply squeezing juice from a fruit.

So what exactly does “natural flavors” mean, and how much does that label actually tell us about what’s in our food? Here’s what you should know.

The FDA’s definition of natural flavors focuses on where the flavoring comes from, not necessarily the food it’s supposed to taste like. Under federal regulations, natural flavors can include essential oils, extracts, distillates, and substances produced through roasting, heating, or enzymatic processing. They can originate from everything from fruit and vegetable juices to herbs, roots, bark, and fermentation products.

That means seeing “natural flavors” on a strawberry-flavored product doesn’t automatically mean the added flavoring came from strawberries.

Specific FDA rules govern how manufacturers describe flavors on the front of packages, particularly when a product’s recognizable flavor comes from sources other than the named food. But the generic ingredient-list declaration alone doesn’t identify the original source. In other words, the word “natural” doesn’t necessarily tell you what you’re tasting.

The FDA generally requires food manufacturers to list ingredients in descending order by weight. But flavorings are one category that can be declared collectively rather than listing every individual flavoring substance.

Under federal regulations, qualifying ingredients can simply appear as “natural flavor” or “natural flavors” on a product’s ingredient list. So manufacturers can use any combination of flavorings without disclosing the specific ones in your food.

There are exceptions, particularly for major food allergens, but the rule helps explain why the ingredient list doesn’t always provide a complete breakdown of a product’s flavor formulation.

The word “natural” tends to sound reassuring, especially when it’s printed on a product alongside claims about ingredients or quality. But it doesn’t automatically tell you anything about that food’s nutritional value.

According to the FDA, food ingredients must meet the same safety standard whether they’re naturally or artificially derived. The agency has also explained that its longstanding policy concerning the broader term “natural” on food labels was not intended to establish any particular nutritional or health benefit.

So while natural and artificial flavors differ in how they’re sourced, that distinction alone doesn’t establish that one is healthier, more nutritious, or safer than the other. And that feels like a pretty important distinction when you’re trying to make sense of the grocery aisle.

Another distinction worth knowing is that “natural” and “organic” don’t mean the same thing. The USDA has additional requirements for flavorings used in certified organic foods. Under federal organic regulations, manufacturers can use nonsynthetic flavors when organic flavors aren’t commercially available.

Those flavorings must come from organic or nonsynthetic sources and cannot be produced using synthetic solvents, synthetic carrier systems, or artificial preservatives. Those are additional restrictions beyond simply meeting the FDA’s definition of natural flavoring.

So while a conventional food and an organic food might both list natural flavors, that doesn’t necessarily mean the flavorings were produced under identical requirements.

The biggest takeaway is that natural flavors aren’t necessarily something to avoid. They’re just a lot less specific than many may assume. The label tells you that the flavoring meets the FDA’s definition of natural, but it doesn’t necessarily identify the ingredient it came from, explain how it was processed, or reveal every flavoring component. It also doesn’t automatically make the product healthier than something containing artificial flavors.

If you’re curious about what you’re eating, it helps to look beyond those two words. Check the full ingredient list, pay attention to how the product describes its flavor on the front of the package, and contact the manufacturer if you need more specific information about a flavoring’s source.

Ultimately, the most surprising thing about natural flavors is just how little those two words actually reveal.

#6571. Steak Bites With Spinach Couscous

A traditional steak dinner can feel like too much for a weeknight: too expensive, too likely to trip the smoke alarm, too fussy to cook to a perfect medium-rare. But cut a steak into bite-size pieces and suddenly it transforms into a quick-cooking protein that’s no more demanding than chicken breast or tofu. Rub the steak with the spices and make the quick no-recipe yogurt sauce a few hours ahead if it’s helpful with time management. To account for the extra liquid thrown off by the spinach as it cooks, the water-to-couscous ratio in this recipe differs from that often found on the back of the bag (or box) so measure accordingly.

More quick dinners this way: Spicy Chicken Lettuce Wraps; Gochujang Chicken Stir-Fry; and Easy Fish Tacos With Spicy Sauce.

Place 1–1¼ lb. boneless New York strip steak (1–1½" thick), cut into 1" pieces, 1 Tbsp. dried oregano, 2 tsp. onion powder, 2 tsp. sugar, and 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl; season generously with freshly ground pepper and toss to coat. Let sit at least 10 minutes or cover and chill up to 8 hours (no need to bring to room temperature before cooking if chilling).

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or medium Dutch oven with a tight-fitting lid over medium. Add 1 bunch scallions, thinly sliced, ½ cup finely chopped dill, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; cook, stirring occasionally, until scallions are softened, about 5 minutes. Add 10 oz. baby spinach in 2–3 handfuls, stirring and letting wilt slightly after each addition before adding more, 5–7 minutes total. Pour in 1 cup water and bring to a boil; season with more salt if needed. Add 1 cup Moroccan couscous and stir to break up any lumps. Remove from heat; quickly cover with lid and let sit 10 minutes.

Meanwhile, heat 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet, preferably cast iron, over high. Arrange steak in a single layer; cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 6–8 minutes. Reduce heat to medium; continue to cook, stirring often, until meat is just cooked through, about 1 minute more. Remove from heat. Add remaining 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; toss to combine. (Residual heat from pan will cook out any raw garlic flavor.)

Uncover couscous and fluff with a fork to separate grains. Spoon into a large shallow bowl or onto a platter. Top with steak. Cut 1 lemon into quarters and squeeze juice from 1 quarter over steak. Scatter thinly sliced cucumber and some dill sprigs on top; drizzle with oil.

Combine 1 cup plain whole-milk yogurt and a generous pinch of kosher salt in a small bowl; squeeze juice from 2 lemon quarters into yogurt. Stir to combine. If sauce is thick, stir in water, a spoonful at a time, to loosen.

Serve steak and couscous with yogurt sauce and remaining lemon quarter and more lemon wedges for squeezing over.

#6569. Apple Butter Snack Cake

Recipe by Margaret Knoebel, Milwaukee, Wisconsin

Made with apples and apple butter, this easy fall cake is just the thing when you need a sweet snack.

I know I’ve fallen into the autumnal magic of a fall farmer’s market when I walk away with too many apples, a jar of apple butter and no real plan for either. Luckily, our recipe tester Maggie Knoebel figured out how to combine both spoils into one super easy bake: an apple butter snack cake, complete with a brown butter glaze and cinnamon-sugar topping.

Preheat the oven to 350°F. In a large bowl, use a hand mixer or stand mixer to beat the eggs, sugar, apple butter, canola oil and vanilla extract.

In a separate bowl, whisk together the all-purpose flour, cinnamon, baking soda and salt. Add the flour mixture to the egg mixture and stir just until no streaks of flour remain. Fold in the apples and pecans.

Pour the batter into a greased 13×9-inch baking dish. Bake the cake until a toothpick inserted in the center comes out clean, 50 to 55 minutes. Cool the cake on a wire rack to room temperature.

Meanwhile, in a small, heavy saucepan, melt the butter over medium heat. Cook the butter until the milk solids are golden brown, stirring constantly, about 5 to 7 minutes. Immediately pour the brown butter into a mixing bowl to stop the cooking process or the butter will burn. Let the brown butter cool to room temperature.

Editor’s Tip: At some point during cooking, the butter will start to foam up. Don’t panic, it’s completely normal! Continue to stir while cooking, making sure to keep an eye on the butter’s color so you know when to take it off the heat.

Use a hand mixer or stand mixer to beat in the confectioners’ sugar until it’s fully combined with the brown butter. Spread the brown butter over the cake, then sprinkle the cinnamon-sugar mixture over the top before serving, if desired. Enjoy!

Store your apple butter snack cake in an airtight container in the fridge for up to four days. You really want to keep it well covered, so the glaze doesn’t absorb lingering fridge smells. If you want to keep the cake in the pan, cover the pan with storage wrap.

Yes, you can freeze apple butter snack cake. If you’re freezing the cake unfrosted, allow it to cool completely to room temperature, then cover the cake in storage wrap followed by aluminum foil. To freeze the glazed cake, place it in the freezer, uncovered, until the glaze is hard, about 30 minutes. Cover the cake with storage wrap and aluminum foil. Freeze the cake for up to two months and thaw overnight in the fridge.

Yes, you can bake an apple butter snack cake in a different-sized pan. Instead of a 13×9-inch baking dish, divide the batter evenly between two 8-inch square or two 9-inch cake pans. The baking time and temperature should be the same.

Yes, you can absolutely make this apple butter snack cake gluten- and/or dairy-free! Replace the all-purpose flour with a good gluten-free flour blend—one that’s designed as a cup-for-cup (or measure-for-measure) replacement. The cake is naturally dairy-free, but you’ll need to replace the butter in the glaze with vegan butter. You won’t be able to brown the vegan butter, so take 2 tablespoons off the measurement. That’s about how much liquid evaporates from butter when it’s browned.

#6566. Mussels With Garlicky Miso Broth

Mussels deserve your attention on weeknights. An affordable and accessible protein, they also happen to cook in less time than it takes to boil water. As the bivalves steam, they release a briny liquid, further perfuming the buttery, sake-fortified miso broth. Load up each bowl with a few good ladles, slurping every drop with an assist from crusty bread or warm rice. And why not enjoy the rest of the bottle of sake alongside your meal?

The seafood counter at your supermarket should sell rinsed and debarred mussels, but it’s easy to do at home. Discard any with cracked shells. Gently tap open raw mussels on a counter to see if they slowly close; if they do, those are okay to use. Swish them in a water-filled salad spinner or colander fitted inside a bowl, draining and refilling until water runs clear (give any especially dirty ones a scrub with a sponge). Use a towel to pull off the fibrous beard and set on a towel-lined tray in the fridge until you’re ready to cook.

More seafood dinners this way: Avgolemono Seafood Stew; Spaghetti alle Vongole; and Gorgeous Green Shrimp.

Place 2 Tbsp. scallions from 8 scallions, thinly sliced on a diagonal, in a small bowl and set aside for serving.

Melt 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large pot over medium heat. Add 8 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining scallions to pot and cook, stirring often, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 2 Tbsp. white miso paste and ½ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes (if using) and cook until miso is broken up and incorporated into butter, about 20 seconds. Pour in 1 cup dry sake or dry white wine and stir to combine, then add 3–3½ lb. mussels, scrubbed, debearded. Cover pot and increase heat to medium-high. Cook, shaking pot occasionally, until mussels open, 5–7 minutes (discard any that do not open). Remove pot from heat.

Squeeze 1 lemon half over mussels. Cut remaining 1 lemon half into wedges for serving. Taste broth and season with kosher salt if needed.

Ladle mussels and broth among shallow bowls, then scatter reserved scallions over. Serve with country-style bread or steamed white rice if desired and lemon wedges for squeezing over.

#6564. Fall Harvest Minestrone

Recipe by Margaret Knoebel, Milwaukee, Wisconsin

Our fall harvest minestrone trades summer’s vegetables for autumn’s produce. Break out the slow cooker!

You may be familiar with the usual cluster of summer vegetables in classic minestrone, but any Italian will tell you that real minestrone changes with the season. Italians like to prioritize whole, nutritious, in-season produce—especially those living in Italy’s blue zone, where some of the longest-living people eat minestrone every single day.

As we dive into fall, we’re taking our classic minestrone recipe with us and giving it a couple of tweaks. Our fall harvest minestrone ditches the zucchini, green beans, parsley, basil and spinach, and reflects what’s growing in the garden right now: sweet potatoes, onions, kale, sage and rosemary. We included Italian sausage, too, to enrich the broth and add a big boost of protein—enough for this fall soup to officially be considered dinner.

In a large skillet, cook the sausage over medium heat until it’s no longer pink, six to eight minutes, breaking it into crumbles with a wooden spoon. Drain the liquid from the skillet, then transfer the meat to a 6-quart slow cooker.

Stir in the beef broth, sweet potatoes, canned tomatoes, kale, onion, carrot, garlic, sage and rosemary. Cook the minestrone, covered, on low until the vegetables are tender, five to six hours.

Editor’s Tip: The sweet potatoes should be fork-tender before moving on to the next step.

Stir the pasta into the minestrone. Cook everything, covered, on low until the pasta is tender, 20 to 25 minutes longer.

Ladle the soup into bowls and serve. If desired, top the fall harvest minestrone with Parmesan cheese, red pepper flakes or fresh sage or rosemary.

Allow leftover fall harvest minestrone to cool completely to room temperature in under two hours. Transfer the soup to an airtight container and store it in the fridge for up to four days.

Yes, you can freeze fall harvest minestrone. Let the soup come to room temperature in under two hours, then ladle it into freezer-safe, airtight containers. Freeze the soup for up to two months. Thaw it overnight in the fridge before enjoying it again.

Yes, you can make fall harvest minestrone gluten free. Buy a box of good gluten-free pasta and make sure the Italian sausage is gluten free, too. I like to cook the gluten-free pasta separately when I suspect I’ll have leftovers. I add the pasta to individual bowls, then top it with the soup. Gluten-free noodles will absorb too much broth overnight, breaking down and becoming mushy.

The fall harvest minestrone has everything: vegetables, carbs and meat. It doesn’t really need anything else, but if you want to stretch the meal a bit, serve the soup with cornbread, biscuits (I love our garlic bread biscuits) or slices of crusty sourdough bread. Something like a vinegary salad will cut the richness a bit and bring in fresh flavor.

#6563. The Halloween Candy That Matches Your Zodiac Sign, According To An Astrologer

Whether you fully commit to spooky season or prefer to keep things low-key, you can’t truly celebrate Halloween without enjoying some candy. Different sweets have cultivated fierce brand loyalties. But the key to finding your favorite Halloween candy may be hiding among the stars.

We consulted astrologer and author Lisa Stardust to find which candy best reflects each zodiac sign's personality. From old-school chocolates to wild, wacky treats, her choices span the full sweet spectrum.

Aries is defined by its bold and ambitious approach to life. Stardust describes the cardinal fire sign as “passionate, electrifying, and intense.” But Aries can also be a bit impulsive. “You never know what you’re going to get next based on their emotions,” she adds.

In honor of Aries’ fiery spirit, Stardust chooses Hot Tamales as the candy that best reflects the sign. With its vibrant red hue, intense spice, and unapologetic cinnamon-forward flavor, there’s no better sweet to symbolize the sign.

Compared to Aries' bold energy, Taurus is decidedly more practical. The earth sign is known for being stable, dependable, and guided by logic over emotion. While Taurus may resist change, the sign also has good taste and knows its way around the finer things in life.

And what candy represents that tried-and-true energy better than a classic bar of Hershey’s milk chocolate? “They’re both iconic and never go out of style,” Stardust explains. “Their tastes might be simple, but they’re always decadent and indulgent.”

Gemini is the astrological embodiment of street smarts. The air sign is very astute, with the uncanny ability to read a room and adapt accordingly. This perceptiveness translates to strong social skills and the ability to elevate the mood of any room.

The candy that best reflects this energy is, unsurprisingly, Smarties. “Geminis are intellectual, and they have a little bit of zest to them,” explains Stardust. “They’re sugary and sweet but also a little messy.”

The cardinal water sign is not shy about expressing emotions. Cancers are best described as the teddy bears of the zodiac: sensitive, empathetic, and the embodiment of comfort. Those with Cancer in their chart are prone to shielding others from their complex emotions, but make no mistake—there are a lot of feelings.

A candy that matches Cancer’s mushy inner self is Reese’s Peanut Butter Cups. “They are very protective on the outside, but they're tender on the inside,” Stardust says.

Leo can’t help but be the life of the party. The fire sign is very extroverted, with a personality so big it verges on theatrical. Stardust describes Leos as “fun and flamboyant,” even if they sometimes get on other people’s nerves.

In her opinion, the sweets that represent Leo best are Twizzlers. Stardust notes that you “can have a lot of fun eating them,” whether it’s peeling them apart or biting off the ends to use as a straw. If it involves playing with your food, it’s perfect for Leo.

Virgos are Type A to their cores. The earth sign has a precise attention to detail and is always looking to solve problems. But the constant focus on logic and perfection often obscures a deep well of emotions.

“There’s more to them than you may think, and there’s definitely another flavor to them on the inside, because they’re ruled by Mercury,” Stardust explains. The candy that best mirrors this energy is a York Peppermint Patty. The seemingly simple chocolate exterior hides a sweet, sharp minty center (if that’s not Virgo, I don’t know what is).

Libra is represented by scales, which reflects the air sign’s desire for fairness and justice. The empathetic and compassionate Libra tends to consider all points of view to make the most measured decisions that’ll make everyone happy. (But sometimes, that may mean not making a decision at all.)

Libra’s balanced approach to life is why Stardust chooses Twix as their ideal candy. Left Twix or right Twix? Thankfully, Libra doesn’t have to choose. “They’re a package deal,” Stardust says. So whether they want to enjoy both or share with someone else, Libras are Twix’s target audience.

Scorpios embody the phrase, “looks like they could kill you, is a cinnamon roll.” The water sign is often misunderstood. While undoubtedly intense, Scorpio’s dark, almost brooding exterior hides a lot of emotional complexity.

The sign shares a lot of characteristics with one candy in particular: Sour Patch Kids. “They have a really deep personality to them; they’re sweet with a sharp, tangy bite.” And, like the multicolored gummy treats, Scorpio is the true manifestation of “sour, sweet, gone.”

Sagittarius is seemingly always on a journey—whether it be physical, emotional, or spiritual. The fire sign is known as an explorer, with lofty aspirations and an aversion to playing it safe.

This energy is exactly why Stardust chooses 3 Musketeers as the quintessential Sagittarius sweet. “The namesake is adventurous, and it speaks for itself,” she explains.

When you need someone reliable, responsible, and grounded, you can’t go wrong with a Capricorn. This pragmatic, logical earth sign is incredibly goal-oriented and has the Type A personality to make it happen.

How many licks does it take to get to the center of a Tootsie Pop? Capricorn may be the only sign in the zodiac that’s disciplined enough to find out, which is why Stardust chooses the lollipop as their ideal candy. “It’s a classic, just like Capricorn,” she says. “They’re traditional, steady, strong, and you have to have patience to eat them.”

Aquarius marches to the beat of its own drummer. The air sign loves to be a contrarian and will unapologetically take the road less traveled. Nothing is too unique or too strange for Aquarius.

And what candy matches that energy better than a bag of Pop Rocks? “They’re unexpected and veer from the norm of traditional candy,” Stardust explains. They’re shocking, surprising, and delightful in their own special way—just like Aquarius loves to be.

Pisces always seems to have its head in the clouds. The water sign has a dreamy, romantic approach to life and has an extremely vivid imagination. “They feel all the feels,” Stardust explains.

Pisces needs a candy that can keep up mentally and emotionally, which is why she chooses Skittles as their ideal sweet. “It’s all about the rainbow and the imagination,” Stardust says. “They get to taste the rainbow and all of the sensations in every bite.”

#6562. Butternut Pasta With Sausage and Dates

Squash and sausage are a heroic autumnal pairing, especially in a weeknight-friendly pasta. Butternut is the easiest squash to source—not to mention easily found peeled and chopped (a blessing for those with more timid knife skills). But other winter squash like acorn or red kuri can stand in as desired. Whichever squash you select, a sharp, heavy chef’s knife is best for breaking down the chunky veg. But to make your life easier, microwave the squash for 1 to 2 minutes. It will slightly soften, making it simpler—and safer—to slice through.

Rigatoni’s ribbed surface and large holes help chunky squash sauce cling and bites of seared sausage and date wedge—opting for a nutty whole wheat variety will only add to this meal’s autumnal earthiness.

More cozy pastas this way: Balsamic Mushroom and Sausage Pasta; Creamy Red Curry Pasta; and Baked Feta Pasta With Green Sauce.

Cook 1 medium butternut squash (1½–2 lb.), peeled, halved, seeds removed, cut into 1" pieces (about 6 cups), in a large pot of boiling salted water until very tender, 12–14 minutes. Using a slotted spoon, transfer squash to a medium bowl. Reduce heat to low, cover pot, and leave on burner to keep warm.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium Dutch oven over medium-high. Add 1 lb. hot or sweet Italian sausage, casings removed, and break up into small pieces with a wooden spoon. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, about 3 minutes. Continue to cook, stirring occasionally, until browned all over and just cooked through, 3–4 minutes more. Transfer to a plate with a slotted spoon.

Reduce heat to medium-low. Cook 3½ oz. Medjool dates (about 6), pitted, sliced lengthwise ¾" thick, in same pan, turning halfway though, until deeply browned, 3–4 minutes. Transfer to plate with sausage; season with salt.

Add remaining 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil to pan. Add 6 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and reserved squash. Cook, scraping up browned bits and smashing squash with spoon to break up, until lightly browned and broken up into a chunky paste (pieces do not need to be even), about 5 minutes.

Meanwhile, return cooking liquid in reserved pot to a boil over high heat. Cook 12 oz. short tube pasta (such as rigatoni) until very al dente, about 3 minutes less than package directions (it will finish cooking in sauce). Drain, reserving 3 cups pasta cooking liquid.

Add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid to squash and break up squash with spoon until a saucy consistency. Add pasta, another 1 cup pasta cooking liquid, and reserved sausage and dates. Increase heat to medium-high; cook, adding more pasta cooking liquid as needed, until pasta is al dente and coated in sauce, 2–3 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 1 Tbsp. sherry vinegar or balsamic vinegar. Taste pasta and add more vinegar, salt and/or pepper if needed.
