#6561. Jenny Kee and the Untold Story of Chanel’s Original Australian Debut

It's everything that anyone who loves fashion Down Under can talk about right now: when Matthieu Blazy brings his resort collection to Sydney this November, it will be the first time Chanel has ever shown in Australia.

What relatively few people know, however, is that this landmark moment will not, by a long shot, be the first time Australia has shown in Chanel.

That moment happened 44 years ago, on October 18, 1982, at the Louvre in Paris. Halfway through a Chanel show that, until then, had been dominated by powerfully pastel and friskily high-hemmed interpretations of Coco Chanel’s canonical bouclé suit, something never before seen began to appear on the models who walked out in front of a line of Chanel-branded wardrobes.

It was a print, mostly on white, but sometimes on black, composed of an apparently haphazard accumulation of shapes. Their interiors were fractured into visually immersive pools and veins of cobalt, scarlet, yellow and blue. This pattern appeared first in flashes, then took over entire dresses, as well as jackets, bags, shoes and more. And then, on one white background ruffle-detailed dress, the apparent abstraction resolved itself into something very tangible: across a model’s torso ran the unmistakable outline of Australia.

Chanel spring/summer ’83 with a Kee print showing an outline of Australia. Image credit: Getty Images.

The print was the creation of the then-35-year-old Bondi-born fashion trailblazer Jenny Kee, who is of Chinese, Italian and English heritage, and deeply Australian in sensibility. Kee has been acknowledged in the past—not least, and quite rightly, by herself—as the author of the prints Chanel used that season. In 1983, the year of Coco Chanel’s centenary, the house presented, through Vogue Australia, a Chanel suit featuring Kee’s Opal print in the lining and lapels to the National Gallery of Victoria, where it is displayed online with full and correct attribution.

Yet the story of how an Australian designer came to play a key role in a Chanel collection that, despite being largely forgotten, was one of the most significant in its entire history has, until now, never been fully told. Fashion moves fast and always faces forward; unless preserved, details will fall away as freely as loosely applied sequins from a dress in motion.

Back in 1982, I was living with my mother in the Blue Mountains, where Kee was a neighbour and close family friend. Her brush with Chanel was probably the first fashion story I ever encountered. So, to mark Blazy’s arrival in Sydney, I decided to try to piece it back together and, in the process, discovered a few details even Kee herself was unaware of. As she said when I called her at home up in the mountains this October: “Darl, I had no bloody idea!”

Unlocking the circumstances behind Kee’s cameo for Chanel takes us first to London, where, by 1968, she was living. That December, she appeared naked on the cover of Oz magazine—edited by my late uncle Richard Neville—while working with fellow Australian Vernon Lambert, the visionary vintage dealer whose stall at the Chelsea Antique Market on the King’s Road was helping to rewrite the rules of fashion. Lambert was Kee’s mentor, and when she returned to Australia in 1972, she was ready to start something new.

She opened the Flamingo Park Frock Salon in Sydney’s Strand Arcade and, together with Linda Jackson, began building a fashion language whose point of reference was Australia itself: its opals, native flowers, fauna, bushfires, rainforests and the Great Barrier Reef. “We were doing a completely Australian beauty,” she says. “We were so fresh and so completely pure and so in love with Australia. We were devoted to our country and making beauty of it.”

Chanel spring/summer’83. Image credit: Getty Images.

When Kee and Jackson took that work to Milan in 1977, it caused a sensation. Kee remembers arriving at a party thrown by the Italian stylist and publicist Nally Bellati: “Linda and I walked in and, honestly and truly, they all started jumping on the tables and clapping us, because they’d never seen anything like it,” Kee recalls.

Among those who applauded was Anna Piaggi, the Italian fashion editor who happened to be another one of Lambert’s protégées. In a 1977 issue of Vogue Italia, Piaggi dedicated a double-page spread to Kee and Jackson’s designs under the headline: ‘Fashion arrived from another hemisphere.’ “Anna was bedazzled by what Linda and I were doing back in Australia,” says Kee. The article was accompanied by a sketch of Piaggi wearing Kee’s wool designs—it was drawn by Karl Lagerfeld.

Vogue Italia 1977 featured Kee in her own designs, along with Linda Jackson. Image credit: courtesy Vogue Italia.

Piaggi and Lambert were extremely close to Lagerfeld, who was inspired by Lambert’s habit of always carrying a vintage fan and regularly drew the elaborate outfits Piaggi assembled each day. Kee was entering a tight creative orbit whose members were already constantly looking at, wearing and exchanging one another’s discoveries. In 1977, Kee and her 22-month-old daughter Grace—my oldest friend—were also on a train between Sydney and the Blue Mountains that crashed, killing 83 of their fellow passengers. During their recovery from that neardeath experience, Kee was inspired to sketch Opal and several of her other most famous designs.

Back in Milan in 1980, Kee remembers showing these designs at the home of Piaggi and Lambert, with Manolo Blahnik also present. Lambert then introduced her to Fabio Bellotti of Rainbow Fabrics in Milan. As Kee’s graphics became too detailed and elaborate to realise in knitwear alone, Bellotti—who had long worked with designers including Giorgio Armani and Lagerfeld—was the perfect partner for transferring those designs into print.

Jenny Kee with Fabio Bellotti of Rainbow Fabrics in the 1980s. Image credit: courtesy Jenny Kee.

One of those designs was Opal. Developed around the shimmering colours and fractured structures of the Australian gemstone, it became central to Kee and Jackson’s 1981 Flaming Opal collection. This was the print that eventually caught Lagerfeld’s eye one day when he was in the Rainbow Fabrics office looking for fabrics for a very important new collection.

Daniela Morera, Bellotti’s wife, remembers Lagerfeld encountering Kee’s samples through her husband. “Karl fell in love,” she says of the Opal design. Like Kee, she also suggests that Piaggi and Lambert may have helped draw Lagerfeld’s attention to her work.

Kee remembers what happened next very clearly. Bellotti called her in Australia to say Lagerfeld wanted to use the print for Chanel. She immediately agreed. “Apparently, when Karl saw Opal, that’s when he went, ‘Bingo, I want that,’” she says. “And then he proceeded to do it in 65 different ways.”

By October 1982, Chanel itself was in transition. The house had launched ready-to-wear under Philippe Guibourgé in 1978, but its owner, Alain Wertheimer, was already looking for a designer who could rejuvenate a fashion image that had become dusty and out of touch following the death of Coco Chanel in 1971 and amid the emergence of the Japanese new wave and homegrown upstarts such as Jean Paul Gaultier. Wertheimer’s eye settled on Lagerfeld and, in September 1982, Chanel announced that Lagerfeld would become its designer of couture, starting in January 1983. According to MarieLouise de Clermont-Tonnerre, then a senior Chanel communications executive, Lagerfeld ghost-designed the October 1982 collection, with Hervé Léger and Eva Campocasso—previously both assistants of Lagerfeld at Fendi and Chloé respectively—serving as its public-facing designers as his contract with Chloé wound down.

Vernon Lambert in Rome in the early 1980s with Chanel bag and shoes using Kee’s prints from spring/summer ’83. Image credit: courtesy Jenny Kee.

This subterfuge was only casually maintained. Writing in The New York Times on the day of the show, Bernadine Morris reported: “Merely a whisper of a Karl Lagerfeld connection was enough to bring out the crowds and the tension … it has been rumoured that he had something to do with the ready-to-wear presented this morning as part of the spring and summer showings here … The Lagerfeld touch seems apparent in the pearl earrings in the shape of the numbers 5 and 19, both names of Chanel perfumes. For the rest, no-one is saying just how much he did. ‘Consultant’ is as far as his friends will go.”

Back in Blackheath, Kee had no idea any of this was happening. When I tell her that the Chanel collection in which her Opal print appeared was, in effect, Lagerfeld’s covert first act for the house, she laughs. “Darl, I had no bloody idea!” Then, delighted: “I love the fact he was ghosting it. It makes it even more interesting—and it means that my print played a part in his first-ever work for Chanel.”

I also show her a picture from a misdated cache of runway images that appears to show a second Kee print, Mali Oz, on the Chanel runway in a dress and handbag worn with an Opal jacket. Kee is astonished. “I’ve never seen that before!” she says. The National Gallery of Australia records that Chanel also used Kee’s Mali Oz fabric.

Whatever the details, Kee’s role also hints at Lagerfeld’s larger creative project: keeping the codes of Chanel intact while applying startling points of difference to push them into another register. “He thought, I’ll just do something really outrageous here,” Kee says, remembering the collision of her print with “that pale pink, old-fashioned Chanel”.

The result changed Kee’s life. “It helped me enormously,” she says. “In that one year, 1982, I was showing at Chanel, and a few months earlier Princess Di was wearing my koala jumper. So those two moments really helped set me on the road. I’m eternally grateful to Chanel and Karl, to Fabio and Daniela, to Anna and Vern. One way or another, they all helped lift me up.”

The Kee Chanel connection was well reported in Australia at the time, and cemented by the Vogue Australia-facilitated Chanel x Kee donation to the NGV. Outside of Australia, however, the strongest contemporary credit to Kee was delivered by another old friend, photographer Bill Cunningham, who dedicated one of his New York Times pages in August 1984 to Kee’s designs for Chanel citing her prominently. One of his photographs was of then Chanel American president Kitty D’Alessio wearing a Kee/Lagerfeld/Chanel spring/summer ’83 jacket. The page features Kee’s Opal and Mali Oz prints on Chanel pieces.

A Chanel jacket lined with Kee’s Opal print from Chanel spring/summer ’83. Image credit: Courtesy Jenny Kee. Powerhouse Collection. Purchased 1999. Photograph Nitsa Yioupros

Nearly half a century later, Chanel is finally touching down in the country that inspired the prints in the first collection Lagerfeld created as he set the house towards its current position at the pinnacle of fashion. Kee is a huge fan of Blazy. “I love his work,” she says. “He’s really standing up to Karl and doing his own thing now.” Coming from Kee—a woman who has spent her very big life doing her very unique thing—that is high praise indeed.

This story appears in Vogue Australia’s November 2026 issue, on sale from November 2.

#6560. The Starbucks Bearista Cup Is Coming Back—with an Early Surprise Edition

The little glass bear is headed back to Starbucks, and this year, it's bringing company.

Starbucks knows how to make a holiday coffee run feel like an occasion. The seasonal drinks return, the cups get a festive makeover, and even a quick stop for caffeine feels a little more special.

Last year, though, one cup became a holiday event of its own. The Bearista Glass Cold Cup—a glass cup shaped like a bear—sold out quickly and began appearing on resale sites for hundreds and even thousands of dollars. That’s a lot of attention for a cup, even one as cute as this! The bear was popular enough that Walmart even sold a lookalike.

For anyone who missed out on all the fun last year, though, we have some good news. Starbucks is bringing the Bearista Bear back, along with a new collection of mystery cups.

The original Bearista Glass Cold Cup returns to select Starbucks coffeehouses on Dec. 1, just in time for holiday gifting. The bear-shaped glass comes with a green beanie-shaped lid and striped straw, ready to hold your cold brew.

After the cup sold out last year, Starbucks offered thousands more as prizes in its holiday game. This time, you’ll be able to look for the original in coffeehouses again.

Look for the original Bearista cup at select Starbucks locations starting Dec. 1. Starbucks hasn’t shared how many will be available, but given how quickly they sold out last year, you may want to check your local store early.

Before then, there’s another opportunity for Bearista fans. On Nov. 10, Starbucks is releasing a Glass Bearista Cold Cup Surprise Box Edition, featuring a collection of festive characters. Each one comes in a sealed box, so you won’t know which bear you have until you open it.

The surprise boxes will be available in limited quantities, while supplies last.

Are you going to be in line in December to get a bear cup of your own? Let us know in the comments below!

#6559. 21 Easy Weeknight Dinners for November

As daylight dwindles and the November chill settles in, dinner calls for something cozy. Think chicken thighs nestled into caramelized onions, pasta slicked with brown butter, and hearty soups that practically demand a hunk of crusty bread. It’s time to lean into comfort food.

The good news? You don’t need to spend your whole Sunday cooking to make dinner feel special, so you’ll have plenty of time for that When Harry Met Sally rewatch. These 21 easy weeknight dinners deliver all the comfort without the commitment. There’s a three-ingredient pumpkin soup, gochujang chicken that gets a quick blast under the broiler, and a smoky one-pan pasta made with pantry staples. Plus a few Thanksgiving-adjacent flavors—sage, stuffing, squash—because the holiday is right around the corner.

Greek yogurt tenderizes the chicken quickly, but the real weeknight win is the broiler: just 15 minutes under high heat, and you’ve got dinner.

Juicy chicken meatballs and crisp-tender sesame green beans roast on opposite sides of the same sheet pan, streamlining both dinner prep and cleanup.

This speedy stir-fry recipe brings together thin strips of boneless pork shoulder and crisp-tender bok choy for a satisfying, weeknight-ready dinner.

Savory ground beef, fluffy scrambled eggs, and crisp vegetables turn a bowl of steamed rice into a satisfying Japanese dinner that’s ready in 35 minutes.

Give boxed stuffing mix a new lease on life with this clever, holiday-inspired crust. Mixed with Parmesan, lemon zest, parsley, and butter, it gives tender fish a golden, crispy topping. Genius.

Brushed with a sticky, sweet teriyaki sauce, then hurled under the broiler, this salmon develops a glossy, caramelized finish in a matter of minutes.

This easy sheet-pan dinner pairs tender cod with a savory chorizo topping. Big flavor, minimal effort, and only one pan to wash.

Canned chickpeas and frozen spinach make this richly spiced saag quick to prepare—and any leftovers taste even better the next day.

Inspired by satay, this saucy, lip-smacking tofu dish comes together in 30 minutes in just one skillet—so cleanup is a breeze.

Cheesy, creamy, and deeply comforting, these fondue-inspired beans bring a little alpine indulgence to an ordinary Tuesday. Serving them over crusty bread is a must.

Nutty brown butter, crunchy pecans, and hot Italian sausage make this an easy dinner bursting with fall flavors. One reader reports, “Made me feel like a 5-star chef.”

Buttery, garlicky shrimp scampi meets pasta in this weeknight-friendly dinner. A splash of white wine and a pinch of red pepper flakes make the sauce sing.

Canned butternut squash purée (find it by the canned pumpkin!) makes this cozy, cold-weather recipe come together in a snap. Vegetable broth and certified vegetarian parm keep it meat-free, but chicken broth works if that’s what you’ve got.

Four ingredients are all you need for these grown-up buttered noodles. Toasted almonds and parsley are totally optional, but add welcome texture and zing.

Pumpkin purée adds richness, body, and a gentle orange hue to this speedy ground beef chili, letting the flavors of the spices and aromatics shine.

Roasted squash, crispy bacon, and crunchy walnuts turn chopped salad into a proper fall dinner. Use pre-cut butternut squash to streamline prep.

This comforting chicken noodle soup is ideal for chilly evenings or sick days. Chicken breast, kabocha squash, and tiny ditalini cook right in the broth.

A vegetarian spin on the classic Reuben swaps in hearty kale for the meat but keeps the melty cheese and tangy sauerkraut. One reader reports, “I didn’t miss the pastrami one bit.”

Made almost entirely from pantry ingredients—S&B curry powder, red lentils, crushed tomatoes, and coconut milk—this cozy soup is, as one reviewer puts it, “way more delicious than it should be.”

When dinner needs to get on the table pronto, a tuna melt is hard to beat: pantry-friendly, cheesy, and comforting.

This fiery soup has a shockingly trim ingredient list: curry paste (we like Maesri), a can of pumpkin purée, and coconut milk. Perfect for busy November weeknights.

#6557. Creamy Miso Mushroom Pasta

Mushroom fans: Bookmark this recipe immediately. It will give you everything you want when you crave a creamy mushroom pasta as soon as the crisp fall air sets in. The hardworking trio of miso, Parmesan, and touch of soy sauce delivers an umami bomb of flavor that doesn’t overwhelm, but magnifies, the best of earthy mushrooms. Coupled with luscious noodles enrobed in a creamy (but not heavy) sauce, what’s not to love?

A few helpful notes for pasta success: (1) While any pasta will work, egg-based noodles, like the fettuccine I recommend here, are the best complement to the sauce. The nests (Rummo and De Cecco are great accessible brands) cook far faster than standard straight pasta, almost as fast as fresh. (2) Don’t be afraid to season your mushrooms! Yes, I know this goes against all that we’ve learned about salting them too early in the cooking process, but just a bit of salt will get them going and releasing their water faster for eventual crisp-browned edges. Don’t be alarmed if you see a pool of water at the start of the mushroom cooking—that’s to be expected and just keep going until it evaporates. (3) Don’t forget to reserve plenty of pasta cooking liquid, which is critical to the eventual sauce’s success. I prefer transferring the al dente noodles from the pasta pot to the skillet, letting any residual water come with it (and to ensure you don’t accidentally drain away that liquid gold).

Find more fall favorite meals here: Weeknight Pumpkin Chili; Cream-ish of Mushroom Soup; Mushrooms au Poivre.

Cook 12 oz. egg-based pasta (such as fettuccine nests) in a large pot of boiling salted water, stirring occasionally, until al dente, about 1 minute less than package directions.

Meanwhile, heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet over high. Add 1 lb. crimini or mixed mushrooms (such as button, maitake, oyster, and/or shiitake), sliced ¼" thick or torn into bite-size pieces, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt and toss to coat evenly. Spread out into an even layer and cook, undisturbed, until mushrooms are starting to release their liquid, 2–3 minutes (do not be alarmed; there will be a lot). Continue to cook, tossing occasionally, until moisture is almost completely evaporated and edges of mushrooms are starting to brown, 6–8 minutes.

Reduce heat to medium-high; add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Cook, tossing often, until garlic is fragrant and golden, 1–2 minutes. Pour in ¾ cup dry white wine, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan with a sturdy spatula or flat-edged wooden spoon, and cook until wine is mostly evaporated (you should have about 1 Tbsp. liquid left in pan), about 4 minutes. Reduce heat to medium-low. Add 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, cut into pieces, and 2 Tbsp. white miso and stir until melted and combined. Slowly pour in ½ cup heavy cream, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan; simmer until thickened slightly, 2–3 minutes. Add 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce; season with freshly ground pepper. Taste and add more salt if needed.

Using tongs, transfer pasta to mushroom mixture and add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid. Increase heat to medium and bring to a simmer. Cook, tossing constantly and adding ½–1 cup more pasta cooking liquid to reach desired sauce consistency if needed, until pasta is al dente and liquid has thickened slightly, about 3 minutes.

Remove pan from heat. Add 1 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about ½ cup) to pasta and toss to combine. Season generously with more pepper; taste and season with more salt if needed.

Divide pasta among shallow bowls and top with more Parmesan and pepper.

#6556. One-Dish Red Curry Noodles

Recipe by Susan Bronson, Rhinelander, Wisconsin

This one-dish red curry noodles recipe is packed with pantry and freezer staples, making it perfect as a dump-and-bake weeknight dinner.

I’m not quite sure where the time goes between school bus drop-off and dinnertime, but I’m pretty sure there’s a fast-forward button involved. Suffice it to say, quick and easy weeknight dinner recipes are life-savers. Easy casserole recipes made with pantry staples are some of my favorites, and dump-and-go recipes—which just require one dish—are even better. This one-dish red curry noodles recipe checks all those boxes: It’s a casserole; it takes just 45 minutes from start to finish; and it’s made with chewy udon noodles, colorful fresh and frozen vegetables, and a rich and spicy red coconut curry sauce.

Easy prep, minimal mess, quick to bake and something my whole family will eat? That’s a real win in my book.

Preheat the oven to 375°F. In a 13×9-inch casserole dish, stir together the vegetable stock, coconut milk, red curry paste, soy sauce, ginger, sesame oil and minced garlic.

Add the udon noodles and use a fork to carefully separate them into a single layer.

Top the noodles with the sliced red pepper, frozen stir-fry vegetables and finely shredded cabbage.

Submerge the noodles and vegetables in the liquid as much as possible.

Cover the dish tightly with foil and bake it for 20 minutes. Uncover the casserole dish and stir the noodles and vegetables. Return it to the oven, uncovered, and cook until the noodles are tender, about 15 to 20 minutes. Top the red curry noodles with green onions and sesame seeds, and serve them with lime wedges.

Editor’s Tip: When you pull the dish out of the oven the first time, take special care to separate any clumped noodles.

Any leftover red curry noodles should be stored in an airtight container in the refrigerator.

When stored properly in the fridge, leftover one-dish red curry noodles last up to four days.

For the best flavor and texture, plan to serve this dish directly after baking it. However, you can prep the casserole up to 24 hours in advance, waiting to submerge the noodles in the sauce until just before it goes in the oven.

Unfortunately, this one-dish red curry noodles is not ideal for freezing. There’s a chance that the coconut milk will separate when thawed, leading to a grainy texture. Additionally, the softer texture of the cooked noodles will likely lead to a mushy texture once thawed.

This recipe calls for udon noodles, which are a thick type of Japanese noodle made with wheat flour. These thicker noodles hold up well in the hot oven, and retain their plump and chewy texture. You could also use egg noodles or lo mein noodles—even spaghetti will work in a pinch! Rice noodles are also an option, although the cook time will likely need to be shorter.

Pump up the protein in this noodle dish by adding cubed or shredded chicken, shrimp or ground pork. For plant-based protein, you can add cubed tofu, edamame, chickpeas or cannellini beans.

Whichever veggies you like best! A few of my family’s favorites include sliced bell peppers, broccoli, green beans and sugar snap peas. Frozen veggie stir-fry mixes, which commonly include broccoli, baby corn, water chestnuts and sugar snap peas, are a great short-cut too.

#6554. The Easiest Exercise for Longevity, According to Science

A few months ago, I had never so much as lifted a barbell—let alone thought about the exercises for longevity. However, during a stay at Buchinger Wilhelmi Clinic, I attended a life-changing lecture by Felipe Isidro, professor of physical education and CEO of Physical Exercise & Health Consulting. That was the day everything changed.

“Who here works out?” Isidro started. “When I say ‘work out,’ I don’t mean normal physical activities like walking, climbing stairs, and carrying shopping bags. I mean ‘exercise,’ which is movement that is both planned and scheduled. I ask, because 7 out of 10 people don’t: that’s 70% of the population.”

Of course, any physical activity is better than none. “But you don’t get the same benefits as with exercise,” Isidro explained. “The ideal, instead, is to combine both—to move more on a daily basis and to set aside specific time for training. In a society that invites us to move less and less with cars, elevators, and escalators, the objective should be to exercise—and, especially, to do strength training.”

Up until then, I had never thought of the true importance of exercise: I’d only thought of it as a means to an end—to lose weight and, ideally, to look better in my clothes. Although it is true that exercise can help on both accounts, Isidro allowed me to see that neither of those are as important as keeping the body’s muscles and mitochondria healthy for as long as possible. “The mitochondria are like little batteries that produce the energy that impact vitality,” Isidro explained. “When the mitochondria work well, we feel strong; when they deteriorate, we feel fatigued. It’s also difficult to burn fat, even when we diet. Fat does not only accumulate under the skin, but also in organs, viscera, and even in the muscle itself.”

Here, there is no miracle pill—the only “medicine” proven to improve mitochondrial function is exercise, and especially strength training. Just as a cell phone battery lasts for hours when it’s new but loses its ability to hold a charge, the same thing happens with mitochondria—as we age, we may wake up with energy, but feel exhausted by mid-morning. Thus, we must keep our mitochondria as healthy as possible.

Within the muscle there are slow twitch fibers and fast twitch fibers— slow twitch fibers are responsible for prolonged efforts such as walking; fast twitch fibers are essential for power and speed.

As we age, fast twitch fibers are the first to decline. “Walking improves endurance, but it doesn’t stop the loss of fast twitch fibers. If you don’t train strength, you become sluggish. We see it in older people, who end up walking in short steps because they have lost those fibers. Strength training is the only way to keep them,” Isidro points out. “We gain muscle until the age of 25, maintain it until the age of 35 and, from then on, we start to lose it slowly, accelerating from the age of 50, and even more at the age of 65. There are cases of people in their 70s who maintain the strength of someone sedentary in their 40s or 50s thanks to daily training, proving that this habit can subtract up to 20 years from biological age.”

After all, what you don’t use, you lose. That goes for muscle—but also for bones, the respiratory system, and the pelvic floor. Regular exercise also improves the non-REM phase (deep sleep in which the eyes do not move), and that also decreases with age. Having longer non-REM phases is related to gradual and healthy aging. “Strength training is an investment in health for the future,” Isidro says. “It reduces anxiety and it makes us feel better at all levels. In reality, a healthy body is a perfect body.”

While water is essential for our hydration, too much of it can cause us to drown. Strength training is similar: the proper dosage is key. It’s not about doing it in excess; it’s about doing it right. The right dose, says Isidro, means few repetitions, lots of recovery time, and, above all, not looking to fatigue. “Many people think that, if they don’t get tired, they haven’t trained properly. It’s actually just the opposite. In strength, we’re not looking to exhaust ourselves, we’re looking for quality.” To that end, here are seven points to keep in mind in order to strength train properly, no matter your age or fitness level.

The minimum for adaptation is two days a week, although the ideal scenario would be to progress to three or four with breaks in between—one day on, one day off. You should also do strength before endurance; if you do both on the same day, it’s best to finish with cardio.

If you’re new to working out, it’s best to focus on the legs. They are the largest reservoir of muscle mass in the body and also the quickest to deteriorate. In addition, the legs contain a lot of fast twitch fibers, so training them is vital.

Do reps at a high intensity (quickly) to work the fast twitch fibers. It is recommended to do a few repetitions—half or less of the maximum you can do—to avoid fatigue. “The key is speed and intensity, because that’s what activates the fast fibers through the nervous system,” says Isidro.

Give yourself plenty of time to rest between sets. At minimum, rest time should be one minute, but two or three minutes between exercises is even better. “You’re fully recovered when you can speak and sing, not just utter and grunt monosyllables,” says Isidro.

“It is essential that the exercise be non-exhausting or fatiguing. When you fatigue, you’re working the slow twitch fiber and continuing to lose fast twitch fibers,” says Isidro. “It’s better to do a few exercises well and repeat them a couple of times. Stop before fatigue sets in.”

Start with short workout sessions that last five to 15 minutes. Do them in circuit format, alternating exercises with breaks. “We all have 10 minutes a day if we prioritize. Forget your previous experience—many of us think that exercise should be tiring and painful to work. If we do less, we enjoy it more and see the benefits, creating a positive ripple effect.”

Working the respiratory muscles is also essential, because it improves recovery and endurance. Take long, full breaths, breathing into the diaphragm.

According to Isidro, the best time to exercise is in the morning. “This stimulates the sympathetic system early, which makes it easier for the parasympathetic system to be stimulated in the evening, improving sleep.” If possible, exercise outdoors, because contact with nature and socialization have a direct effect on health.

You don’t need a full gym to get the benefits. Working out with your own body weight can be really effective. “The important thing is that the exercises are adapted to your fitness level so that you can repeat and maintain them over time,” Isidro says. “And if you can do them in a group or with friends, even better. Socializing motivates, engages, and, as studies show, lengthens life.”

There are several simple tests that can be done at home in order to check our current strength level and to show us where we may need to improve. “The important thing about these tests is not only to know where we are, but also to measure how we are progressing,” notes Isidro. “Sometimes the change is perceived in how we feel, but other times we need objective data, and these are very simple tools that allow us to tangibly see how strength training is helping us improve.” Below, some of those tests:

One useful test is to stand up and sit down five times as fast as possible using just your legs—all you need is a chair and a stopwatch. This test measures the strength of the legs, which is where we have the most muscle and, at the same time, where we usually lose muscle first.

This one combines strength and balance. It involves standing on the non-dominant leg and lifting the other leg. The goal is to maintain posture without using the arms. In people under 50 years of age, it is done with eyes closed, and in older people, with eyes open to prevent falls. The ideal is to balance for at least 45 seconds.

The six-minute endurance test involves walking as fast as possible for six minutes. Walking less than 500 meters indicates poor cardiorespiratory fitness; walking between 500 and 700 meters is acceptable; walking more than 700 is excellent.

Shawn G. Anthony, MD, orthopedic sports medicine surgeon and associate system chief of sports medicine at Mount Sinai, says that almost every form of movement will help with longevity and has some value. But you shouldn’t rely on just one type of exercise to do everything. “There is no single longevity exercise,” Dr. Anthony says. “The goal is to build cardiovascular fitness and strength while preserving the ability to move well and remain active over time.”

He goes on to explain that the strongest evidence for longevity is combining aerobic exercise with resistance training. Think brisk walking, running, cycling, swimming, or sports with free weights, resistance bands or body weight. With that in mind, here are some other exercises to consider:

Walking is one of the easiest exercises you can incorporate to daily life, and is backed up by science. “It is accessible, low impact, and easy to sustain, and meaningful health benefits occur well below 10,000 steps per day,” Dr. Anthony agrees. “There is also good evidence that walking after a meal can reduce the rise in blood glucose that follows eating, so even a brief post-meal walk can be a useful way to incorporate more movement into the day and improve metabolic health.”

He says that weighted walking can help. And while trendy walking exercises such as Tai Chi walking and lymphatic walking come with limited research in regards to longevity, anything that gets you moving is beneficial.

Picking up a new sport like tennis isn’t easy in the sense that you’ll get the hang of it in one (or even several) tries. But if you’re not trying to be next Serena and just doing it for fun, it can be a form of exercise you look forward to. Dr. Anthony adds that sports can be especially useful because you train a lot of things at once, and one of the best examples is tennis. “It combines aerobic conditioning with bursts of higher-intensity movement, changes of direction, coordination, reaction time, and a social component,” he says. “Studies of racquet sports have reported favorable associations with longevity.”

Yes, these workouts are hard. But finding a workout that you like and want to stick to will make it easy for you to stick to your longevity goals. Dr. Anthony says that trendy workouts such as Pilates, HIIT, and Zone 2 training can all be useful as long as the underlying training makes sense. You want to identify your fitness goals and find an exercise that will help you meet them safely and consistently. “If a trendy workout motivates someone to exercise regularly, that has real value,” he says. “What matters more than the label is whether the workout contributes to a well-rounded and sustainable exercise program.”

Dr. Anthony says to avoid anything that will repeatedly cause joint pain, tendon problems, or overuse injuries. “[That] is not a successful longevity strategy,” he says. “The goal is to increase physical capacity without repeatedly exceeding what the body can recover from.”

He also says that our fitness and strength are built up over time in our 20s, 30s, 40s, and 50s. So while it would be ideal to not wait until later in adulthood to begin thinking about longevity, starting now is still better than later (or never).

And just remember that the foundation of longevity remains regular aerobic exercise, resistance training, and daily movement. Whatever will get you those three will be the best workout for you. “Longevity requires durability,” he says. “Ultimately, the goal is to preserve enough physical capacity to keep running, skiing, playing tennis, traveling, and doing activities that matter to you 20 or 30 years from now.”

#6553. Cider-Braised Sausage and Lentils

I haven’t made a meal in the French countryside in fall; but sometimes I dream, and these slow-cooked lentils are what I’d make in such a situation. Back in my American reality, it still makes an excellent dinner or hearty weekend lunch. Look for mild smoked Austrian or German sausages, which lean on mellow herbs and warm spices (sometimes, if you’re lucky, they’re also stuffed with a nutty cheese)—this style is already cooked to a safe temperature, but the casing’s texture is greatly improved when seared before reheating. If your shop only carries sweet Italian sausage or something like an apple-stuffed chicken sausage, both work in a pinch. What a treat it will be to actually finish off that gallon of apple cider you impulsively bought last week in the lentil-braising liquid.

More great fall recipes this way: Charred Cabbage With Sausages and Apples; Pork Chops With Green Chiles and Apples; Mustardy Cider-Braised Pork Chops.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium heavy pot over medium-high. Cook 6–8 smoked Austrian or German sausages (1–1½ lb.), turning often, until deeply browned on all sides, about 4 minutes. Transfer to a plate.

Combine 1 large red or yellow onion, finely chopped, 3 celery stalks, finely chopped, 1 large carrot, peeled, finely chopped, 1 tsp. freshly ground pepper, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in same pan. Reduce heat to medium and cook, stirring often and scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan, until vegetables are softened, 6–8 minutes. Add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and cook, stirring, just until fragrant, about 1 minute.

Add 2 cups low-sodium chicken or vegetable broth, 1½ cups apple cider, 1½ cups French green lentils, picked through, rinsed, ½ cup finely chopped parsley, 3 Tbsp. Dijon or whole grain mustard, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt to pan. Increase heat to high and bring to a boil. Cook until liquid is slightly reduced, about 5 minutes. Cover pan, reduce heat to medium-low, and cook until lentils are tender and most of the liquid is absorbed but mixture is still saucy, 30–35 minutes.

Uncover pan and stir in 1 Tbsp. apple cider vinegar or red wine vinegar. Nestle sausages into lentil mixture and add any juices pooled on plate. Simmer until sausages are warmed through, about 5 minutes. Top with parsley leaves and reserved celery leaves to serve.

#6552. Countdown to Christmas with Snoopy! The Best Peanuts Advent Calendars

The Lenox Peanuts Advent calendar is both a beautiful luxury gift for loved ones and a nostalgic yearly tradition for families.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

Here at Taste of Home, we know all too well that Advent calendars are no longer just for tots. In fact, some of the top-selling picks among our readership over the last few years include wine calendars and other boozy options. Not to mention the bestselling Bonne Maman Advent calendar, which has been voted one of our favorites for three years running! But when it comes to collectible calendars that double as unforgettable gifts, nothing impresses us quite as much as the Lenox Peanuts Advent calendar.

That’s right! The brand behind the iconic Spice Village now has Advent calendars. And yes, the Peanuts Advent calendar is just as gorgeous and nostalgia-filled as you’d imagine. Here’s my experience unboxing this assortment of adorable ornaments. Warning: spoilers ahead!

Boasting 25 ornaments crafted in Lenox's signature porcelain, the Lenox Peanuts Advent calendar is a luxury Advent calendar unlike any other.

The Lenox Peanuts Advent calendar isn’t just your average Christmas countdown. It’s a luxury Advent calendar that unfolds to reveal 25 doors, each housing its own adorable ornament. Because these are made from Lenox’s signature  premium porcelain, they’re meant to be enjoyed season after season. That makes this Advent calendar an extra special gift for Peanuts fans. It also makes a fun yearly tradition for families! Don’t forget to put on A Charlie Brown Christmas as you hang them on your Christmas tree!

This collector’s calendar comes with 25 different tree hangers, each boasting either an iconic wintery scene from the comic strips or one of our favorite classic characters. In total, there are 13 characters and 12 scenic snowflakes, all of which sit at around two inches tall. And these bite-sized heirlooms aren’t found anywhere else—you can only get them inside the Advent calendar, making them a thoughtful gift for collectors.

My experience unboxing the Lenox Peanuts Advent calendar was truly magical. Even before I opened the first door, I was struck by the packaging. While simple, the shiny red box looks classy and expensive. It also feels nice and hefty—a nod to the precious porcelain ornaments nested inside. Once you loosen the gold clasp, the calendar folds open like a book to reveal 25 doors, and each opens to reveal a figurine or snowflake nestled in a protective foam cushion. I love that the box is protective enough to reuse for storage once the season ends, too!

From Lionel to Peppermint Patty to Charlie himself, each of the character ornaments offers extraordinary detail. Despite the small size, they’re slightly heavy, so you can tell they’re also high-quality. Among the figurines are also several iterations of fan favorite puppy dog Snoopy partaking in holiday traditions and lounging on his light-wrapped doghouse.

Even the snowflake ornaments offer their own holiday charm. Each one is carefully painted with a miniature scene from the wintery comic strips. Among the art are ageless, captivating sequences of the gang gathered around a lighted tree, Lucy performing on ice skates and mischievous Snoopy tangled up in a string of vibrant Christmas lights among many others. Adorning each hanging loop is a festive tassel, giving the ornaments a little added flair.

Whether you plan on giving this one as a gift or want to keep it as a holiday heirloom, it’s truly a special collection that the whole family can enjoy. It’s also the perfect way to signal the most wonderful time of the year is here!

While we absolutely love the Lenox Peanuts advent calendar as a yearly tradition, it’s not exactly child-friendly (without parental assistance, that is). For folks seeking an alternative Advent calendar for kids that still offers the same Peanuts charm, we love this Peanuts puzzle Advent calendar. Deputy Editor Katie Bandurski tested it last year and praises its adorable prints, which cover all of the classic characters.

Want something a little sweeter? Sure, you can always opt for a classic chocolate Advent calendar. But for fans of Snoopy, this adorably delicious Advent calendar from Sugarfina makes a showstopping gift. It’s brimming with 24 of the brand’s popular sweet treats, including gummies in fun holiday shapes, peach hearts, sparkling stars, sparkle pops, chocolate biscuits, confetti caramels and so much more.

“This calendar gets major points for its design even before you get into the good stuff,” raves Katie, who enjoyed last year’s edition. “It’s shaped like the iconic red doghouse. It gets even better when you open the doors to the calendar and find a pop-up paper Snoopy.”

This gorgeous Advent calendar will quickly become a yearly family tradition.

Absolutely smitten with the limited-edition Lenox Peanuts Advent calendar? We don’t blame you. Folks wanting to get their hands on one ahead of the holidays can find them on the Lenox website, Wayfair and Macy’s. The calendar retails for around $300, but offers an incredible $500 value, making it a great choice for gifting or adding to your yearly holiday traditions.

One note: We recommend investing in one as soon as you can, because they’re bound to sell out well ahead of Christmas time.

#6551. A Diwali Menu That’s Full of Joy (and Sticky Chicken Wings)

Growing up, I remember a steady stream of guests coming in and out of our home in the weeks leading up to Diwali. The season would start with Navratri, a nine-night Hindu festival celebrating the divine feminine, Shakti, through the worship of Goddess Durga. Our celebrations were led by women, my grandmother, mother, and aunts, who would meticulously clean the house and spend weeks preparing snacks and sweets. They taught me the art of hosting and how to share the joy of food with our community.

I came to associate Diwali with that sense of abundance, care, and graciousness. There was always more food than we needed, and always room for more people. When I moved to New York, I started to miss that deeply, so I began a tradition to share Diwali with my chosen family here, many of whom were experiencing the holiday through food for the first time.

I’m the kind of host who likes to enjoy her own party, which means being strategic about the menu. I lean on dishes like my homestyle chicken kari, which can be made ahead and tastes even better the next day. And then there are dishes that bring a little theater to the table, like the creamy rice pudding which gets torched before serving. I want food that feeds a crowd, feels special, and lets me spend less time in the kitchen and more time with the people I love.

Guests always ask me for this crowd-pleasing app. Japanese sweet potatoes have a creamy texture that pairs beautifully with the spicy, crunchy elements of chaat. Best of all, the spuds can be cooked ahead, with the toppings added just before serving. One less thing for you to do on the big day.

Wings reign supreme when it comes to a party appetizer, and these tamarind-glazed ones deliver tangy punch in every bite. The marinade combines tamarind purée, fish sauce, brown sugar, red pepper flakes, and cumin, with extra glaze brushed on for maximum flavor and char. Be sure to finish with fried onions for bonus crunch.

This tastes like you spent hours cooking, but actually it comes together in less than an hour. The best part? It’s even better the next day, making it ideal for hosting. Gently reheat the kari before guests arrive, letting the warm, heady spices fill your home before everyone gathers around the table.

Mushrooms are an underrated ingredient in Indian cooking, and this creamy masala puts the earthy veg front and center. Sautéing them in batches gives the shrooms beautifully caramelized edges, while deglazing the pot captures all those flavorful browned bits. Serve the masala with rice or warm flatbread to sop up all the savory sauce.

No Diwali celebration is complete without something sweet, but dessert doesn’t have to be elaborate to feel special. This recipe transforms a handful of pantry staples into a rich, creamy rice pudding. For a playful twist, finish it with a crackly brûléed sugar crust and serve with a scoop of mango sorbet.

#6549. Broiled Salmon Teriyaki

Sometimes all it takes to make dinner feel special is a big, bold piece of protein. Case in point: This salty-sweet salmon glazed in a glossy teriyaki-style sauce. Brushed in two rounds with the quick sauce made with nothing more than sugar, soy sauce, sesame oil, and vinegar, the salmon sizzles under the broiler, charring as it takes on a smoky flavor. This recipe calls for one large piece of salmon, but you can use smaller fillets or opt for a white fish such as cod or halibut. Just note that the cooking time will be shorter if using smaller pieces, so keep an eye on them. Add a quick garnish of sliced scallions and toasted sesame seeds, and dinner is done.

More salmon winners this way: Hot Honey-Glazed Salmon; Green Curry-Glazed Salmon; and Slow-Roasted Salmon With Harissa.

Bring ⅓ cup (packed; 67 g) dark brown sugar, ¼ cup soy sauce, 2 Tbsp. unseasoned rice vinegar, and 2 tsp. toasted sesame oil to a simmer in a small saucepan over medium-high heat; cook until reduced by half and syrupy, 5–7 minutes. Let sauce cool until thickened slightly, about 10 minutes.

Heat broiler (if broiler is in your oven, place rack in upper third). Season both sides of one 1½–2-lb. skinless or skin-on center-cut salmon fillet with kosher salt. Place, skin side down, in a skillet or baking dish. Transfer one third of sauce to a small bowl and set aside for serving. Brush about half of remaining sauce over fillet. (If the salmon has a lot of room around it in the pan, line with foil to prevent runoff sauce from burning onto pan.)

Broil salmon until sauce is just starting to burn in spots, 4–7 minutes. Brush remaining sauce over fillet and broil until deeply charred and salmon is opaque all the way through, about 5 minutes.

Remove fish from oven and spoon reserved sauce over. Top with thinly sliced scallions and/or toasted sesame seeds if desired.

#6548. Carne Guisada

Recipe by Margaret Knoebel, Milwaukee, Wisconsin

With its warm spices and a rich gravy, this slow-braised carne guisada is perfect in tacos or on a bed of rice.

Carne guisada, a classic Mexican beef stew whose name translates to “stewed meat,” has a rich culinary backstory. Its roots stretch across northern Mexico and into Texas, where slow-braised beef dishes are a staple of home kitchens, taquerias and Tex-Mex restaurants alike. Tender beef simmers in a chili-based sauce, then is often served as a taco filling with soft flour tortillas. Some versions (especially in Texas) include potatoes to make it a one-pot meal. Others focus solely on the fall-apart meat and the smooth, peppery sauce built from dried chiles. You win either way.

For our carne guisada recipe, we keep the signature slow-cooked, deeply seasoned beef and rich gravy, but say yes to the potatoes for extra body and comfort. The use of beer, Worcestershire sauce and tomato paste brings layered depth that complements the traditional spices like cumin and chili powder. We aren’t claiming this is the only version because, honestly, that doesn’t exist. But this dish absolutely captures the spirit of classic carne guisada: tender meat, bold flavor and something meant to be shared.

In a large bowl, toss the beef with 1/4 teaspoon of salt. In a separate large bowl, combine the flour and paprika. Add the beef to the flour a few pieces at a time, tossing to coat them.

In a Dutch oven, heat the oil over medium heat. Brown the beef in batches, adding additional oil as necessary. Remove the pieces with a slotted spoon.

Editor’s Tip: Those browned bits stuck to the bottom of the pot are called fond, and they’re flavor gold. Don’t even think about washing them away.

To the same pan, add the onion. Cook and stir until it’s tender, three to five minutes. Stir in the tomato, jalapeno and garlic, and cook until they’re fragrant and the color starts to darken slightly.

Add the browned beef back to the pan. Add the beer, and bring it to a boil, scraping the bottom to release the browned bits. Simmer until the liquid is reduced by half, about five minutes.

Stir in the broth, Worcestershire sauce, crushed red pepper flakes, chili powder, cumin, bay leaf and the remaining 1/2 teaspoon of salt, and bring the mixture to a boil. Reduce the heat, then cover the pot and simmer the stew until the meat is almost tender, about 1 hour and 30 minutes.

Add the potatoes and red wine vinegar. Cover the pot and simmer the stew until the meat and vegetables are tender, about 30 minutes longer.

Discard the bay leaf. Using the back of a spoon or ladle, slightly mash the potatoes. If desired, shred the beef slightly with two forks. Serve with tortillas, rice, lime and cilantro.

Let the carne guisada cool completely before transferring it to an airtight container. Store it in the refrigerator, where the flavors will actually deepen and improve overnight. It’s one of those dishes that might taste even better the next day. Carne guisada lasts up to four days in the refrigerator.

Carne guisada freezes very well. Store it in freezer-safe containers for up to three months, and thaw it overnight in the refrigerator before reheating.

Reheat carne guisada gently on the stovetop over medium-low heat until it’s warmed through. Add a splash of broth if the sauce has thickened too much.

You can use beef shoulder, bottom round or beef stew meat for carne guisada. The key is choosing a tougher cut with connective tissue that breaks down during the long, slow cooking time. This gives you that tender, fall-apart texture.

Whether you serve carne guisada on tortillas or rice, it also pairs beautifully with black beans, fresh salsa or even a side of warm cornbread.

#6547. Brittany Howard and Anna-Maria Babcock’s Tennessee Wedding Was a Celebration of Their Mexican and Southern Roots

Given their day jobs, musician Brittany Howard and record executive Anna-Maria Babcock’s meet-cute feels entirely appropriate: they first crossed paths at a concert. “We met at a friend’s album release show on October 10, 2023, at The Blue Room in Nashville,” Anna-Maria explains. Brittany, who is best known as the lead singer and guitarist of Alabama Shakes, was helping out at the merch table after the show. “I walked up to the table and a mutual friend introduced us by putting our hands in each other’s while asking, ‘Have y’all met yet?’ It was love at first sight for the both of us,” says Anna-Maria. A few days later, the two went on their first real date and fell in love over pizza rolls and mocktails at Brittany’s home. “The first date that never ended!” Anna-Maria jokes.

Just over a year later, Anna-Maria proposed on November 15, 2024, at Smith Lake in Alabama. After an extensive tour year, she encouraged Brittany to come with her on a fishing trip. “Little did I know, this was more than a fishing trip,” says Brittany. “On the first night of our stay, under the last full supermoon of the year, Anna-Maria got on one knee in a freshly made wood-fired hot tub. After the proposal, I said, ‘yes!’” Despite spending hours preparing the hot tub, the couple jumped out to share the news with their friends and family. “All those hours to prepare the hot tub, just to get out after five minutes! It’s okay though,” says Brittany. “We got all of our life together to make another fire.” Adds Anna-Maria, “Brittany followed up with a double proposal (the gay way) during our trip to Portugal for my birthday just a few months later! I also said yes to forever!”

Anna-Maria and Brittany spent the next two years planning their perfect wedding celebration. The big day arrived on October 24, 2026, at the Southall Farm & Inn in Franklin, Tennessee. The couple describes planning as both “so much fun” and “a lot of work.” “We had a hand in every single design aspect of the night; we wanted the space to feel like us,” says Anna-Maria. Alongside planner Carly Pickett, the brides lent their handwriting to save-the-dates, made an ofrenda to honor ancestors, and hand-selected planters from home to fill with florals. Says Anna-Maria, “We wanted our people to feel like they knew exactly whose wedding they were at—one that was very Black, very Mexican, and very queer!”

The couple also wanted to feel their cultures reflected through their fashion choices for the wedding weekend. “We wanted to feel gender affirmed, beautiful, sexy, and ourselves,” says Anna-Maria. “We were not interested in traditional wedding wear, so designing our own garments and sourcing from small women-owned, Black-owned, Indigenous-owned, and queer-owned brands was extremely important to us.” She adds that wearing family heirlooms was also an important part of their wardrobe curation. “We wanted our ancestors to be honored in this space,” says Anna-Maria.

For her wedding look, Brittany worked with stylist Courtney Mays to craft a custom gown with a detailed bodice and dramatic off-the-shoulder cape. Later in the evening, she changed into a bright red ensemble with diaphanous flowing fabric designed alongside Loulette Bride. Anna-Maria found a halter Danielle Frankel dress at Nashville bridal salon The Dress Theory. To walk down the aisle, she paired it with a veil from queer-owned brand Tanner Fletcher.

When Brittany changed into her red reception look, Anna-Maria changed into a textured, red dress of her own that was designed alongside Mays. The brides also created a mood board for their wedding party and even helped style some looks for them. “We wanted our wedding party to be more concerned with having fun, letting loose, and connecting with others—not with whether or not they liked the outfits we picked out for them that they will never wear again,” says Anna-Maria.

The weekend kicked off with an intimate sunset dinner overlooking the Tennessee hills. The rehearsal dinner was hosted by Anna-Maria’s parents, Sylvia and Randy Babcock. “We ate delicious Mexican food, danced to cumbia, and cried hysterically as our wedding party, parents, and grandmas expressed their love for us,” recalls Anna-Maria. “The feeling of watching your blood family and chosen family fall in love with each other was nothing short of magical and healing.”

The ceremony took place the next day in a meadow along a creek. Guests were surrounded by nature and gathered amongst florals that lined the aisle. “We walked to everyone’s smiling, expectant faces under a beautiful fall sunset while the mariachi band played a rendition of ‘The First Time Ever I Saw Your Face,’” describes Brittany. The couple walked towards one another on the arms of their parents. “When we got to the altar, we then encouraged our two-year-old nephew, who was the ring bearer, to come meet us up there! Holding a wooden fish ring box—the one Anna-Maria gifted me when she proposed—in one hand and picking his nose with the other, he joyfully ran up to us while stopping to smell the flowers halfway down the aisle,” she recalls. “A perfect reminder of what’s important in life. Always stop to smell the flowers.”

Anna-Maria’s Tía Pinky read a poem written by the bride’s late grandfather, Roberto. “His words reminded us of why we are here and why it’s important to not waste time with the ones we love,” says Brittany. Remembers Anna-Maria, “I was so giddy and my cheeks hurt from smiling so much. I felt so excited and humbled watching our family grow right before my eyes. I felt proud of myself for never giving up on love. Little us would be so proud.” Brittany emphasizes that she felt “full of pride” throughout the ceremony and as if the moment was “magical and sacred.” This magic was made complete as a rainbow appeared in the sky once the brides kissed. “We think that was a little sign from the ancestors that we were all right where we were supposed to be,” says Anna-Maria.

The mariachi band led the way towards the reception, followed by the newlyweds and their community as “Isn’t She Lovely” played. “We danced and sang our way around the lake to cocktail hour where the sun finally went down over the hill in a blaze of pinks, reds, purples and oranges,” recalls Brittany. “The moon was so bright it would stop us in our tracks.” Cocktail hour followed with reunions, hugs, and tears of joy. “We drank and danced to cumbia before walking over to the ofrenda to pay our respects to our loved ones who couldn’t physically be there with us,” says Anna-Maria. “We could feel their spirit throughout the entire night.”

The reception moved indoors for a dinner full of Mexican and Southern cuisine, along with a night full of music. “Lloyd Buchanan, who plays with my touring bands, led an incredible band during reception where he played our first dance song, ‘The First Time Ever I Saw Your Face’ by Roberta Flack in a hauntingly beautiful rendition,” says Brittany. “This song also happens to be Anna-Maria’s grandparents Maria and Roberto’s wedding song. Anna-Maria and I both took turns dancing to the end of the song with her 86-year-old grandmother.” She recalls, “There wasn’t a dry eye in the room.” The newlyweds then danced with their fathers and also did a special dance with their moms to “I Say A Little Prayer” by Aretha Franklin before welcoming all their guests onto the floor.

Special performances went on throughout the evening. “I come from a long line of family drummers, and my Uncle Scott and little brother Robert graced the stage, playing drums to Sinatra’s ‘Fly Me To The Moon’ and Bobby Caldwell’s ‘What You Won’t Do For Love’ respectively,” says Anna-Maria. “The very first time I saw live music, it was at an underground jazz club in DC where my uncle would play with his big band. When Uncle Scott was up there playing at the reception, I was instantly transported back to that club when I was a little girl.”

The after-party was held at Dottie’s, a speakeasy on the grounds of the property. The couple’s friend, NYC DJ T1BG, spun until 2 a.m. “The room was vibrant with belly laughs, dirty dancing, wigs, bologna sandwiches, hot dogs, and deep conversations around the fire pit,” says Anna-Maria. “Our feet were aching—with Brittany nursing my blisters at 4 a.m.—but our hearts were exploding with love.” Adds Brittany, “We were so moved seeing our family and friends from thousands of miles away dancing together and making their own relationships. It’s the very thing we wanted our wedding to embody: communion.”

While the brides share they are truly excited to settle into their married lives with each other and enjoy the simplicity and joy of being newlyweds, they also emphasize how grateful they are to share their love today: “Getting married in the South as Black and brown lesbians feels extra heavy in today’s political climate. We live in a country where we have a Supreme Court justice who wants to ban interracial marriage. We live in a state where LGBTQIA+ rights are under attack, and the local government is working with ICE to tear families apart. We aren’t going anywhere. This is our home and we are here to stay. We are here to dig in deeper—into love and into our beautifully diverse and queer community. We believe love always wins, and it certainly felt like that at our wedding. While we were the first gay couple to get married at this venue in Franklin, Tennessee, we certainly won’t be the last!”

We started the most perfect weekend with our rehearsal dinner at golden hour overlooking the rolling hills of central Tennessee. Nothing beats Mexican food, our favorite people, cumbia music, and lots of happy tears. —Anna-Maria

We loved working with our wedding planner Carly Pickett on all paper goods! Carly also happens to be a close friend and an incredible visual artist, so working on these designs with her was so fun! We came up with our own custom gay quail lovers logo and custom icons to represent us as a couple. A lot of love went into these so that hopefully our guests could frame and display them in their homes to forever remember the special weekend we shared together. —Anna-Maria

My mom, dad, tías, and sister planned and decorated our beautiful rehearsal dinner. My mom has always been the party planner of the family—always making everyone feel so special and celebrated. The smells of the tortillas cooking, the floral arrangements made by my mom and sister Caroline, and the way the custom-made “Anna-Maria & Brittany” papel picado looked blowing in the breeze made us feel right at home. —Anna-Maria

The tablescape of our dreams! My mamá is so talented. —Anna-Maria

I’d be nothing without mi abuela. —Anna-Maria

Doing anything to make our two-year-old nephew smile! He is currently obsessed with cars. —Anna-Maria

I was named after both of my grandmothers, Anne and Maria. My favorite women who raised me to be kind and resilient. Grandma Maria is a light to all that cross her path. —Anna-Maria

The details! We love Courtney Mays. Courtney is a new friend and collaborator and helped Brittany bring her vision to life for her tour wardrobe these past two few years. We are so lucky we found her and Candice Jones and knew we would be in the perfect hands for our wedding! They were pivotal in bringing our dream wedding day looks to life! —Anna-Maria

We feel lucky to have spent such intimate moments with them. They are stuck with us forever now. — Anna-Maria

I would do anything for Kitty! If you love my hair, it’s all because of her. She is my pink-haired angel and Earth sister. Kitty’s eyes sparkle when she is with her beautiful partner, Jaime Wyatt. Jaime has the voice of an angel, and we are so happy they found each other. —Anna-Maria

#6545. Cranberry Meringue Pie

A big, billowing cloud of meringue tops this crimson beauty and acts as a sweet reprieve from the tart cranberry curd. The vibrant filling is made even more sour with a generous amount of lime juice. Think lemon meringue pie but holiday-ified. Use our Perfect Pie Crust as the base to create a sturdy-flaky foundation, and be sure to start the pie the day before you plan to serve it, as the curd requires several hours of chilling to set into a sliceable texture. Cut into it too soon and it will run onto your plate, creating a messy—albeit delicious—slice.

We never make pie dough without a metal bench scraper. Our favorite is from Gestura. Use the scraper to cut butter, fold dough and nudge it into shape, transfer it from counter to plastic wrap, trim edges, cut strips, and, sure, scrape flour off your counter.

Welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack.

3 hours (plus 30 minutes for freezing and 5 hours for chilling)

Whisk 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ¼ tsp. baking powder in a large bowl to combine. Add 2 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces, and rub into dry ingredients with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 10 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash with your fingers into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea-size).

Make a well in the center of mixture and pour in ¼ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute, then knead in bowl a couple of times to bring dough together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn out dough onto a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour and dust top of dough with flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold dough in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting with more rice flour as needed to prevent sticking. Pat into a ½"-thick disk and wrap tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Let dough disk sit at room temperature 5 minutes. Roll out dough on a lightly floured surface to a 12" round, about ¼" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and wrap around rolling pin. Transfer to a 9"-diameter pie pan (such as East Fork Spun Iron Pie Dish). Unfurl into pan, then lift edges and allow dough to slump down into pan. Trim, leaving about a 1½" overhang. Fold overhang under so crust is flush with edges of pan and crimp as desired with lightly floured fingers. Set pan on a rimmed baking sheet and prick bottom and sides of crust with a fork in several places. Freeze, uncovered, at least 30 minutes and up to 2 hours.

Place a rack in lower third of oven; preheat to 400°. Line crust with a sheet of parchment paper and fill with pie weights or dried beans. Bake crust, tenting edges with foil if browning too quickly, until edges are set and look dry, 20–25 minutes. Carefully lift out parchment paper and weights and continue baking crust, gently pressing bottom and sides occasionally with a flat-bottomed measuring cup if puffing up, until bottom looks dry and is golden, 20–25 minutes more. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let crust cool.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

Bring 1 lb. fresh or frozen cranberries, 1½ cups (300 g) granulated sugar, and ¼ cup water to a boil in a large saucepan, then reduce heat to medium and simmer, stirring often, until cranberries soften and burst and most of the liquid has evaporated, 10–15 minutes. Let cranberry mixture cool.

Transfer cranberry mixture to a blender; reserve pan. Add ⅔ cup fresh lime juice and ¼ cup (32 g) cornstarch and blend on high speed until smooth. Scrape purée back into pan (not over heat) and add 3 large eggs, 2 large egg yolks, 1 Tbsp. vanilla extract, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Place over medium heat and cook, whisking constantly, until mixture bubbles and thickens to a pudding-like consistency, about 4 minutes. Remove pan from heat. Add ¾ cup (1½ sticks) unsalted butter, room temperature, cut into pieces, and whisk until melted and combined. Strain curd through a fine-mesh sieve, pushing with a rubber spatula, directly into crust. Smooth into an even layer and cover with plastic wrap, pressing directly onto surface. Chill pie at least 4 hours and up to 1 day.

Just before serving, beat 6 large egg whites, room temperature, ¼ tsp. cream of tartar, remaining 1¼ cups (250 g) granulated sugar, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment on medium speed until foamy and sugar is dissolved, about 5 minutes. Increase speed to high and continue to beat until stiff peaks form, about 3 minutes more.

Spoon meringue over filling and swirl decoratively as desired. Using a kitchen torch, toast meringue if desired.

#6544. Chili Crisp Yogurt Chicken

Slather Greek yogurt and your favorite chili crisp on chicken thighs, roast in a hot oven, and you’ll be rewarded with juicy, tender meat with a delightful orange-tinged exterior. But the best part of this sheet-pan dinner comes after the chicken is cooked: Spread cooked rice into the pan’s juices, then slide the baking sheet back into the oven. As the rice soaks up the deeply savory sauce, it will crisp in spots, creating a texture that’s somewhere between chewy-fluffy steamed grains and a freshly toasted pita chip. And when it comes to chili crisp, we love the iconic and easy-to-source Lao Gan Ma, but specialty brands like Fly By Jing are great too—just make sure the one you use is not too spicy, which will overpower the dish.

More great chicken and rice recipes this way: One-Pot Chicken Thighs With Cilantro Rice and Beans; Spiced Coconut Chicken Rice; Nana’s Chicken and Rice Stew.

Preheat oven to 425°. Season 6–8 skinless, boneless chicken thighs (1½–2 lb.) with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt.

Whisk together ¾ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt and ¼ cup plus 2 Tbsp. well-stirred chili crisp in a large bowl. Add chicken thighs and toss to coat.

Arrange chicken on a rimmed baking sheet and top with any yogurt mixture left in bowl. Bake chicken until deeply browned and an instant-read thermometer inserted into the thickest part of a thigh registers 165°, 25–30 minutes. Transfer chicken to a cutting board or plate.

Spread 3 cups cooked jasmine or short-grain rice over baking sheet with chicken juices and bake until most of the juices have been absorbed and rice is starting to crisp in spots, 12–15 minutes.

Meanwhile, whisk together 1 Tbsp. finely grated lime zest, ¼ cup fresh lime juice, ½ tsp. sugar, ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt, and remaining ¼ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt in a small bowl.

Combine ½ medium head of green cabbage (about 1 lb.), very thinly sliced, and a big pinch of Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt in a large bowl. Using your hands, scrunch cabbage gently to soften. Add 1 small red onion, thinly sliced, 1 cup finely chopped cilantro, and yogurt dressing and toss to combine. Taste cabbage slaw and season with more salt if needed.

Slice chicken as desired and serve with crisped rice and cabbage slaw.

#6543. I Tried the New Bentgo Lift Water Bottle—And the Ring Handle Makes It So Easy to Stay Hydrated

The new Bentgo water bottle is easy to use, carry and clean, plus it comes in gorgeous, candy-colored hues.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

For someone who works and works out at home, I’ve amassed quite the collection of reusable water bottles. Maintaining the healthy habit of drinking more water is always my excuse for adding yet another to the mix. After all, the cuter the water bottle, the more likely I am to reach for it and take a swig.

So when I saw the new Bentgo Lift Chug Lid water bottle, I knew I had to try it. As much as I love my Stanley Flowstate, I like to ditch the straw every so often, even if it does save me from dousing myself every time I go in for a sip. But with the Bentgo’s unique lid and leakproof design, I had high expectations that this strawless bottle would become a regular in my hydration rotation. And it has! Here’s why I’m toting around the new Bentgo Lift water bottle like it’s my favorite purse.

The major draw of the Bentgo Lift Chug Lid water bottle is the soft-grip ring handle that’s attached to the lid. It does double the work by keeping the flip top securely closed and offering a comfortable way to tote it around. My major gripe with other water bottles has always been that their handles and/or straws make them unwieldy for carrying and commuting. But not the Bentgo. Just lift the handle and carry it like a bag. I’ve even hung it from the handle of my Peloton Bike during a ride!

It did take me a moment to get used to drinking from the bottle, only because it’s different from others I’ve had. But all you have to do is lift the ring handle and push the little lever with your thumb to pop open the cap (you could also wedge your thumb in under the handle to hit the button so it lifts the cap and the handle at the same time, but I found it easier to open the handle first). I like that the handle folds flat against the bottle so everything stays compact. The mouth is wide enough to comfortably drink from, although I do turn the bottle so that my nose doesn’t bump the edge of the ring handle.

At first I thought the smooth cylindrical shape of the bottle might be a problem because, other than the handle, there is nothing to grip the bottle when you’re actually drinking. But the powder-coated exterior offers plenty of grip so it won’t slip in your hand.

The lid twists off easily from the wide-mouth bottle, which makes it easy to fill with liquid and ice. It also makes it very easy to clean. The Bentgo is top-rack dishwasher friendly, although the manufacturer does recommend handwashing to protect the exterior. I’ve definitely popped the lid in the dishwasher several times already but I’ve been handwashing the bottle itself, at least for now.

The Bentgo Lift Chug Lid Bottle is available in 24-, 32- and 40-ounce sizes in a host of colors. I chose both the 24-ounce in Bubblegum and the 32-ounce in Denim, but soon found myself gravitating toward the more petite 24-ounce bottle. It wasn’t only because of the candy hue—I just prefer a smaller bottle!

With all this talk about design and color, you’re probably wondering: Does it even keep your water cold? Yes, it sure does. The Bentgo Lift water bottle features a stainless steel interior with triple-layer insulation (BPA-free with no PFAs) that keeps liquids cold for up to 24 hours. And yes, I can confirm this to be true: I left ice water in a bottle on my desk after the work day and came back the next morning to surprisingly cold water!

You can purchase the Bentgo Lift Chug Lid Water Bottle right on the brand’s website, as well as on Walmart and Amazon. It comes in 24-, 32- and 40-ounce sizes, which cost $29.99, $34.99 and $39.99, respectively. The two smaller sizes come in six colors: Bubblegum, Denim, Latte, Blanc, Back to Black and Amalfi Coast. The 40-ounce is currently available only in Blanc and Back to Black. These will make great gifts for the holidays, so shop soon for the best size and color availability!
