A proposed shift in recommendations for hepatitis B vaccination in the U.S. could leave millions of young adults unprotected, a new modeling study suggests.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A proposed change to decades-old guidance on hepatitis B vaccination would lead to a dramatic increase in chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infections among young people, a new modeling study predicts.

Previously, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommended that all newborns be vaccinated against HBV within hours of birth ‪—‬ a strategy known as "universal birth-dose vaccination." But in December 2025, the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) advised ending this recommendation, and the CDC accepted that advice.

The new guidance would recommend birth doses only to babies whose mothers tested positive for HBV or whose HBV status was unknown. The guidance suggests that mothers who test negative should instead ask their doctors about whether their child needs a birth dose — an approach the CDC calls "shared clinical decision-making." The new recommendation states that babies who forgo the birth dose should be at least 2 months old before starting the HBV vaccine series.

Health experts widely criticized the proposed change when it was announced, and for the moment, its implementation has been put on pause by legal action. The modeling study, published Oct. 19 in the journal Annals of Internal Medicine, predicts what would happen if it came to pass.

"Overall, this modeling study has many strengths and I think presents an accurate projection of how the vaccine recommendations may impact future chronic HBV in the U.S.," Dr. Norah Terrault, a transplant hepatologist at the University of Southern California Keck School of Medicine who wasn't involved in the study, told Live Science in an email.

When caught in infancy or early childhood, over 90% of HBV infections become chronic. About 15% to 25% of people with chronic HBV go on to develop liver scarring (cirrhosis), a form of liver cancer called hepatocellular carcinoma, or another chronic liver disease. So, an uptick in chronic HBV infections would translate to an uptick in these harmful liver conditions.

"Not every pregnant person is tested for hepatitis B," said study co-author Dr. Amir Mohareb, an infectious-diseases physician-investigator at Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard Medical School. For those who are tested, there's a chance their results are inaccurate or that they're not provided the right care after testing positive. "Something can be missed at any step in the care process, so the vaccine dose at birth provides protection," he said.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Mohareb and his colleagues built a simulation model using published data, including the current prevalence of HBV and the screening rate among pregnant people. The team also factored in the HBV test's sensitivity, the share of children who are fully vaccinated by age 2, and the risk of developing chronic HBV infection in different age groups. They made estimates of how often children are exposed to the virus through contact with infected household or community members.

HBV is "very, very transmissible," Mohareb said. It can spread from mother to child at birth or through exposure to tiny amounts of bodily fluids, like blood from a scratch, after birth. So, even if a baby does not get HBV from their mother, if they are unvaccinated, they can still get from another family member or from other children.

Infants and young children have a greater risk of their HBV infections becoming chronic than people infected in adulthood.

With this data, the researchers tested what would happen if vaccination were postponed to 2 months of age for babies whose mothers tested negative. Among babies born in 2026, 19% more would have chronic HBV infections by age 20, compared with universal birth-dose vaccination, they found.

In this scenario, the babies would still start the HBV vaccine series, albeit two months later than usual. However, the CDC's proposed recommendation offers more wiggle room; it says that parents should consult with their children's doctors to "decide when or if their child will begin the hepatitis B vaccine series" at all.

The researchers ran a stimulation to compare these two scenarios: one where kids get their first shot two months late and one intended to capture this looser "shared clinical decision-making" scenario.

"Other vaccines whose recommendations employ similar language had uptake as low as 25%," Mohareb noted. This aspect of their modeling has some uncertainty, he emphasized, since it's unknown exactly how the public will respond to such loosening of the guidance.

The researchers assumed that about 87% of kids would complete the vaccine series by age 2 under the deferred strategy, while only 50% would under the shared decision-making strategy. That 50% coverage, in turn, would increase chronic HBV infections acquired by age 20 by 83%, and about 50% and 70% of those born under that guidance would be susceptible to HBV infection at age 20.

That's about 1.8 million people in this age group per year, compared with fewer than 250,000 under universal birth-dose vaccination. "This represents a population that is at risk for acquiring HBV via sex, drug use etc — behaviors more prevalent among young adults," Terrault said.

To test the robustness of the findings, Mohareb's team varied the most uncertain inputs across wide ranges and ran the model 1,000 times. In every simulation, the birth-dose strategy led to fewer chronic infections than either alternative.

These conclusions seem "robust" because "they are the same conclusions no matter how we change the numbers of the model," Mohereb noted. Though of course "the specific magnitude of change depends on how many people defer vaccination," he said.

The new study does not specifically show how many additional cases of liver disease or cancer would result from the uptick in HBV infections. But Terrault said that the risks of liver failure, cirrhosis and liver cancer "would be anticipated to increase due to the missed opportunity to protect against infection."

Mohareb stressed that he is in no way opposed to the principle of shared decision-making between doctors and patients. "They should always make the decision together," he said. "But we rely on our public health agencies not to tell us that we should be making decisions with the patient, but rather to tell us what policy would make us healthier as a country."

Childhood HBV infections in the U.S. dropped from more than 25,000 cases a year in 1985 to fewer than 100 reported cases in 2024. This steep decline is credited to HBV screening during pregnancy, antibody treatment for babies born to HBV-positive mothers and universal birth-dose vaccination.

"Certainly without following a universal dose vaccination recommendation there would be a lot more hep B infections early in life," Dr. Brian McMahon, a hepatologist and the director of the Liver Disease and Hepatitis Program at the Alaska Native Medical Center, told Live Science in an email.

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

Projected effect of 2026 federal changes to the childhood immunization schedule on chronic hepatitis B virus infections in the United States. Annals of Internal Medicine. https://doi.org/10.7326/annals-26-02135

#6449. This Ancient Meteorite Hints at Mars' Warm, Wet Past

Mars is the subject of an ongoing, decades-long effort to understand its past. Its potential ancient habitability drives that effort. More than 20 missions have been sent to its surface (though many didn't survive the entry and landing). Two are operating there currently, Curiosity and Perserverance, and multiple orbiters scan the planet's surface from above.

Clues to Mars' past are in its rock, and the more ancient a piece of rock, the deeper the clues it can contain about the planet's ancient past. Visiting Mars with rovers is only one way to access the planet's rock. Fortunately, some chunks of Mars have been sent to Earth. Violent impacts have sent chunks of Mars rock into space, where they've eventually found their way to Earth as meteorites.

A Martian meteorite named Black Beauty set the standard for ancient meteorites from Mars when it was found in 2011. Most meteorites are found in deserts or in snowy/icy areas simply because they're more easily seen, and Black Beauty (Northwest Africa 7034, or NWA 7034) was found by nomads in the Western Sahara. Portions of it are about 4.43 billion years old, and Mars is about 4.5, maybe 4.6 billion years old. So Black Beauty is extremely ancient.

The Sahara Desert has yielded other ancient Martian meteorites, including Teghaza 001 (Teg 001), found in Mali in 2022. New research uncovered some unusual properties in Teg 001, and they're presented in new research.

The research is titled "A Martian meteorite that formed â³4.1 billion years ago samples Marsâ early crust and mantle," and it's published in the journal Science. The lead author is Yang Liu from NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory at the California Institute of Technology. Scientist Carl Agee, director and curator at the University of New Mexicoâs Institute of Meteoritics (IOM), also played a leading role in the work.

"This sample probably came from an environment on Mars that was more Earth-like." - Carl Agee, University of New Mexico.

(A) shows the largest of the eight pieces of Teg001. (B) shows a cut section of a smaller chunk. Image Credit: Yang Liu et al., A Martian meteorite that formed â³4.1 billion years ago samples Marsâ early crust and mantle. Science0,eadz5646DOI:10.1126/science.adz5646

Ancient meteorites are rare finds and they're extremely valuable scientifically.

"Martian meteorites provide a record of the planetâs geological history," the authors explain in their research. "However, most are geologically young samples that are not representative of Marsâ surface, which is dominated by ancient rocks."

Most meteorites are young just because of selection effects. Meteorites are launched into space by impacts, and that favours young rocks, which are stronger. So meteorites tend to come from younger, basaltic volcanic rocks. More ancient parts of Mars crust are weaker because they're fractured and brecciated by impacts. Some ancient rocks are also sedimentary or clay-bearing rock. These rocks are weaker and much less likely to survive an impact that can launch them into space.

Teghaza is one of the rare ancient Martian meteorites.

"We describe the Martian meteorite Teghaza 001 (Teg 001), a slowly cooled igneous rock that formed at least 4.1 billion years ago," the authors write. "Its composition, mineralogy, and texture are distinct from other Martian meteorites." Distinct from other Martian meteorites, but also similar to likewise ancient Black Beauty.

âI realized that this one was a little bit like Black Beauty, not exactly, but it resembled it in the oxygen isotope values,â Agee said in a press release. "I looked at it microscopically and found domains within it that had high levels of manganese oxide, a compound being looked for on Mars by the rovers as an indicator of environments conducive to life.â

MSL Curiosity found rock fractures in Gale Crater that were filled with material rich in MnO. It suggests, but doesn't prove, that the planet's atmosphere once had free oxygen and oxygen-rich groundwater. That's still being debated.

Lead author Yang Liu and other Caltech scientists used a dating technique to find the age of tiny zircon crystals in Teg 001. Zircon crystals are important finding the age of ancient rocks because they can survive geological processes. They also contain trace amounts of elements with long half-lives. This is how Liu determined that Teg 001 is 4.1 billion years old. "We conducted ten measurements of U and Pb isotopes, in six shocked zircon grains with different morphologies, to determine their U-Pb and Pb-Pb ages," the authors explain.

Though Black Beauty is also ancient, the pair of meteorites are quite different from one another.

âThere are a few parts to Black Beauty that are around that age, but that whole meteorite itself is a conglomeration of many different rock types. Teghaza 001 is just one unadulterated rock type, and it's 4.1 billion years or older, so that was a big surprise,â said Agee. âIt's the oldest Martian igneous rock ever found by a huge margin, but in addition to that, it seemed to have these clues in its composition that suggested it had been in an environment that had fluids and water coursing through it.â

Teghaza 001 was found in several chunks adding up to almost 800 grams. Unlike Black Beauty, which is a congolomeration of different chunks, Teg 001 is a single rock type. Image Credit: UNM.

The isotope Oxygen-18 indicated that it had interacted with water in the past, most likely on the Martian surface. "The high Î´ 18O value of Teg 001 probably reflects assimilation of Î´18O-rich crustal material that had interacted with surficial fluids, or direct reaction of the magma with high-Î´18O fluids," the authors write. That finding supports the hypothesis that Mars was once warm and wet, a hypothesis supported by a growing body of evidence.

âWe also had these anomalous oxygen isotopes, and these domains that had high manganese levels, Agee said. "All of that was consistent with it being from a time on Mars, from the very, very beginning when the Martian environment was different from the time in which most of the Martian meteorites that we see were formed and erupted a few 100 million years ago when Mars was a dry desert, just like it is now. This sample probably came from an environment on Mars that was more Earth-like.â

This image shows a cut section of Teg001, with some of its features and contents labelled. Pigeonite (PgT) is particularly relevant, because it hosts fluid-altered Magnesium. "The Mg-rich interiors of pigeonite have been heavily altered by reactions with a fluid phase," the authors write. Image Credit: Yang Liu et al., A Martian meteorite that formed â³4.1 billion years ago samples Marsâ early crust and mantle. Science0,eadz5646DOI:10.1126/science.adz5646

Mars' early, potentially more Earth-like time period is called the Pre-Noachian period. Planetary scientists struggle to paint a clear picture of the Pre-Noachian because it was so long ago, and geologica processes and weathering have erased much of the ancient. Some research shows that Mars may have had global oceans during this period, a stunning difference from the frigid, dessicated planet it is today.

It's possible that billions of years ago, Mars had a global ocean, as shown in this illustration. That could explain the aqueous alteration in Teg001. Image Credit: By Ittiz - Own work, CC BY-SA 3.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=7861829

It's possible that Mars still has some simple, extant life. If it does, that life is hiding somewhere underground where the last of the planet's ancient water might be sequestered, away from the harsh radiation on the surface. But if the emerging picture of an ancient, warm and wet Mars is true, that would be the Pre-Noachian.

âIf there was ever abundant life on Mars, on the surface, not sequestered away in some subsurface, that would be the time that you would be looking at, the Pre-Noachian period,â said Agee. âIt's the very earliest time, and that was when maybe Mars still had a magnetic field, and it was shielded from radiation, and there were surface waters. There was a denser atmosphere. If primitive life was abundant in Mars. That is the time that is most likely for it to have happened.â

Most Martian meteorites are much younger than Teg001, only a few hundred million years old. It likely came from a place no rover has visited, possibly from Mars' southern highlands. Remote sensing shows that that ancient region has a similar composition to Teg001.

âThis is just one single meteorite. It's like going out, going back in time and chipping off a hunk of an outcrop, 4 billion years ago on Mars, and then we have this example of what was actually happening,â said Agee. âThat is why it's such a valuable sample. Weâve never found one like this before. The most exciting part about this find is its age, plus the alteration in the meteorite that indicates it has been in what I would call an Earth-like environment, with fluids coursing over the surface and volcanoes creating hydrothermal systems. There are surface waters and so on. And that's all reflected in the way that the meteorite has been sort of altered from its original state.â

"The presence of aqueously altered minerals, combined with bulk and mineral-specific oxygen isotope measurements, indicate that Teg 001 experienced reactions with fluids enriched in 18O, before ejection into space by an impact," the authors summarize in their paper.

#6448. Has Substitution Culture Gone Too Far?

Guests are increasingly asking for their meals to be customized. These restaurants say it’s gone too far.

When Chanita Chayaluk decided to open her restaurant and wine bar Taan, she hoped “to showcase Thai food in Chicago in a different light,” she says. “The first [wave of] immigration of Thai people in Chicago was in the 1970s, and a lot of [Thai] food here still feels like it’s from that time.” In September, she opened with a menu including miang, a Northern Thai dish made with fermented tea leaves, and a whole, deep-fried fish in a fish-sauce caramel.

Another quirk of operating in Chicago? “We’re still pretty ‘Midwest nice,’” says Chayaluk. “We try to overaccommodate and appease the masses.” In the early days of service, guests made frequent requests for substitutions or accommodations due to preferences and dietary restrictions. “It would slow down service and speed, and that was not just affecting us, but the guest experience in many ways,” she says. With a small kitchen and staff, it was hard to keep up. “It just felt like we were Chipotle.” When a guest asked for green curry mussels “but without the mussels,” it was a turning point.

Chayaluk implemented a limited substitution policy at Taan, stating on Instagram that ingredients like fish sauce and shrimp paste are “the fabric that defines our cuisine,” and therefore, could not be removed from any dishes that include it.

A decade or so ago, substitution culture was generally frowned upon and derided. Recently, though, some restaurants report it bubbling back up—and in full force. There’s a swirl of factors that got us here: Lunch slop bowl spots primed customers to expect a detailed level of customization with their orders. Unreasonable Hospitality pushed an intensified “customer is always right” mentality. And influencers entering the food-review space have made criticism of anything—including a restaurant choosing not to honor certain dietary preferences—ripe for an immediate, viral takedown. Couple all of that with the fact that it is hard to keep a restaurant afloat these days, and you’ve got several operators giving in, whether to specific requests, or to altering their menus altogether (see also: the great de-spicification of menus.)

At the same time, restaurants like Taan and New York’s Ha’s Snack Bar—which proudly announces in its Instagram bio that everything contains fish sauce—are standing their ground.

For Lom Wong in Phoenix, Arizona, substitution and modification requests have ramped up after receiving national attention. Chef Yotaka “Sunny” Martin was recognized by the James Beard Awards last year, and the restaurant was named a Michelin Bib Gourmand in August. “[After the award,] we had more guests than we were used to picking things apart. They were asking us to modify dishes or not understanding our service style and why we weren’t coursing things in a European fashion,” says chef and co-owner Alex Martin. “[There is a] European distinction of what an award-winning restaurant looks like, so people equated that recognition with a white-tablecloth restaurant. We were just like, ‘Well, that’s not who we’ve ever been, and it’s never what our restaurant will ever be.’”

Like Taan, Lom Wong took to social media to set expectations, including that the restaurant would not “make substitutions simply to make a dish more familiar,” and that certain dishes might differ from Western expectations of them; beef might have gristle, fishes will be whole, and both choices are fully intentional. “Sunny is our guiding light of cultural context,” says Martin. “[She advises, considering if] changing something about a dish compromises the integrity of the dish.” For example, the mango salad can be ordered with the shrimp on the side, but the restaurant won’t remove beef or shrimp paste from dishes that necessitate them.

Chayaluk takes a similar approach at Taan; there is always a vegan, gluten-free option (currently a fried rice) that she describes as a “catchall” for those who can’t have other items on the menu. “We make sure that that dish is also really, really good and substantial; it’s not just an appetizer,” she says. “It’s not an afterthought.”

Staff at both restaurants are encouraged to uphold the boundaries, which both Chayaluk and Martin say are as much in place for protecting their staff’s peace as they are for ensuring quality control for guests. While there has been some backlash, the expectation-setting at the start of the meal (and before, thanks to the social media posts) has for the most part been taken well. “The way we explain [our policy] to guests is kindly saying we respect your preferences, but they’re your preferences,” says Martin, “and steering them toward dishes on the menu that might already align with those.”

#6447. Scientists Say This Medication Could Be the Next “Wonder Drug”

A diabetes medication may protect against heart attacks and strokes through an unexpected biological mechanism.

Two medications used in people with type 2 diabetes produced dramatically different results when scientists tested their ability to prevent dangerous blood clots. In mice with injured blood vessels, sotagliflozin reduced clot formation by approximately 60%, compared with just 5% to 10% for the widely prescribed drug empagliflozin.

Researchers at Michigan Medicine also found that sotagliflozin suppresses excessive platelet activity, a process that can block blood flow to the heart or brain. Published in the Journal of Clinical Investigation, the findings suggest a possible explanation for the drug’s ability to reduce heart attack and stroke risk beyond its effects on blood sugar.

Sotagliflozin, marketed as Inpefa, belongs to a group of medications called sodium-glucose cotransporter (SGLT) inhibitors. These drugs interfere with proteins that transport glucose through the body. Common treatments such as empagliflozin (Jardiance) and dapagliflozin (Farxiga) primarily block SGLT2, a protein that helps the kidneys reabsorb glucose. Sotagliflozin acts on both SGLT2 and SGLT1, which is also present in other tissues.

Although SGLT2 inhibitors have established cardiovascular benefits, clinical trials have shown that sotagliflozin can also reduce ischemic events, including heart attacks and strokes. These occur when blood clots or other blockages restrict circulation. The researchers investigated whether the drug’s broader action on glucose transport proteins might help explain this protection.

“A drug that can both decrease the risk for diabetes along with the risk for having a heart attack or stroke could be a turning point in our ability safely treat this growing population in the US and abroad,” said Michael A. Holinstat, Ph.D., M.S., co-senior author and professor of pharmacology, internal medicine, and surgery at the University of Michigan Medical School.

Scientists compared sotagliflozin and empagliflozin using blood samples from healthy volunteers and people with type 2 diabetes. Sotagliflozin significantly reduced platelet activation and made platelets less likely to clump together. Empagliflozin produced little or no comparable effect.

Platelets normally help stop bleeding by gathering at damaged blood vessels. However, excessive activation can produce clots inside arteries, potentially triggering a heart attack or stroke. Sotagliflozin’s ability to suppress this activity may contribute to its cardiovascular benefits.

“These experiments showed that sotagliflozin has a unique effect, and blocking SGLT2 alone is not enough to inhibit platelet aggregation,” said Eugene Chen, M.D., Ph.D., co-senior author and Frederick G. L. Huetwell Professor of Cardiovascular Medicine at the University of Michigan Medical School.

“Sotagliflozin may offer additional protection against blood clots, potentially lowering the risk of heart attack and stroke.”

The researchers next investigated whether inhibiting SGLT1 alone could account for sotagliflozin’s effects. When they genetically removed SGLT1 from mouse platelets, blood clot formation decreased by approximately 40%. However, neither this genetic approach nor treatment with mizagliflozin, a drug that selectively blocks SGLT1, fully reproduced sotagliflozin’s results.

This suggests that other biological mechanisms contribute to the drug’s ability to prevent clot formation. One possibility involves SGLT1 in endothelial cells, which form the inner lining of blood vessels and interact with circulating platelets. Researchers have not yet established whether these cells contribute to sotagliflozin’s anti-clotting effects.

“Sotagliflozin appears to be in the sweet spot because compounds that have higher levels of SGLT1-selective inhibitors can cause gastrointestinal issues,” said Bertram Pitt, M.D., co-author and professor emeritus of internal medicine at the University of Michigan Medical School.

“We think this could be a wonder drug with potential to offer benefit for many conditions.”

Sotagliflozin is FDA-approved to reduce certain cardiovascular risks in adults with heart failure and in adults with type 2 diabetes, chronic kidney disease, and additional cardiovascular risk factors. The researchers hope to investigate whether its effects on clotting could benefit patients with other conditions, including chronic kidney disease and atrial fibrillation, an irregular heart rhythm associated with increased stroke risk.

The laboratory and animal findings provide evidence that sotagliflozin affects clotting through mechanisms beyond conventional SGLT2 inhibition. However, further clinical research is needed to determine how much this platelet effect contributes to preventing cardiovascular events in humans and whether it can do so without increasing bleeding complications.

“The search for medications that reduce the risk of life-threatening blood clots without increasing the risk of bleeding has continued for decades,” Holinstat said.

“Sotagliflozin has now been demonstrated to serve both functions and may represent the next advancement in prevention of blood clots, heart failure and stroke in patients with and without diabetes.”

Reference: “SGLT1/2 inhibitor sotagliflozin, but not SGLT2-selective inhibitor empagliflozin, attenuates platelet activation and thrombosis” by Livia Stanger, Krista Goerger, Xu Zhang, Pooja Yalavarthi, Andrew Rickenberg, Adriana Yamaguchi, Mariane Flores Nascimento, Ashleigh Kilgore, Heeseo Kim, Xiaokang Wu, Yanhong Guo, Anna R. Dahlgren, Jifeng Zhang, Jordan A. Shavit, Bertram Pitt, Y. Eugene Chen and Michael Holinstat, 14 October 2026, The Journal of Clinical Investigation. DOI: 10.1172/JCI201899

This work was supported by the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (F31HL179940, R35HL150784, R01HL109946), the National Institute of General Medical Sciences (T32GM140223, and the National Center for Advancing Translational Sciences (T32TR004371) of National Institutes of Health. #6446. Sommelier-Approved Thanksgiving Wines

The challenge of picking wine for Thanksgiving is multifaceted. Your selections must be lively enough to enjoy as guests work their way through charcuterie, balanced enough to play well with turkey, and versatile enough to rub shoulders with dessert. It’s a tall order for anyone tasked with bringing the bottles to their holiday meal. To help, five beloved wine-heads from across the country weighed in on the bottles that everyone around your holiday table will adore.

Here are the crowd-pleasing offerings sure to liven up your Thanksgiving.

For Adam Robins, beverage director at State Bird Provisions and The Progress in San Francisco, there’s no better way to start a festive meal than with Champagne. Bérêche & Fils delivers classic brioche notes tempered with fruit like Bosc and Asian pears, brought together with a snap of acidity to prime the palate for the feast ahead

Les Cigales dans la Fourmilière Escarpolette Blanc 2024

Los Angeles’s Lasita is beloved for its natural wine selections and its menu of kicky Filipino favorites. Co-owners Chase and Steff Valencia adore this Languedoc orange wine, which offers notes of bold fruit—peach and apricot—and a bright acidity that can cut through even the butteriest of mashed potatoes.

Peter Lauer Riesling Schonfels Kabinett No. 111

“More people should be drinking Riesling,” says Matt Turner of Lei, one of Bon Appétit’s Best New Restaurants of 2026. He points to this German stunner with direct minerality and notes of stone fruit, which sips just as well alongside a cheesy cauliflower gratinée as a garlic-studded beef tenderloin.

At the James Beard–nominated Wild Child in Lafayette, Louisiana, natural wine rules supreme. Ian LaCour, who helps curate the bottle list, gravitates toward this muscular red. Thanks to a silky body and dusky notes of stewed red fruit, it plays well with the “heartier proteins on the Thanksgiving table.”

You’d be forgiven for being unfamiliar with macvin, a niche style of fortified wine made in France’s Jura region. But the oaky fresh apple and cider notes in this punchy bottling—akin to a less-oxidized, sweeter oloroso sherry—make for a divine digestif. “It fares well with every dessert,” says Nick Arone of Detroit’s Bar Chenin.

#6445. Inside the New D.C. Restaurant That Only Sells Five Curry Steak Frites Every Night

In a Georgetown alleyway, Alfie’s serves northern Thai dishes that are built around local ingredients

The hottest new spot in Washington, D.C. focuses on the traditional heat-packed cooking methods of northern Thailand, while still using local ingredients from around the DMV. Alfie’s, from chefs Justin Ahn and Alex McCoy, started as a pop-up in Petworth in 2017 before traveling around the world, serving diners in New York and London. This year, the restaurant put down permanent roots in a Georgetown alleyway. The co-owners led us through a day in the new kitchen, preparing everything from hand-cut green papaya in som tam salad to the limited-quantity Thai steak frites with a massaman curry peppercorn sauce.In the video, the kitchen team breaks down rib-eye steaks for their take on a steak au poivre, which they only make five of each night. The steaks are carefully seared for each order, with the au poivre massaman curry sauce is finished in the pan with the leftover beef fat. Classic “bar fries” are served up with the massive 26-ounce rib-eye.

Elsewhere in the kitchen, another chef carves green papayas. The irregular slices of papaya get tossed in a funky, spicy dressing for each order. Ko calls it the “most labor intensive dish on the line;” each order is carefully mixed with fresh tomatoes, peanuts, and a palm syrup and tamarind-heavy dressing. A rich pork belly curry is simmering in the background. Gaeng hung lay (a traditional northern Thai curry) cooks down large pieces of pork belly to get that fatty layer, with pickled garlic and pineapple balancing out the rich flavors of curry paste, tamarind, and fish sauce.

Right before service, the chefs begin prepping herbs and sticky rice that has been soaking overnight and is quickly steamed for that malleable, glutinous texture. McCoy talks about how being a chef is more of a lifestyle than a job, but there’s immense payoff when you get to see diners enjoy your hard work every night. He hopes that Alfie’s will become a place where “you can just forget where you are, have a good time, and just lose yourself in the experience and the food.”

Watch the kitchen team at Aflie’s cook classic Thai dishes and fusion plates like curry steak frites in this episode of Now Open.

#6444. Queen's University Belfast Students Find Neptune's Elusive Trojan Asteroids

An international team led by researchers at Queen's University Belfast has made a discovery that has eluded astronomers for decades. Beginning in 1906, telescope observations revealed a population of asteroids leading and trailing Jupiter, which came to be known as the "Trojan" and "Greek" populations. Since then, astronomers have discovered similar "families" orbiting Saturn and Uranus, but not Neptune. Thanks to the Queen's-led team, the mystery of the missing Trojans has now been resolved!

As detailed in a paper that appeared in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, the team found these distant icy bodies by analyzing data from the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, the next-generation telescope perched high atop the Andes in Chile. Thanks to Rubin's sharp optics and ability to rapidly survey the night sky (the fastest of any ground-based telescope), the team identified two asteroids and a candidate as permanent members of Neptune's trailing Trojans.

The team was led by Dr. Meg Schwamb, an astronomer and lecturer at the Astrophysics Research Centre, Queen's University Belfast (QUB). She was joined by researchers from the Instituto de Astronomia, GeofÃ­sica e CiÃªncias AtmosfÃ©ricas (IAG), the Planetary Science Institute (PSI), the DiRAC Institute, the Michigan Institute for Data and AI in Society (MIDAS), JHUAPL, the NSF's NOIRLAB, and multiple universities worldwide.

The Vera C. Rubin Observatory's LSST survey will help scientists create a census of Solar System objects. Credit: Rubin Observatory/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA H.

The Vera C. Rubin Observatory combines the resolution of its 8.4-meter Simony Survey Telescope with the LSST Camera, the largest digital camera ever built. Having commenced operations in June 2025, Rubin is currently conducting the largest survey of the southern sky - the Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST). At the same time, it is mapping the northern sky to create an ultra-wide, ultra-high-definition time-lapse record of the cosmos.

Through these surveys, Rubin will provide new insight into the mysteries of the cosmos, including Dark Matter and Dark Energy. It will map the Milky Way and its faint satellite galaxies, detect transient phenomena (supernovae, variable stars, rogue planets, etc.) and create an inventory of objects in the Solar System. This last objective was what drew Schwamb and her team to analyze data from Rubin's early test observations last year.

After combining this massive trove of data, the team identified the objects as primordial members of the elusive trailing Neptune Trojan population. "Early data from Rubin Observatory is already expanding our knowledge of the solar system's 'small bodies,' including asteroids, comets, and other minor planets," Schwamb explained in a QUB press release. "And these early observations have provided our clearest view yet of Neptune's trailing Trojan cloud."

A rendering of the inner Solar System showing the asteroids discovered by Rubin in light teal. Known asteroids are dark blue. Credit: NSFâDOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory/NSF NOIRLab/SLAC/AURA/R/NASA/Goddard/ESA/Gaia/DPAC

Previously, astronomers struggled to find Neptune's Trojan populations because of the difficulty of spotting such distant, faint objects as they moved across the night sky. For the past ten years, the Trojans have been crowded in a region of the sky that placed them in front of the Milky Way's center (relative to Earth-based observers), an extremely dense and bright part of the night sky that obscured any tiny light sources in the foreground. Said Schwamb:

The Trailing Cloud has now begun to move out of this region of sky and combined with the Rubin Observatory's unmatched depth and sky coverage, we've been able to double the number of known objects in this population on long-lived orbits. These discoveries offer a glimpse of just how transformative Rubin's data will be, with even more exciting findings expected in the years ahead.

The Rubin Observatory obtained images of these objects using different filters, which allowed Dr. Schwamb and her team to show that the Trojans leading and trailing Neptune have similar surfaces. As Rubin continues the LSST survey over the next nine years, it is expected to discover tens to hundreds of Neptune Trojans in both its leading and trailing population, plus tens of thousands of icy bodies in the Trans-Neptunian Region and Kuiper Belt.

Further Reading: Queen's University, The Astrophysical Journal Letters**

#6443. Depression Symptoms Improved in Just 48 Hours After a Single Psychedelic Dose

A single dose of psilocybin produced rapid antidepressant effects in a small Swedish clinical trial, with improvements lasting for weeks.

A single dose of psilocybin, the psychedelic compound found in magic mushrooms, produced rapid improvements in depression symptoms in a small Swedish clinical trial. After six weeks, 53% of participants who received psilocybin were in remission, compared with just 6% of those given a placebo.

Some participants reported improvements within two days, and the antidepressant effects persisted for more than three months in self-reported assessments. The findings come from Sweden’s first randomized, double-blind trial of psilocybin for depression, conducted by researchers at Karolinska Institutet and published in JAMA Network Open.

Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are among the most widely prescribed treatments for depression, but they can take several weeks to work, cause unwanted side effects, and provide insufficient relief for some patients. Previous research has suggested that psilocybin may act more quickly, although much of that work has focused on treatment-resistant depression or depression associated with cancer.

The new phase 2 trial investigated whether psilocybin could also help people with more common forms of recurrent depression. Researchers enrolled 35 adults between the ages of 20 and 65 who had moderate to severe symptoms. Participants were randomly assigned to receive either 25 milligrams of psilocybin or niacin, a vitamin used as an active placebo because it produces noticeable physical sensations.

Both groups received psychotherapeutic support across five sessions before, during, and after treatment. During the dosing session, participants wore eye masks, listened to music through headphones, and were encouraged to direct their attention inward.

Researchers measured depression severity using the MADRS (Montgomery–Åsberg Depression Rating Scale), with assessments conducted by clinicians who did not know which treatment each participant had received.

Eight days after treatment, depression scores had fallen by an average of 9.7 points in the psilocybin group, compared with 2.4 points in the placebo group. The 7.3-point difference was statistically significant and considered clinically meaningful. The advantage remained evident at assessments conducted 15 and 42 days after treatment, while participants’ own ratings indicated improvement as early as the second day.

“Our results suggest that psilocybin can provide rapid, clinically meaningful improvement in depression and may serve as an alternative to standard treatment when fast symptom reduction is important,” says lead author Hampus Yngwe, consultant psychiatrist and PhD student at the Department of Clinical Neuroscience, Karolinska Institutet.

Although the initial results favored psilocybin, the difference between the groups was no longer statistically confirmed after one year. At that point, 53% of participants in the psilocybin group remained in remission, but many people who had received the placebo had also recovered.

“However, the long-term effects are uncertain. Repeated treatments may be needed to prevent relapse. This needs to be investigated in larger studies.”

The findings suggest that a single supervised dose may provide relatively rapid symptom relief for some patients, but the small trial cannot establish how consistently those benefits will last or whether additional doses would improve long-term outcomes.

Psilocybin was generally well tolerated, with most reported side effects being mild or moderate and temporary. However, two participants who received the psychedelic experienced severe, persistent anxiety that required medical attention.

“It is important to emphasize that the treatment is not risk-free and that some patients may need extra support,” says Johan Lundberg, professor at the Department of Clinical Neuroscience and the Centre for Psychiatry Research, Karolinska Institutet, who led the study.

Another limitation involved the difficulty of keeping participants unaware of their assigned treatment. Psychedelics produce distinctive psychological effects, and almost everyone in the trial correctly guessed whether they had received psilocybin or the placebo. Such awareness can influence expectations and make it harder to determine how much improvement comes from the drug itself.

“We want to understand how factors such as treatment expectations and lack of blinding affect the results, as previous studies may have exaggerated the treatment effects,” says Hampus Yngwe.

Researchers are now turning to biological measurements collected during the trial to investigate how psilocybin might influence depression. Their next analyses will examine PET brain scans alongside blood and cerebrospinal fluid samples obtained before and after treatment.

One area of interest is synaptic density, which reflects the number of connections through which nerve cells communicate. Depression has been associated with disrupted communication between brain regions, while preclinical studies suggest that psychedelics may promote the growth of synaptic connections. Whether comparable changes occur in people receiving psilocybin remains an open question.

“Research suggests that the interaction between parts of the brain is impaired in depression and that this may be linked to changes in the connections between nerve cells, known as synapses. In preclinical studies, psychedelics have been shown to stimulate synaptic growth. We therefore want to investigate whether psilocybin alters synaptic density in the brain,” concludes Hampus Yngwe.

Reference: “Short-Term and Late-Term Effects of Psilocybin on Symptoms in Major Depression: A Randomized Clinical Trial” by Hampus Yngwe, Pontus Plavén-Sigray, Carl Johan Ekman, Eva Henje, Anders Berglund, Mikael Tiger, Maria Beckman and Johan Lundberg, , JAMA Network Open. DOI: 10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2026.12589

Scientists sequenced the genome of a woman who lived 30,000 years ago and discovered that she had mixed Eastern and Western European ancestry.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scientists have sequenced the genomes of three Late Stone Age people who lived in Europe 30,000 years ago and discovered that they had closer biological ties than researchers previously thought. The new finding suggests that places like southwestern France may have been critical cultural hubs during the last ice age.

Shortly after Neanderthals disappeared from Europe, a Stone Age culture known as the Gravettian spread across the continent. Artifacts found during archaeological excavations ‪—‬ including portable art, such as "Venus figurines" ‪—‬ have shown that the Gravettian culture lasted from about 34,000 to 25,000 years ago. But ancient DNA has been recovered from only two dozen human skeletons from the Gravettian period, so questions about these people's ancestry remain unanswered.

Based on the small number of genomes from Gravettian people that were previously sequenced, experts believed that groups in Western Europe were largely separate from groups in Eastern Europe. But in a study published Oct. 23 in the journal Science Advances, researchers sequenced the genomes of three people who lived in what are now Spain, France and Italy during the Gravettian period. They discovered that one person had mixed genetic ancestry that revealed East-West exchange at least 30,000 years ago.

"Our results show that eastern and western European populations were not as genetically isolated as previously assumed," study first author Pere Gelabert, an evolutionary anthropologist at the University of Vienna, said in a statement.

The new information about mixed ancestry comes from a woman who died around 30,000 years ago and whose bones were found in Isturitz Cave in southwestern France. Originally used by Neanderthals, Isturitz Cave was occupied off and on from about 80,000 to 10,000 years ago. Cups made out of human skulls dated to roughly 15,000 to 12,000 years ago have also been found in Isturitz Cave.

Researchers found that the DNA from the Gravettian woman in Isturitz Cave was most similar to the previously known Western European genomes, but with an intriguing connection to Eastern and Central European groups.

This discovery of gene flow from the East is uncommon for the Late Stone Age, also known as the Upper Paleolithic, the researchers wrote in the study. It "could be explained by movements of people from Eastern Europe during the Gravettian period, which eventually contributed to this ancestry in Isturitz." Specifically, the researchers dated this "pulse" of gene flow to about 31,500 to 32,500 years ago.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The DNA evidence supports the archaeological theory that Isturitz Cave was an important cultural and biological hub for tens of thousands of years during the Late Stone Age, as the cave was located at a critical passage between continental Europe and the Iberian Peninsula, the researchers wrote.

All three newly sequenced Gravettian genomes revealed close biological connections to Western European groups, as well as genetic traits suggesting they had dark skin, dark hair and dark eyes. What's more, all of them had parents who weren't closely related to each other, suggesting that those populations may have actively avoided inbreeding.

"Overall, our results suggest that population structure and gene flow in western Europe during the Gravettian were more complex and dynamic than previously assumed," the researchers wrote.

Gelabert, P., Sawyer, S., Villalba-Mouco, V., Cheronet, O., Oberreiter, V., Gárate, D., Normand, C., Straus, L. G., González Morales, M. R., Gutiérrez-Zugasti, I., Cuenca-Solana, D., Darricau, J., de Lumley, H., Tejero, J.-M., Stahlschmidt, M., Higham, T., Giannì, M., van der Sluis, L. G., Gómez-Montes, C., … Pinhasi, R. (2026). Early Gravettian genomic data from Western Europe reveal population movements before the LGM. Science Advances, 12(43). https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aeh6128

#6441. What Could Split a Black Hole in Two?

We all know that black holes can collide. It has happened since black holes began to form, early in cosmic time. The result is always a clash that gives off gravitational waves and a giant bang. Since black holes have such strong gravity, it's almost impossible to imagine a way that any force could break one apart. Yet, that's the task that a group of scientists in Europe set for themselves.

In a study of possible mechanisms for black hole fragmentation, Francesco Sannino of the University of Naples Federico II in Italy and the Quantum Field Theory Center at the University of Southern Denmark, along with Giacomo Cacciapaglia (Laboratoire de Physique ThÃ©orique et Hautes Ãnergies) and Manuel Del Piano and Vania Vellucci, both from the Quantum Field Theory Center, conducted a series of calculations showing that under the right conditions, a black hole could split up into two black holes. It's an unusual possibility, to say the least, but the team has calculated what needs to happen if such an event were to occur.

The two pieces would have to stay apart, according to Sannino. "The two resulting black holes must also be able to separate rather than immediately fall back together. When we include this requirement, the window largely closes again, except possibly for black holes rotating close to their maximum possible rate," he said. If such a split-up could happen, the event horizon of the black hole would form a trouser-like shape as the split-up proceeded. Essentially, it would form two legs of a pair of pants, which is why the team called it a "pair-of-pants topology."

That's one possibility for what happens if/when a black hole splits into pieces. No one has seen such an event (yet), so it's still largely theoretical. There's one major impediment, however. That's called entropy, the measure of how many different microscopic ways a physical system can be arranged while still appearing the same from the outside. For example, a rock's shape can remain solid and static until some outside force changes it, such as heating. In the case of an ordinary, non-rotating black hole, breaking it into two pieces would reduce its entropy and make the process thermodynamically unlikely.

The black hole at the centre of M87. It has a measured spin, so theoretically, if conditions were right, it could break apart, according to a new study. Credit: Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration

However, let's say we have a rotating black hole, spinning very rapidly. According to the team, such a system could break up into two pieces. However, they have to separate quickly, or risk falling back together. So, it turns out it could happen if both black holes have to keep rotating as fast as they possibly can (or close to it). But what would cause the split to occur? The answer lies in the rotation. It alters the relationship between black hole mass, its angular momentum as it spins, and entropy. It's possible that change could lead to the black hole fragmenting. If so, then the next steps are for the black hole "twins" to move apart and retain the momentum and speed of the original.

Focusing just on black holes, it seems pretty unlikely that such events have happened, but they don't want to say it's never happened. According to Sannino, the possibility is there, but in specific cases. "We cannot yet give a single probability for a black hole to split. It depends on how gravity behaves beyond Einsteinâs theory, and we are working to quantify this," he explained. "We expect small primordial black holes to be more prone to splitting than much larger astrophysical black holes. We may detect a split indirectly: gamma-ray telescopes such as Fermi-LAT can search for signals from tiny black-hole fragments that might form during mergers."

When Black Holes Admit Pair-of-pants Topologies

Carolyn Collins Petersen is a long-time science writer and former astronomy researcher. She writes about astronomy and space exploration and has written 8 books, including the recently released 2nd edition of her Astronomy 101 book, countless articles, more than 60 documentaries for planetarium star theaters, and exhibits for Griffith Observatory, NASA/JPL, the California Academy of Sciences, the Shanghai Astronomical Museum, and the Lowell Observatory Dark Sky Planetarium. #6440. Scientists Discover a Common Treatment for Chronic Tendon Pain May Not Actually Work

A major clinical trial is challenging the effectiveness of commonly used injections for chronic Achilles tendon pain.

A widely used injection treatment for chronic Achilles tendon pain may offer little lasting relief, according to a clinical trial published in The BMJ. Researchers found that high-volume injections, including those containing corticosteroids, did not significantly improve pain or physical function compared with a sham procedure after one year. The findings challenge the routine use of injections for a condition that can persist for years and interfere with everyday movement.

Achilles tendinopathy causes pain, stiffness, and swelling in the tendon that connects the calf muscles to the heel. Approximately 6% of people experience the condition during their lifetime, and although exercise-based rehabilitation is the recommended treatment, up to 44% of patients do not recover. Many consequently explore other options, including injections intended to reduce pain and improve tendon function.

To investigate whether these treatments provide meaningful benefits, researchers conducted a randomized clinical trial involving 192 adults with midportion Achilles tendinopathy in Melbourne, Australia, between December 2019 and July 2022. Participants were 49 years old on average, and their symptoms had persisted for a median of two years.

The researchers divided participants into three groups receiving either a sham injection (64), a high-volume injection without corticosteroid (63), or a high-volume injection containing corticosteroid (65). The active injections delivered saline and local anesthetic around the affected tendon, with corticosteroid added in one group. Everyone also received the same exercise program, education, and guidance on modifying physical activity.

The primary measure was pain and disability after 52 weeks, assessed using the Victoria Institute of Sport Assessment-Achilles scale (0-100, where 100 is no pain or disability). Participants began the trial with an average score of 48.7, indicating substantial symptoms and functional limitations.

At the one-year follow-up, researchers obtained results from 181 participants (94%). Neither high-volume injection treatment produced a clear improvement in pain or disability compared with the sham procedure. The two active injection approaches also showed no meaningful difference in their overall outcomes.

Injections without corticosteroid failed to outperform the placebo at any assessment point. Adding corticosteroid produced small improvements after six weeks, but these benefits were short-lived. By 26 weeks, participants who received corticosteroid had worse outcomes than those given high volume injections without the drug.

An economic analysis found that corticosteroid-containing injections were less costly and generated more quality-adjusted life-years than sham treatment. However, the overall clinical results did not justify their routine use. No serious adverse events related to the trial treatments were reported.

The researchers acknowledged several limitations. Many participants were recruited through social media, which could affect how well the findings apply to other patient populations. Clinicians administering the injections also knew which treatment they were providing, and some observed differences may have resulted from chance.

Despite these uncertainties, the authors concluded that the evidence “should prompt clinicians to reconsider the rationale for using these injections in people with Achilles tendinopathy.”

In a linked editorial, John Orchard of the University of Sydney cautioned that corticosteroids are neither universally beneficial nor inherently inappropriate. Their use should depend on the patient’s circumstances, particularly when immediate symptom relief takes priority over longer-term outcomes (where short-term needs predominate over longer-term needs). He emphasized that patients should never be told corticosteroid injections will fix or cure tendinopathy.

“All clinicians recommending or performing corticosteroid injections for tendinopathy need to understand this trade-off and make every effort to explain the broader overview to the patient as part of the informed consent process,” he concluded.

Reference: “Efficacy and cost effectiveness of high volume injections with and without corticosteroid compared with sham for midportion Achilles tendinopathy (Inject trial): randomised controlled trial” by Peter Malliaras, David Connell, Anders Ploug Boesen, Rebecca S Kearney, Hylton B Menz, Dylan Morrissey, Shannon E Munteanu, Karin Gravare Silbernagel, Martin Underwood, Andrew Forbes and Terry P Haines, 28 October 2026, BMJ. DOI: 10.1136/bmj-2026-100807

Never miss a breakthrough: Join the SciTechDaily newsletter.Follow us on Google and Google News.

Kinesiology studies have demonstrated that eccentric motion (the slow, downward motion of calf raises) strengthen the Achilles tendon over time and essentially cure tendonitis–and yet humans still can’t resist injecting chemicals. Doctors are under pressure to produce an instant fix. Nobody wants to be told they have to do some work to fix their Achilles.

#6439. The 38 Best Restaurants in Barcelona, According to a Local Food Guide

From local Catalan cuisine to a burgeoning global food scene, here are the best meals in Barcelona right now

From Barcelona’s towering churches and bustling avenues to the sun-drenched beaches and idyllic plazas, it’s obvious why this city captures visitors’ hearts. You can also eat incredibly well here, and often for not very much money — though Barcelona loves a tasting menu and the World’s 50 Best Restaurant list awarded Disfrutar the No. 1 spot last year. Despite Barcelona’s famed cuisine, it’s also easy to have a downright disappointing meal if you settle for any old paella-slinging bar along Les Rambles (known in Spanish as La Rambla) or La Barceloneta. (Tip: If a restaurant has to pay someone to stand outside and hassle pedestrians, the food isn’t worth it.)

Start with some classic tapas and paella (both great but neither entirely Catalan) and be sure to seek out local gems like bittersweet vermouth, seasonal seafood, and homestyle Catalan cuisine. But after writing and revising this list for nearly a decade, I have to insist you don’t overlook the city’s burgeoning global cuisines; save room for Calabrese paninis, Northeast Asian sharing plates with natural wines, towering fried chicken sandwiches, South Indian fish stews, and nose-to-tail yakitori.

We update this list quarterly to make sure it reflects the ever-changing Barcelona dining scene. Our write-ups include insider tips from our experienced writers and editors, as well as a rough range of pricing for each destination — ranging from $ for quick, inexpensive meals with dishes largely under $10 (or the equivalent in euros), to $$$$ for places where entrees exceed $30.

New to the map in October 2026: Lluritu, a Mediterranean marisquería with three locations across the city; a parallel universe of Catalan culinary history in a former water bottling plant at Franca; and the trendy modern Catalan cuisine of Manda Huevos.

Sam Zucker is a freelance writer, photographer, filmmaker, travel Instagrammer, and gastronomic tour guide in Barcelona. He has contributed to Monocle, National Geographic’s “48 Hours” guides, Culture Trip, and Vice Travel, among others.

From local Catalan cuisine to a burgeoning global food scene, here are the best meals in Barcelona right now

From Barcelona’s towering churches and bustling avenues to the sun-drenched beaches and idyllic plazas, it’s obvious why this city captures visitors’ hearts. You can also eat incredibly well here, and often for not very much money — though Barcelona loves a tasting menu and the World’s 50 Best Restaurant list awarded Disfrutar the No. 1 spot last year. Despite Barcelona’s famed cuisine, it’s also easy to have a downright disappointing meal if you settle for any old paella-slinging bar along Les Rambles (known in Spanish as La Rambla) or La Barceloneta. (Tip: If a restaurant has to pay someone to stand outside and hassle pedestrians, the food isn’t worth it.)

Start with some classic tapas and paella (both great but neither entirely Catalan) and be sure to seek out local gems like bittersweet vermouth, seasonal seafood, and homestyle Catalan cuisine. But after writing and revising this list for nearly a decade, I have to insist you don’t overlook the city’s burgeoning global cuisines; save room for Calabrese paninis, Northeast Asian sharing plates with natural wines, towering fried chicken sandwiches, South Indian fish stews, and nose-to-tail yakitori.
